articles.title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
articles.snippet: Open video on YouTube ↗ Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use. Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue , the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation . By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph. Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute. Sculptor started as a tool loop. Now it's a coding agent. When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings. The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows. Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together. Jump to the Sculptor discussion → Most companies post-train too early For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks. Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million. Jump to the post-training discussion → $1,500 to score every company in the world Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more. Ask a classifier whether each company is a good fit, and the bill for all 40 million comes to around $1,500. Today, most customers qualify a list of maybe 10,000 companies. At these prices, you can start with the entire market. Jeff puts a good enrichment budget at $1 to $10 per qualified lead and $10 to $100 per booked call. He thinks qualification itself is close to solved. Models have been scoring about as high as they can on Clay’s evals for roughly a year. Just about any model from the past year can pull a company’s latest funding round. Frontier models still matter for deep prospecting research and for orchestration, where Jeff says the best plays can be ten to a hundred times as effective as an average one. Jump to the Jev discussion → Customers hate the model selector Customers complain when they see Clay’s model selector. They can’t check the evals for their use case every time a new model ships, and they shouldn’t have to. Clay is about to launch an automatic router that picks a model for each task. There’s no fancy branding. Finding Apple’s CEO is a very different job from finding the CEO of an obscure local company. The selector isn’t going away. Agency owners and power users still want control. Everyone else just wants to get on with their work. Clay has to earn their trust before they’ll leave it on auto. Jump to the model routing discussion → No Temporal, no LangGraph Clay built most of its agent stack itself. It uses BullMQ to keep agent jobs running, Postgres and ClickHouse for product data, and Snowflake for analytics. Jeff isn’t sure how BullMQ will hold up if usage grows another tenfold, but it’s held up so far. Clay recently shipped 25 to 30 new integrations. Contracts and testing took longer than the engineering work. Where Clay did run into trouble was scale. People run an agent per row, so if someone starts a run on a table of 50,000 companies, inference demand spikes all at once. Clay brought in LangSmith to see what was happening. The team also built a way to throttle requests and to pause and resume work when a provider goes down or starts rate-limiting. The harder part is keeping

articles.snippet: My morning reads: ​• The Thanksgiving Accident That Created TV Dinners : Thanksgiving 1953: Swanson was stuck with 260 tons of unsold turkey, and salesman Gerry Thomas had 5,000 aluminum trays and an idea. The frozen dinner was born from a surplus. How 260 tons of frozen birds inspired decades of easy meals in front of the TV. ( Mental Floss ) • Make Thanksgiving Great Again! If your family is anything like mine, you will have more than a few people of different political persuasions at the table: Liberals, Conservatives, Magas, Q-Anon, and all sorts of other Pro- and Anti- folks of all manner of thought. ( The Big Picture ) see also Behavioral Hacks to Keep Your Thanksgiving Civil The midterms are over, Presidential elections are 2 years away, and Thanksgiving Day is here. If your family is anything like mine, you have a few Fox News viewers in the crowd. Rather than allow politics to ruin your Turkey Day, some timely advice might help save your holidays. ( The Big Picture ) • Donald Trump readies raft of new tariffs on major economies : China, the EU, Japan and South Korea expected to be hit by levies as US president doubles down on trade strategy.​ Aime Williams: the president is preparing to unveil more tariffs on major trading partners this week, doubling down on his signature policy despite steep Republican losses in the midterms. Trade negotiator Jamieson Greer has been formally investigating China, the EU, Japan and South Korea over whether they subsidize their own companies unfairly. ( Financial Times ) ​• The Wealthiest 10% of Americans Are Pulling Ahead of Everyone Else. This Is What’s Making Them Richer. : Venessa Wong: using the Fed’s latest Survey of Consumer Finances, the median household’s net worth rose just 2% from 2022 to 2025 after inflation. The top 10% saw a 19% gain, about $800,000 in median net worth. This is what’s making them richer. The wealthiest 10% have a median net worth that is $800,000 greater than it was three years ago ( Marketwatch ) • Thinking—Fast, Slow, and Artificial: How AI is Reshaping Human Reasoning and the Rise of Cognitive Surrender : People increasingly consult generative artificial intelligence (AI) while reasoning. As AI becomes embedded in daily thought, what becomes of human judgment? We introduce Tri-System Theory, extending dual-process accounts of reasoning by positing System 3: artificial cognition that operates outside the brain. System 3 can supplement or supplant internal processes, introducing novel cognitive pathways. A key prediction of the theory is “cognitive surrender”-adopting AI outputs with minimal scrutiny, overriding intuition. ​Steven D. Shaw and Gideon Nave of Wharton: as people consult generative AI while reasoning, what happens to human judgment? They introduce a Tri-System Theory of cognition. ( SSRN ) ​• 2026 US Insurgent Brands: Powering the Next Wave of Growth : Charlotte Apps: in the 10th edition of Bain’s report, nearly 400 insurgent consumer brands since 2017 have added about $60 billion in incremental retail sales, 50% more than the top three consumer products companies combined. They hold under 10% of a $1 trillion market but drove nearly a fifth of its growth. ( Bain & Company ) ​• A Colossal Oscillation : The 2026 El Niño may be the strongest in 1,000 years, with Pacific surface temperatures soaring relative to long-term averages. The essay turns to the deep past, recovered by scientists, historians and archaeologists, to ask what comes next. ( Aeon ) • Inside the Democratic wave: Who showed up, who stayed home and who switched sides : An analysis of thousands of precincts across 13 states shows the forces behind the historic Democratic victories — and offers lessons for 2028. Lenny Bronner and Eric Lau: Vance and Cruz say Republican voters did show up. A Post analysis of precinct results in 13 states finds that only partly true. The bigger problem is 2024 Trump voters who crossed over to vote Democratic, which matters for 2028 because stay-at-homes are easier to win back. ( Washington Post ) • Ukraine’s drone pilots hit Russian targets from 500km away New internet-based guidance system allows operation of unmanned aerial vehicles far from battlefield. ( Financial Times ) see also They Were Too Old to Enlist, but Not to Fight. Meet the Steppe Wolves of Ukraine . When the military refused to let them sign up, a band of aging men found their own way to wage war against Russia. ( New York Times ) • Extremely Rare Hilma af Klint Sells for $12.7 Million, About 16 Times Its High Estimate : It’s been three decades since a painting by the world’s first abstract artist was auctioned. Most of her work is locked away in a foundation. ( Wall Street Journal ) Video of the day : Psychology of Life (And How To Spend It Wisely) (Psych Loop) Be sure to check out our Masters in Business interview this weekend with Holly MacDonald , CEO of Bessemer Trust , the privately owned multifamily office founded in 1907 by Carnegie Steel co-founder Henry Phipps. articles.title: “That’s on me”
articles.snippet: There have always been shortcuts. The small-plot farmer who chooses a crop that’s easier to plant but yields less, or the entry-level bureaucrat who goes along to get along. The person at the gym who avoids the machines that aren’t fun… We’re surrounded by systems that prey on our temptation to try just a bit less. So they create dark patterns and convenient and well-lit paths that end up more like traps than tools. We’re not under the circumstances, though. We are the circumstances. There are always going to be systems that work to manipulate us as they offer us shortcuts. And resisting each and every one of them is too much to ask. But when we’re serious about a piece of work, if anyone has figured out the long path, then we can too.

articles.title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
articles.snippet: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most. Update : Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released. Tags: backups , sqlite

articles.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
articles.snippet: My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News. I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that. He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted. The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too! Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously. (Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.) How to Love the World More: Artist and Poet Rachel Hébert’s Breathtaking Catalogue of Gratitudes
articles.snippet: Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable , that we bless that bright improbability with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live in the cage of complaint, too preoccupied with how the will of life betrayed our wishes, the wanting monster always growling in the other corner of the cage. Imagine parting the bars and stepping out. Imagine waking up with a rush of gladness at everything we were never promised but got anyway — trees and music, clouds and consciousness, the cobalt eye of the scallop , the golden fan of the gingko , the alabaster chandelier of the ghost pipe . In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long. But it is trainable. It is possible to become strong enough to be tender, it is. Artist and poet Rachel Hébert offers a bright patch of training ground in The Book of Thanks: A Catalogue of Gratitudes — one of the most miraculous books I have ever encountered, trembling with tenacious tenderness for the bewilderment of being alive. Radiating from the pages is an invitation, extended in paintings and poems, to open “the sunlit fort of your attention” and let the world rush in, in all its minute and majestic loveliness: stalactites and Spanish moss, spiderwebs and skylights, snow and the call of the snowy owl, the heart’s capacity for “an urgent, flashing, interrupting kind of love.” What emerges is prayerful (“more cellos, touch, and rain, please”) and singing with praise (“roots gripping, canyon carved, spine woven of baleen a thousand years old”) — a manual for how to live in gratitude (“what is working wants your praise”) and a theological statement (“there is nothing you must do to belong”). A taste: What do we say to longing? If you have sat in the chill of early morning bleakness and watched as the deep blue sighed and blushed, touched by the warm curve of dawn and pinker than pink then apricot soft and spreading its glow, you know. You know. How — in this dim parade of brutality — might all be well? But if we trouble it with light, train our sights on the rebellious good, and work to make it truer. Beneath the face of the water, wonder. In dark woods, a gate. In the chapter called lostness, a friend. All the help we could not yet see. It cannot be always comfortable. So love the thousand knives as they enter and see your shape still sitting. See that you too belong to paws of soft silent hungers, to thirst-tangled roots, to silver-spun constellations. Know you’re no sicker than the rest of us. The big secret is this: No one else can brave you. Messy, yes. And marvelous. What is more than we see in this world we’re pressed into, its blistered barking noise? For what we build, speak, and ruin — our efforts, our angers. For music. For wings. donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. articles.title: The Paradox of “Finding Yourself”
articles.snippet: “The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth…” “No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life,” thirty-year-old Nietzsche wrote in his treatise on how to find yourself . And yet in the century and a half since, a curious dissonance has begun to reverberate across culture: On the one hand, we have grown increasingly fixated on the self as the focal lens for interpreting the world — a fixation which Ian McEwan so brilliantly satirized and which has precipitated today’s tragic epidemic of militant identity politics; on the other hand, the rise of neuroscience has demonstrated again and again that the self we experience as so overwhelmingly real — the psychophysiological raft of experience through which we float along the river of life — is a sensory-perceptual byproduct of consciousness , completely illusory in its solidity. Nearly half a century ago, the Pulitzer-winning poet Robert Penn Warren (April 24, 1905–September 15, 1989) cast a cautionary eye to the notion of “finding oneself” in Democracy and Poetry ( public library ) — his magnificent Jefferson Lecture about power, tenderness, and art’s role in a healthy society . Robert Penn Warren Decades before Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert’s witty and wise observation that “human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they’re finished,” Warren challenges the cultural trend of young people taking “time off” from school or work in order to “get away from it all” and find themselves. He writes: In the phrase [“to find myself”] lurks the idea that the self is a pre-existing entity, a self like a Platonic idea existing in a mystic realm beyond time and change. No, rather an object like a nugget of gold in the placer pan, the Easter egg under the bush at an Easter-egg hunt, a four-leaf clover to promise miraculous luck. Here is the essence of passivity, one’s quintessential luck. And the essence of absurdity, too, for the self is never to be found, but must be created, not the happy accident of passivity, but the product of a thousand actions, large and small, conscious or unconscious, performed not “away from it all,” but in the face of “it all,” for better or for worse, in work and leisure rather than in free time. In consonance with my own deep belief in the ongoingness and fluidity of our becoming , Warren adds: The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth, a process that is the image, we may say, of the life process of a healthy society itself. In a sentiment that calls to mind Academy of American Poets executive director Jennifer Benka’s beautiful observation that “poems are physical sites of discovery [and] sense-records of our humanity,” Warren considers the role of poetry as a locus of our evolving being: How does poetry come into all this? By being an antidote, a sovereign antidote, for passivity. For the basic fact about poetry is that it demands participation, from the secret physical echo in muscle and nerve that identifies us with the medium, to the imaginative enactment that stirs the deepest recesses where life-will and values reside. Beyond that, it nourishes our life-will in the process of testing our values. And this is not to be taken as implying a utilitarian aesthetic. It is, rather, one way of describing our pleasure in poetry as an adventure in the celebration of life. Complement this particular portion of Warren’s thoroughly transcendent Democracy and Poetry with Walt Whitman on identity and the paradox of the self and philosopher Rebecca Goldstein on what makes you and your childhood self the “same” person despite a lifetime of change , then revisit Elizabeth Alexander on what poetry does for the human spirit . donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). articles.title: The Revolution vs The Renaissance — Thariq Shihipar, OpenAI
articles.snippet: AI can make software cheap enough to produce by the thousand and still give you more time to make one thing feel right. At AI Engineer CODE, Thariq Shihipar shows how those two futures can coexist. In his fighting game, he edits the size of a rock in the /human folder and immediately tries the throw. He also built a Mac Dock that switched modes, used it, and realized he cared more about noticing when he got distracted. We get into what Thariq changed his mind about with coding agents, how a decision model can choose from actions a designer defines, and who gets to decide which experiments deserve the compute. Thariq announced his move to OpenAI after we recorded. Sponsored by Jira by Atlassian. Learn more at jira.dev . articles.title: [AINews] Math Proofs Are Landing Faster Than We Can Read Them
articles.snippet: AINews by Latent Space Scott Aaronson was still trying to digest two proofs of VP ≠ VNP at dinner. Before dessert, an OpenAI paper claimed that the square matrix multiplication exponent ω is exactly 9/4 . During dessert, another paper claimed matching upper and lower bounds for the finite Fourier transform . The lower bound is the biggest news. In October, OpenAI found an upper bound for ω down to at most 9/4 . Finding the lower bound = upper bound leaves only one possible value, which is a shocking result for most. We plotted 64 selected AI-assisted research advances so far this year. November accounts for 20, including six preprints from Google’s Cogentic . The curve follows public releases, including proofs still under review. We count the two VP ≠ VNP proofs once and give October’s faster matrix multiplication algorithm and November’s matching lower bound an entry each. Yupan Liu showed that two messages suffice for quantum interactive proofs , a result that would have been a big deal on its own. articles.title: Talking Points for Thanksgiving
articles.snippet: infographic by Chat GPT Light posting over the holiday weekend, but before I head to the airport, I wanted to share a few cheat sheets for dinner-table discussions with those annoying cousins and that know-it-all uncle . Working backward from the most recent: I delved into the Midterm-blowout, subject-changing TACO trade on Monday: This is the TACO trade writ large, the Grande Supreme version. It is fair to suggest that the White House is not looking forward to a change of control in Congress and endless investigations. A crashed stock market and possible recession is the last thing they want… I was genuinely surprised at how poorly the media covered the October 30 and Nov 6 sell-offs. Lazy, superficial discussions of that Thursday crash begged to be corrected last week — and so I did : Rumors circulated that ~108 separate pods closed and unwound on Thursday in what is best described as “forced liquidations.” That might help explain the fastest $2.5 trillion wipeout on record. (Note we saw a somewhat less ugly selloff on the last trading day of October). For those unfamiliar with the term “pod shops,” these are multi-manager, multi-strategy hedge funds that have hundreds of small, semi-autonomous trading teams – aka “pods” – on the same platform. Many of the best-known multi-strat funds run large amounts of capital: Millennium ($98B), Citadel ($77B), Point72 ($55.5B), Balyasny ($37B), Schonfeld Strategic Advisors ($23.5B), Hudson Bay Capital ($20B), etc. Add to that Viking and many other Tiger shops, and it all adds up to a rather sizeable amount of capital — close to half a trillion dollars. It felt to me like the sell-off was driven by forced liquidations: Last Thursday felt (at least to me) like many of these pods got caught in a crowded, systematic, long-leveraged growth equity trade. Think mega-cap growth, momentum, and tech names, especially AI/Semis . The multi-strat shops are disciplined, mechanical, and formulaic. Any pod that hits a specific drawdown limit (~5% or 7.5%)4, it triggers a hard stop automatically. When I refer to forced liquidation, this is precisely what I mean. Then there was this amusing “THAT wasn’t for public consumption” radio incident involving the 3% opening gap up and close at the lows : “…and Barry Ritholtz said before the open that markets have been ‘trading heavy’ and he is concerned that a big gap up might lead to an ‘intraday reversal;’ if we see markets close on their lows, well he says, Katie, bar the door .” Most families are better off not discussing politics at the table, but we can all LOL at how badly the polls got it. Start here: Endless things can happen between when a pollster gets an answer and when it’s time to vote. A respondent to a poll who says a) I like this candidate; b) I am a registered voter; and c) I intend to vote for that person — does not guarantee a ballot will be cast as stated, if at all.1 In October, I exhorted you to rebalance your portfolios to take advantage of high bond yields and extended equities: Regardless of your starting allocation, the odds are that you have become overweight equities and underweight fixed income. A portfolio that began as 70/30 stocks and bonds is 80/20 today. At the same time, since 2022, the bond aggregate has gone nowhere, with 2026 negative YTD. Stocks gained about 50% over the same period, despite the 2022 bear market. In three years, a 70/30 portfolio drifted to about 79/21; since 2020, it’s 84/16. The simplest thing to do is to rebalance out of equities and into fixed income back to your original weighting. Earlier in October, I gave you a dozen reasons why rates had been moving higher : What Is Driving Rates Higher and Bonds Lower Oil and the Iran war premium Reaccelerating growth Long-term rate normalization COVID fiscal stimulus and the CARES Acts Trade and tariff policy Hawkish Fed’s hiking cycle Japan leading global yields higher Corporate supply competing with Treasury Sticky inflation Weak natural demand for long-dated paper Deficits and the term premium The Fed is reducing duration In September, I pushed back on what I thought was terrible advice : that entrepreneurs should aim to amass $5m in Treasuries: O’Leary is 72 years old and is worth north of $100 million. For someone at that stage of their career – really anyone in their 50s, 60s, or 70s – I believe the best bet for those circumstances is tax-free municipal bonds.2 (More as to why this was bad advice for founders in the footnotes) Late Summer, I kept hearing people explain that investors carrying cash was a drag on performance; I pushed back on that approach: “A reminder for individual investors: you are not hedge fund managers competing in league tables for bragging rights; you are individuals trying to live and enjoy your life, giving your family the best opportunities and experiences you can. Today, we are 17 years post-GFC bottom; many people are sitting on huge gains. I never have a problem when clients want to take something off the table to make a major purchase that a) they can afford and b) brings them joy.” Those are your fun talking points for Turkey Day. Be grateful for what you have, be hopeful this latest drawdown is a run-of-the-mill correction, and travel safely! articles.title: FCC should focus on robot security, not country of origin
articles.snippet: The Go2 quadruped robot from Unitree, a prominent Chinese robot developer. | Source: Unitree The FCC is right to treat connected robots as a security issue . Its recent action restricting foreign-produced advanced robotic devices reflects a real risk. These machines carry cameras and sensors, transmit data, take remote software updates, and make their own decisions inside factories, warehouses, stores, and airports. But where a robot was assembled tells you little about who controls it once it’s deployed. A robot built entirely in the United States, with unsigned updates and open remote access, is a bigger risk than one built overseas with secure software. The real security boundary is the code, the data, and whoever can change them, not the chassis. The FCC has already recognized this. Its definition of a covered device relies on software: firmware and AI or machine-learning model weights that control navigation, perception, data collection, and remote command and control. The agency has identified the layer that matters. The next step is to turn that critical layer into the standard. Brain Corp builds autonomy software, so of course I think software deserves scrutiny. But that’s also why I know where the risk lives. Our technology runs more than 50,000 robots on six continents and has logged more than 25 million hours of autonomous operation. At that scale, the failures that matter are rarely in the hardware. They’re in how software gets updated, who can reach the machine, and what happens when it meets a situation nobody anticipated. Regulate control, not just origin Software provenance alone can’t mean where the code was written. Robots run on open-source libraries, globally trained models, and international engineering teams. What should matter is provenance of control, demonstrated rather than declared. Any robot deployed in a sensitive or public setting, wherever its parts came from, should be able to show: Who can push code to it, and that every update is signed and verified before it runs. That unauthorized code can’t execute. Where its data goes, where it’s processed, and who can access it. How remote access is granted, logged, and revoked. How quickly a newly discovered vulnerability can be patched across the entire fleet. An independent safety layer that the AI cannot override. Independent audits and certifications that back up all of the above. Submit your innovation now! AI can be probabilistic. Physical safety can’t be. The safety layer deserves emphasis, because AI is changing what robots can do faster than policy is changing how we judge them. When a chatbot gets something wrong, the result is a bad answer. When a robot gets something wrong, it could generate unsafe behavior in a crowded aisle or beside a worker. AI models will make robots far more capable, but they shouldn’t be the final authority over physical behavior. Robots need deterministic constraints beneath the intelligence layer. If a model proposes an unsafe action, an independent mechanism must stop it, and sensor data should check the model’s reading of the world rather than defer to it. The more sophisticated the models become, the more this separation matters, and the more it belongs in any serious security standard. The next step The industry doesn’t need to wait for regulators to adopt these standards. Developers can publish how their systems meet them today, and enterprise buyers can require them in procurement. But voluntary practice is no substitute for a clear rule. The FCC has already recognized that a robot is defined by its software. The next step is to regulate it that way: not just where the parts were made, but who controls the code. About the Author David Pinn assumed the role of CEO at Brain Corp in 2022, where he has held various executive positions since joining in 2017, including chief strategy officer and chief financial officer. During his tenure, Pinn was instrumental in leading Brain Corp’s transformation from a robotics hardware company to a software as a service (SaaS) provider. He played a pivotal role in securing over $100 million in funding from prominent investors such as the SoftBank Vision Fund, Qualcomm Ventures, Hercules Capital, ClearBridge Investments, and Satwik Ventures. Prior to joining Brain Corp, Pinn served as head of finance for Antenna79, a technology startup backed by L Catterton, the world’s largest consumer-focused private equity group, where he facilitated the raising of $94.9 million in private equity funding. Before his tenure at Antenna79, Pinn co-founded Snaptracs, Qualcomm’s consumer electronics subsidiary. Under his leadership, Snaptracs was successfully sold, leading to a merger with Whistle and a $117 million acquisition by Mars. Pinn holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Electrical Engineering from the University of Texas at Austin and a Master’s in Business Administration from the University of California, Berkeley, Haas School of Business. The post FCC should focus on robot security, not country of origin appeared first on The Robot Report .

articles.title: How DARPA Challenged Teams to Bring Robots Into Disaster Triage
articles.snippet: On 5 November, 10 teams descended upon a 52-acre mock town in College Station, Texas called Disaster City . They were there for a nine-day competition to see how well teams of robots and humans could navigate simulated catastrophes, like a market ravaged by a tornado and a nighttime strike on a military base. At stake? US $2.5 million in prize money. The scenarios were the final of the DARPA Triage Challenge , which the U.S. agency has been running for three years with the goal of saving more lives in urgent mass casualty events. Engineers from academia and industry have competed in elaborately staged mass casualty events , such as simulated combat zones and plane crash scenes. Teams spent years designing systems where autonomous ground robots and drones could help first responders find mock victims and decide the best way to care for them. “Triage is all about resources,” says Jeremy Pamplin , who managed the challenge for DARPA. Pamplin is a critical care physician and retired colonel who spent 28 years in the U.S. Army. In mass casualty events, medics race to assess trauma with finite resources and limited time. Some victims need urgent help that medics can provide immediately, like tourniquets to halt bleeding. Some need evacuation and surgery. Others don’t need immediate help—either because their wounds are minimal enough, or because they’re so severe that a medic’s attention is better served elsewhere. Medics must prioritize who gets what care, but the line between each of these scenarios can be murky amid the rubble, frenzy, and heat of the moment. It’s a difficult problem, and so the technologies developed in this competition could help real-world decisionmaking, says Gabriela Garcia Dolagaray , assistant medical director for emergency preparedness at Massachusetts General Hospital and the Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston. “Finding people can sometimes just be dangerous,” she says, “and getting a robust number of people to go out and search in a disaster area will take time.” Trauma Technologies and the DARPA Triage Challenge The Triage Challenge is the latest in a long DARPA legacy of running grand challenges to incentivize proof-of-concept development of important technologies. This particular challenge began as a program to quickly detect signs of trauma. DARPA imagined not only that drones and robots could find casualties, but that machine learning algorithms could assist in triage—which, at its core, is the process of assessing injuries and prioritizing care in a medical emergency. Pamplin took over the competition in May 2025. “I have friends that still wake up in the middle of the night with these types of recollections and wondering if they did the right thing in the moment during a mass casualty incident,” Pamplin says. “That moves me. I would very much like to eliminate that uncertainty for them to the extent possible with this type of technology.” He used his experience to make the competition increasingly elaborate and realistic. Year one featured a simulated convoy attack, and human participants sat in protective enclosures to avoid incidental run-ins with robots. In year two, when Pamplin took over the challenge, his team incorporated a full-size airplane fuselage to simulate a plane crash with dozens of victims. Organizers learned to recreate the physical environment of a disaster, and also the physical signs of injuries, like warm blood. Pamplin’s team visited a slaughterhouse with thermal cameras to study the temperature of blood spilling onto the ground. In the competition, they mimic that effect by heating water in a coffee pot and pouring it beside the body. This lets teams detect bleeding even at night. A man performs a simulated triage as part of DARPA’s Triage Challenge finals. The program was designed to see how robots could assist in making triage decisions during an emergency. Paul Flacks/DARPA “They always are throwing additional challenging things at us that you wouldn’t expect,” says Sam Colachis , a biomedical engineer at Battelle, an applied science and technology nonprofit in Columbus Ohio who led the organization’s DART team —short for “Drone-Assisted Rapid Triage”—in the competition. The tactics required for successful triage are inherently multidisciplinary, says Derek Paley , a professor of aerospace engineering leading the University of Maryland’s team, RoboScout . Before 2022, Paley felt confident in his lab’s skills with autonomous navigation and algorithms, but he knew little about trauma medicine. “I didn’t even know what triage was,” he says. Paley recruited colleagues in emergency medicine to help design his team’s approach and shape their tech. Before the Triage Challenge began, they felt like an underdog. “We kind of have a chip on our shoulder because we think we can play on the same field as these other teams…who’ve done grand challenges before,” Paley told Spectrum before the competition. They finished third in the first year of competition and second last year. Each year’s competition began with four smaller trials that tested specific components of a robotic system. Teams first released their robots to locate as many casualties (a mix of live actors and manikins ) as possible in 15 minutes. Next, they spent five minutes triaging injuries. Another trial presented teams with a fixed number of casualties in known locations to test how they assess trauma. Then, teams had ten minutes to collect vitals like pulse and breathing rate remotely from a few meters away. The top four teams moved into a semi-final where their robots worked with two human medics in simulated emergencies. And the two teams who performed best in four human-machine runs then moved to a 25-minute championship run. Robots, Drones, and Autonomous Triage When the teams arrived at Disaster City, they knew very little about the details of what awaited them. articles.title: 10 Wednesday AM Reads
articles.snippet: My getting ready for Turkey day morning reads: • Nvidia Squeeze, Vol Spike and Short Losses : Last week we flagged Nvidia (NVDA) as still the market’s largest short value at risk at $1.9B, even with fewer dollars short. Shorts made $13.7B in seven straight down sessions after Jensen Huang’s exit, including $5.9B on Friday. Today’s 33% rebound on Jensen Huang’s return as CEO costs shorts about $12B, nearly 90% of the seven-day gain, and lifts short value at risk 150% to $4.68B, the highest on record for any stock. Shorts are still up about $4B on NVDA this year. The stock needs to reach $173 to erase the seven-day gain and $182 to erase the year’s. ( S3 Partners ) • How to talk to your family about the economy over the holidays : Year-end comes with tough conversations If you’re reading this, you almost certainly work in finance. Bad news: your friends and family will probably unload their anxiety about affordability, AI, Iran, government debt, interest rates and the stock market onto you over the holidays. Good news: reading this report might save you some heartburn. We list 10 questions you might get asked. For each, we suggest both a short response – in case dessert is served – and a more detailed one if the turkey just went into the oven. ( B of A Research ) ​• The Rube Goldberg Machine We Call Health Care : Wendell Potter: a webinar invite from CoverMyMeds, “Optimizing the Affordability Journey,” leads him into the company’s story. It began in Ohio in 2008 as software to automate prior authorizations, and McKesson bought it nine years later for about $1.1 billion, with up to $300 million more tied to targets. ( Health Care Un-Covered ) • Inside the ‘war room’ that lobbied Donald Trump to bring back Nvidia’s Jensen Huang : Silicon Valley titans enlisted US president and JD Vance to rescue the billionaire tech boss whom they viewed as critical for the AI industry. ( Financial Times ) see also The Frantic White House Push to Get Jensen Huang Back : Trump made clear he wanted the Nvidia CEO reinstated; on Monday he touted the decision, saying the market proved it was right. ( Wall Street Journal ) ​• AI Data Centers Are Devouring the Power American Factories Need : Bloomberg’s feature, by the headline, says the AI build-out is competing with U.S. manufacturers for grid power. To understand why, visit Canada’s border and a New York town once famed for Alcoa aluminum. ( Bloomberg ) • Birth order doesn’t predict your personality. Here’s what does : Michael J. Coren: the bossy firstborn, peacemaking middle child and reckless youngest make a tidy story, but researchers who analyzed the statistical souls of millions of people found birth order has no durable predictive power over personality. New research is challenging assumptions about what determines our personality — and showing that you can change it. ( Washington Post ) • GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff : Roslyn Henry and Peter Alexander: GLP-1 drugs could cut food demand enough to free farmland larger than Italy. The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access. ( The Conversation ) ​• America Loves Mahjong. Chinese Americans Hardly Recognize It : Amy Qin: American mahjong, with its own tiles and rules, has overshadowed the traditional Chinese game, and the rivalry is fueling anger and cultural misunderstanding. She opens at one of the largest Chinese mahjong tournaments ever held in the U.S., where 322 contestants were whittled down to about 50 players. ( New York Times ) ​• The Big Reason Florida Is Still Red : Olga Khazan: the midterm blue wave reached the South, yet Florida’s Democratic candidates for senator and governor both lost, narrowly. Her answer is migration: the state has absorbed hundreds of thousands of newcomers who moved there to be Republican. ( The Atlantic ) ​• Three Faster Ways to Board a Plane (That the Airlines Won’t Use) : David Pogue asks whether today’s boarding method is mathematically the worst. He blames seat interference, when an already-seated aisle passenger must stand up to let a window or middle passenger in, in the busiest air-travel week of the year. ( Pogue’s Substack ) Video of the day : Never Argue Politics With Family (Do This Instead) (Professor Pyrros) Be sure to check out our Masters in Business with David Eichhorn , Chief Executive Officer and Head of Investment Strategies at NISA Investment Advisors , a 100% employee-owned asset manager based in Clayton, Missouri, overseeing roughly $483 billion in assets. AI Twitter Recap Frontier Models as Research Engines: VP ≠ VNP, Protein Design and 948 Kernel Bugs VP ≠ VNP, posted by two labs : An Anthropic GitHub repo reportedly contains a proof by an internal Claude research model that VP ≠ VNP. This is the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, posed by Valiant in 1979, and implies that polynomials such as the permanent lack small circuits over every field ( @kimmonismus , repo pointer ). OpenAI's counter-release : OpenAI then posted its own proof and says it was "obtained on November 6, 2026." Neither lab named a model or published an announcement ( @AndrewCurran_ ). Scope : The result does not imply P ≠ NP, which still requires general Boolean circuit lower bounds ( @ZhihuFrontier ). Speculation : Curran argues that both labs are sitting on unreleased results and repeats unconfirmed rumors of cryptography breakthroughs. Treat this as opinion. Riemann proof clarifications : Levent Alpöge says the "250,000+ pages" claim was a joke. He released only the Lean code because he could not produce a readable writeup, and called it "full of garbage obviously, but compiles" ( @kimmonismus , @simonw ). Lineage claim : A Zhihu analysis traces Alpöge's key method to a short OpenAI proof excluding Landau–Siegel zeros. This is an attributed inference ( @ZhihuFrontier ). GPT-6 protein design, wet-lab validated : OpenAI released a preprint showing GPT-6 models designing new protein shapes and sequences through reasoning and code, without specialized bio models ( @OpenAI ). Results : 14 of 107 resequenced proteins showed binding. 128 of 182 redesigned small antibodies and 179 of 272 antibody fragments retained binding ( details ). Cost caveat : On a prior DNA task, GPT-6.1 Sol was about 2,000x more expensive per task than a specialized model ( @_lewtun ). GPT-6 Cyber and the Linux kernel : In one run, GPT-6 Cyber helped validate 948 Linux kernel bugs that could grant local root and generated patches for maintainer review ( @OpenAI ). Discovery beyond verifiable domains : A historian says GPT-6.2 Astra identified the vicomte de Chabot as the artist of an anonymous 1808 Yale sketchbook in 22 minutes. It also surfaced an obscure microfilmed diary whose handwriting and itinerary matched the sketches ( @HistoryGPT ). Exoplanet candidates : Amateurs using Codex and Astra searched Kepler and TESS data. One 13.8-day signal was independently confirmed by a SETI astronomer, and 49 TESS candidates were flagged ( @OpenAI ). Robotics saturation : GPT-6.2 Astra on Codex scored 97% on RoboDojo-RC Tier 1 across 120 real-robot trials, and RoboDojo is being retired ( @robocurve ). New environments : Einsia released RoboUniverse-10K, a set of 10,807 verifiable Isaac Sim tasks built from real manipulation videos. The top frontier score on held-out tasks is 85.8%, while 7 of 11 models score ≤10% ( @EinsiaAI ). Gemini 4 Neon Rollout and Frontier Model Moves Gemini 4 Neon adoption : Neon set a Day-1 usage record on Google's paid APIs. Antigravity tokens/day are up 82% since Argon launched six weeks ago ( @sundarpichai ). Availability : Neon is now available to Google Workspace customers through the Gemini app ( @OfficialLoganK ). Third-party volume : Perplexity has passed 120B Neon tokens, doubling daily volume in 3 days with 36B on Monday. Arav Srinivas places Neon "between Opus and Fable" in intelligence but best on response style ( @AravSrinivas ). Developer tooling : Google shipped an experimental anti-slop frontend-design skill for Neon ( @_philschmid ) and made eight Workspace MCP servers plus gwscli generally available, with 5,000 requests/day free per product ( @_philschmid ). Price-performance (attributed estimate) : One estimate puts Neon xhigh roughly equal to Opus Max, at $6.44 vs $10.04 per Artificial Analysis task ( @teortaxesTex ). Sycophancy concerns : Several users report heavy "glazing" and overcorrection when Neon is critiqued ( @teortaxesTex , @johnowhitaker ). Claude Opus 5.6 sightings (unconfirmed) : Users report Opus 5.6 being A/B-tested in Claude Code and chat, and describe it as "quite a jump" over 5.5 ( @synthwavedd , @kimmonismus ). Cognition SWE-2.1 : The model is pure-RL trained on Kimi K3 and reportedly approaches frontier models on FrontierCode 2.0 at max reasoning. It is free on Devin paid tiers for two weeks ( @cognition ). Looped transformers trend : GLM-5.4 makes five looped models in Raschka's architecture gallery ( @rasbt ). SenseNova-Loop-9B : The model runs its middle 24 of 32 layers twice and beats Qwen3.8-27B on GAIA (69.90 vs 66.99). It is about 4.9 GB at 4-bit and released under Apache 2.0 ( @kimmonismus ). Inkling 2 Mini decoding : LoopCD contrasts loop pass 3 against pass 1 with no training, lifting AA-Omniscience from -9.0 to -3.4 ( @onloglogn ). articles.title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
articles.snippet: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example. 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa. Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game . It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play. I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play! Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked . My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay. Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time. Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games. The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster . It feels like another inflection point to me. Is Fable 5.2

articles.title: Silence and Love
articles.snippet: Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted. What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound. As in music, so in life: “Listen to the silence inside the illusion of the world,” Jack Kerouac wrote to his first wife turned lifelong friend in reckoning with the meaning of life , “and you will remember the lesson you forgot.” Silence is the listening presence through which you hear the music of your own life, presence purified to become peace — a peace greater than joy and unburdened by understanding, a peace the other word for which may be love. There is no piece of music that has scored more of my waking days and my writing hours than “Spiegel im Spiegel” by the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, whose virtuosity with sound springs from his relationship to silence — something he articulates with poetic concision in a series of reflections recently shared by his son: Silence is always more perfect than music. You must simply learn to hear it. Silence is utterly full. […] When we speak of silence, we must keep in mind that it has two wings: Silence can be both outside of us and within us. The silence of our soul, over which even external noise has no power, is actually more crucial. But is also much more difficult to achieve. A generation before him, Kahlil Gibran had captured this difficulty with piercing pointedness. “You talk when you cease to be at peace with your thoughts,” he charged in his timeless meditation on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself . Pärt puts it more gently: One does not have to speak. But one must love. One does not have to compose, one does not have to write a book. But one must love… If you do not speak, thinking, and even prayer, is clearer, and there is more space left over for love. I have always felt that the quality of silence two people can share is one of the great measures of love — something the young poet Babette Deutsch captured beautifully a century ago: SILENCE by Babette Deutsch Silence with you is like the faint delicious Smile of a child asleep, in dreams unguessed: Only the hinted wonder of its dreaming, The soft, slow-breathing miracle of rest. Silence with you is like a kind departure From iron clangor and the engulfing crowd Into a wide and greenly barren meadow, Under the bloom of some blue-bosomed cloud; Or like one held upon the sands at evening, When the drawn tide rolls out, and the mixed light Of sea and sky enshrouds the far, wind-bellowed Sails that move darkly on the edge of night. donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. articles.title: How to Touch the Nothingness Behind Everything: Kahlil Gibran on the Seven Selves
articles.snippet: A self is a forest . A self is a ship . A self is an illusion , and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world. Above all, a self is a sum of selves , contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life. Kahlil Gibran (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life , takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic The Madman ( public library | free ebook ). The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated the Japanese concept of ma .) Kahlil Gibran THE SEVEN SELVES by Kahlil Gibran In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper: First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years, with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel. Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary existence. Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self who would rebel against this madman. Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell, who would protest against serving this madman. Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self, the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is I, not you, who would rebel. Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who, with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman. Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel? When the seventh self thus spake the other six selves looked with pity upon him but said nothing more; and as the night grew deeper one after the other went to sleep enfolded with a new and happy submission. But the seventh self remained watching and gazing at nothingness, which is behind all things. Couple with Gibran on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself , then revisit Hermann Hesse on discovering the soul beneath the self . donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). articles.title: Responding to objections to recursive self-improvement
articles.snippet: (00:00:00) – Intro Dwarkesh Patel 00:00:00 Okay, so I recently released this essay and this video about recursive self-improvement and why I expect superintelligence by 2030. A wild claim, and understandably, lots of people had objections. Many of them are actually quite interesting and compelling, and I want to go through them here. And by the way, I’m joined by Max Farrens , who is my General Manager, and we ended up discussing all of these ideas as we were writing them down. And in fact, we paired in a lot of the writing. (00:00:24) – Jim: “Do you have a real job?” Max Farrens 00:00:25 I think a good place to start is with a comment on the Substack version of the post that comes from a user named Jim, who writes as The 1690 Project. “Dwarkesh, do you have a real job where you use this stuff” (meaning AI) “in and day out? I am guessing you do not, because I do, and this is not what I am seeing at all.” What do you think? Dwarkesh Patel 00:00:47 Those are two different questions. Do I use these things day in, day out? Yes. Do I have a real job? Debatable. Don’t answer that. Funny that the guy’s like bragging about having a real job. He’s like, he’s like a gotcha on me. Like, I’ve been one of the main people who for the last year and a half has been arguing that the basic learning capabilities that these models lack do in fact impair their productivity. I think people who a naive understanding of what it means to automate a job just look at a system like GPT-6 and say, oh, why can’t we have AGI? It can automate all the white-collar work. I think this is totally wrong. The point I’m making in this essay is that are currently worse than humans at almost everything, right? IT is 1% of the economy, well-scoped coding tasks is a small fraction of IT. In some things, AIs are in fact getting to human level or beyond human level, where we have lots of verifiable proxies. And I would argue that just like math, AI research has a lot of verifiable proxies. And so the consequences of narrow progress in AI research or towards AIs that can do AI research leads to general improvements in AI capabilities. So if you look at a system like GPT-3 and you compare it to GPT-6, GPT-6 is also narrow intelligence, right? It can solve Millennium Prize problems, but it can’t be my video editor. So it can do basically everything way better than GPT-3. What I am imagining is that disproportionate progress in ML research, or AIs that are good at doing ML research, will compress as much progress as we had between GPT-3 and GPT-6 into a single year. And so the end result is within a year of having a system like GPT-7 or GPT-8 or whatever it ends up being, we end up with systems that are more generally capable in the way that humans are generally capable, and are on track to then rapidly become better than humans at everything. (00:02:41) – Cindy Wu: Is AI research a verifiable domain? Max Farrens 00:02:42 So Cindy Wu writes on X , “Dwarkesh conveniently sweeps under the rug that climbing a metric involves defining it. Supposing you define it in a way that avoids Goodharting, reward hacking, etc., you need data and environments which do the lifting on defining good metrics. This is most of the game of making AGI, converting fuzzy concepts to formalized objects you can climb without gaming, which requires costly fixes later. He elides the hard problem by saying AI will just automate data.” Dwarkesh Patel 00:03:12 I think there’s two parts to Cindy’s objection here. One is: can we find metrics which capture general AI progress? Are we aware of such metrics? And two, will we be able to generate the data that makes AIs good at getting better at those metrics? A big part of my essay was dedicated to articulating what those verifiable proxies for general AI progress are, right? So in pre-training, the loss on a held-out corpus is not only a proxy for pre-training progress, it is the basis of pre-training progress, and that is extremely verifiable. And there’s a lot of other proxies you can come up with that are just general intelligence capabilities that are kind of agnostic for any given paradigm. For example, how fast do you master a video game you’ve never seen before? This is one of the key ways that humans are different from current AIs, that humans master new video games really rapidly. How fast can an AI that has only seen a data corpus up to 1700 figure out general relativity? How many open math problems can it solve, right? So there’s a lot of paradigm-agnostic, hard metrics of progress we can come up with. The second argument here is learning algorithms. The application of learning algorithms is very general. The transformer was invented to beat the existing state of the art in translation, but because that architecture, or the implications of the architecture, were general, it also was really good at predicting the next token in WikiText. It’s also really good at generating images and so on. And similarly with reasoning models. Initially they were invented and they were debugged to, like, solve high school math problems and simple coding problems, and now they’re applicable and useful across lots of different domains. And so the breakthroughs that are made in AI end up being measurable on lots of different metrics. And the reason they’re measurable across lots of different metrics is because AI, or intelligence, is general, and because of that, its general improvements show up and make contact with reality in lots of different ways. Max Farrens 00:05:14 So you started out by saying that there were two subpoints you wanted to address. The first is around verifiable proxies, and I think I understand that your answer is something of the sort of: it is not just that there are verifiable proxies that we can hill-climb, they are, like, the things themselves that we can work on. And so AI research makes itself particularly amenable to hill climbing. The second is around how we actually get the data to do that sort of work

articles.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
articles.snippet: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra

articles.title: SoftBank acquires Marc Raibert’s Robotics and AI Institute
articles.snippet: SoftBank has completed its acquisition of the Robotics and AI Institute (RAI) from Hyundai Motor Group, The Robot Report has learned. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. SoftBank responded to emailed questions from The Robot Report about the acquisition, but it declined to comment. The Robot Report first reported the acquisition agreement in September 2026 . The deal adds another prominent name to SoftBank’s growing portfolio of robotics companies. Boston Dynamics founder Marc Raibert founded the RAI Institute in 2022 with more than $400 million in initial funding from Hyundai. Based in Cambridge, Mass., the institute focuses on solving fundamental challenges in robotics, including mobility, manipulation, perception, and intelligence. RAI is also looking to expand its team. It currently has 24 open positions , including internships, across its offices in Cambridge and Zurich, Switzerland. The openings cover a range of technologies, including robot learning, manipulation, simulation, navigation, and hardware engineering. SoftBank continues to build its robotics portfolio The acquisition reunites SoftBank and Raibert. SoftBank acquired Boston Dynamics from Alphabet in 2017 before selling a controlling stake to Hyundai in 2021 in a deal that valued the robotics company at $1.1 billion. Hyundai recently acquired SoftBank’s remaining 9.65% stake in Boston Dynamics, giving Hyundai Motor Group and its executive chairman full ownership of the robotics company. The deal marks the end of SoftBank’s nearly decade-long investment in Boston Dynamics . SoftBank has since acquired or invested in a number of robotics companies, including 1X Technologies, Agile Robots, AutoStore, BALYO, Berkshire Grey, Brain Corp, Skild AI, and Symbotic. It will be interesting to see how much collaboration takes place between the RAI and some of these companies. There are potential synergies, for example, between the research being done at the institute and the technologies being developed by Skild AI and Agile Robots. It’s unclear whether SoftBank’s ownership will change the institute’s research priorities or whether it will continue to operate independently. The deal also comes at a time when SoftBank’s planned $5.375 billion acquisition of ABB Robotics faces an uncertain future. Chinese regulators blocked the acquisition of ABB’s robotics business in China, putting the deal in jeopardy . Simulated robots training on a tire-rolling skill in parallel. Each skill takes a few hours on a single GPU. | Credit: Robotics and AI Institute The post SoftBank acquires Marc Raibert’s Robotics and AI Institute appeared first on The Robot Report .

articles.title: Transcript: David Eichhorn, NISA Investment Advisors CEO, Head of Investment Strategies
articles.snippet: The transcript from this week’s MiB : David Eichhorn, NISA Investment Advisors CEO, Head of Investment Strategies , is below. You can stream and download our full conversation, including any podcast extras, on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , YouTube , and Bloomberg . All of our earlier podcasts on your favorite pod hosts can be found here . ~~~ Masters in Business Transcript: David Eichhorn, CEO and Head of Investment Strategies, NISA Investment Advisors [00:00:02] ANNOUNCER: Bloomberg Audio Studios, podcasts, radio, news. [00:00:07] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Strap yourself in for another banger. I sit down with the head of NISA Investment Advisors. They run a half a trillion dollars or so in institutional assets. David Eichhorn has been CEO there for a few years, as well as the head of investment strategies. He’s not just a fixed income and pension fund investor, he’s a quant. He has a deep understanding of what drives liability-based strategies, as well as the bond market, geopolitics, everything that’s going on, what really produces alpha as opposed to just excess risk and leverage. I thought this conversation was fascinating and I think you will too. With no further ado, my conversation with NISA’s David Eichhorn. David Eichhorn, welcome to Bloomberg. [00:01:09] DAVID EICHHORN: Barry, I’m delighted to be here. Love the show, and excited to chat today. [00:01:13] BARRY RITHOLTZ: I’m delighted to have you. What you guys do is really fascinating and so unusual. We’re going to delve into that. But before we get there, I want to spend a little time talking about your background. You got a Bachelor of Science degree in business administration, majors in finance and mathematics, from Washington University in St. Louis. Sounds like investing was the original career plan. Was that it from the start? [00:01:41] DAVID EICHHORN: Mostly the career plan was, you know, pay bills, honestly, and try to work through school and all that. I didn’t know that was even a thing until some number of years ago, when it became popular to talk about that. [00:02:04] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Right. First one in your family to go to college? [00:02:06] DAVID EICHHORN: No, all my brothers and sisters, but our generation was the first. And so it certainly was great being local at Washington University. I grew up in St. Louis. I was a commuter, which isn’t even allowed anymore. Probably a regrettable decision from a college life experience. But I had to work a lot to pay the bills at Wash U, when it was still possible to pay for college. Still, back then. But the math really was the superpower that I think supercharged the finance degree, frankly. So I met Phil Dybvig, who I love to describe now as Nobel Laureate Phil Dybvig, at Washington University. Because of the math degree, he took a shine to me, for lack of a better term. And it’s one of those—in the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king. I had some programming background. I knew relatively sophisticated math for what was in the finance department, and he really helped get me my first job at JP Morgan. And I’m eternally grateful for Phil, and he remains a great friend to this day. Tell us about your JP Morgan experience. [00:03:26] DAVID EICHHORN: Well, I’ll probably come back to the theme many times, but serendipity has struck a lot in my career. So Phil connected me with Mike Granito at JP Morgan, who ran what they called the Strategic Investment Advisory Group. I dumb-lucked into that. That was a group of, I think at the time, 17 or 18 PhDs. A couple of us were the first-ever undergrad hires, and even within that group, I lucked into—as opposed to cleansing databases and doing awful work that the quants needed—I somehow got put in a client-facing role very quickly. We shared free consulting, maybe in air quotes, free consulting, to our large clients: classic mean-variance optimization-style analysis of managers, things that were newer for the time to roll out to clients. And so I got a great background in that. And at that time, while most people weren’t doing it, we started really pushing the concept of asset-liability management, really what became, I’d say, the forerunner to LDI-type strategies. How do you—amongst other things, but certainly for large corporate pensions—how do you manage risk, as opposed to in an absolute context, how do you manage it vis-à-vis liability, whether that be how you think about your equity allocation, but maybe most importantly how you think about your fixed income allocation? How does it mitigate some of the liability’s inherent interest rate risk? And again, not many people listened in the late nineties, and that kind of continued on into the early aughts at NISA. But it was setting the groundwork for what ultimately became known as LDI. [00:04:57] BARRY RITHOLTZ: And so I think the average layperson hears “liability” and they’re thinking car accident. Explain, especially from a pension fund manager’s perspective, what do future liabilities mean in plain English?
