articles.title: 10 Tuesday AM Reads
articles.snippet: My Two-for-Tuesday morning reads: • The Icarus Files: What’s next for Nvidia and AI : Michael Cembalest: Since 1960, there have been ten companies that shared the distinction of being the largest company in the S&P 500. Some held the perch for years (GE, GM, Exxon, Apple) while others got there just to look around for a bit before descending (Cisco held the title for just 3 days). But one company’s rise to the top was faster than the rest: Nvidia which rose from 1% of the S&P 500 in December 2022 to 8.5% by May 2026. Nvidia then became a pace-setter with respect to innovation, profitability, vendor financing, support for open weight models and outspoken advocacy against the US risk-fencing China. ( J.P. Morgan Eye on the Market ) ​• What Does the Anthropic IPO Mean for Your 401(k)? : Anthropic went public today, and you may already own it. Funds including American Funds Growth Fund of America and Fidelity Select Technology hold substantial stakes, and index funds will soon add shares after rule changes that speed up inclusion for newly listed giants. Indexes picking it up include the Russell 1000, Russell 3000, Nasdaq-100, Morningstar U.S., FTSE Global All Cap and MSCI USA. ( Fast Company ) ​• 5 Silent Investment Risks That Can Do More Damage Than a Market Crash : Sheryl Rowling: investors equate risk with market downturns, but a diversified portfolio can sit beside a pile of employer stock and options, with your paycheck riding on the same company. Many resist selling because of the tax bill. ( Morningstar ) • The Elephant in the Market: Understanding America’s Weight in Global Benchmarks : The U.S. is 70% of developed-market equity capitalization but only about 50% of GDP. D. E. Shaw says the gap is mostly structural, not a valuation story: U.S. companies earn more per dollar of GDP, which explains 64% of it An allocators a framework for understanding the gap in relative market capitalization between the U.S. and other developed markets and to consider what would need to change for market capitalization to converge with GDP. The gap stems mainly from structural and compositional factors, not from U.S. stocks being more expensive than their global industry peers: . ( DE Shaw ) ​• Boomers Are Rewriting the Playbook for Old Age. It Doesn’t Include Winding Down. : Boomers hold more than $97 trillion, over twice what Gen X has, and the average 65-year-old can expect nearly 20 more years, about two more than in 2000. Richer and more adventurous than their predecessors, baby boomers are living it up: ‘Somebody like me never retires like my parents did.’ ( Wall Street Journal ) ​• Mystery Firm Spending Millions to Attend Trump Crypto Gala, Seeks to Build “Chinese $TRUMP Coin Community” : Madeleine May: a digital finance firm whose CEO goes by one name has jumped to the top spot in the contest for a seat at the president’s upcoming crypto gala dinner, and says it wants a Chinese $TRUMP coin community. ( CBS News ) • When’s the Crash? Ask a Journalist : Toby Nangle jokes that market bears have the best arguments and the worst returns, and that financial journalists are Chicken Littles. A new paper from Marco Grotteria of London Business School suggests you shouldn’t ignore them anyway. Because in 170 years of perma-anxiety, stopped clocks are right fairly regularly. ( Financial Times ) ​• Nurses Are in High Demand—but They’re Quitting in Droves : Front-line nurses are leaving bedside jobs over burnout, understaffing, verbal abuse and workplace violence. Annual turnover for bedside RNs hit 18% last year per NSI Nursing Solutions, and Emory research puts the cost of each departure at about $78,000. The field can command six-figure salaries, but understaffing and persistent violence are pushing nurses off the front lines ( Wall Street Journal ) ​• Trump Keeps Losing in Court. The tariffs were struck down, then rebuilt under other legal authorities. ( Washington Post ) ​• The Russian Exile Behind the Missiles That Helped Destroy the Crimea Bridge : Ruta cruise missiles built by Destinus, led by exiled Russian Mikhail Kokorich, helped take down Russia’s showpiece bridge. ( Wall Street Journal ) see also They Were Too Old to Enlist, but Not to Fight. articles.title: The Individual Exception
articles.snippet: Listen to this post : Log in to listen Since Thursday: I have created a Sharp Studio service application that manages all of the Sharp Tech studio cameras, lights, mixer, and various other devices. That service can be accessed by a Windows app on the studio PC, an iPhone app, a web app, or an Elgato Stream Deck; every device in the room needed to record an episode is fully remote controlled. I have created multiple single-use iOS apps for cataloguing and measuring items and designed and 3D-printed a measurement rig. I have also designed and purchased the items for several dedicated hardware devices, including a device for direct interaction with an agent, and dedicated display devices for the studio. I have created a full-fledged iOS app (designed for the Duo, but it works on regular iPhones) for accessing the various computers I manage; it works across screen sharing, terminals, and KVM switches. It works on Mac, Linux, and Windows. I honestly think it’s the best screen sharing client ever made. I already use it daily. Along the way I created a small harness for my agent such that it not only choreographs subagents, but also farms out work to various computers I own, depending on the load: a Mac for iOS development, a gaming PC for GPU-related work, and a Linux server for everything else. That work is tracked on a custom status board that runs on every TV in my house, as an iOS app, and as a Telegram bot. All of this would have taken teams of people weeks of work, if not months, just a few years ago; I, however, have AI. It only takes an individual. The Deflationary Employee The largest company of the 1950s, as measured by market capitalization, was AT&T; in 1959 it had revenue of $7.54 billion and a market cap of $17.1 billion. It had 729,000 employees. In inflation-adjusted terms that’s revenue of $87.5 billion and a market cap of $198.4 billion; we don’t apply inflation to employees. Or, maybe we do, but in the other direction: what has been striking about the most valuable companies in the world is how their employee numbers have deflated , even as their revenue and market cap have exploded. All dollar numbers in this table are inflation-adjusted to today: Decade Company Year Real revenue Employees Real market cap 1950s AT&T 1959 $87.5B 729,000 $198.4B 1960s AT&T 1969 $147.8B ~1,000,000 $245.6B 1970s IBM 1979 $106.3B 337,119 $174.8B 1980s IBM 1989 $170.6B 383,220 $148.5B 1990s General Electric 1999 $226.6B 340,000 $1.03T 2000s ExxonMobil 2008 $749.5B 104,700 $637.6B 2010s Apple 2018 $355.9B 132,000 $1.00T 2020s Apple 2026 $478.8B 167,000 $5.07T The deflation is even more extreme if you consider two of the seminal AI companies, Nvidia and Anthropic: Decade Company Year Real revenue Employees Real market cap 2020s Nvidia 2026 $361.8B 42,000 $3.99T 2020s Anthropic 2026 $35.3B 5,300 $1.17T This translates into a stunning rise in revenue/employee and market cap/employee — note that this graph is a logarithmic scale: And yet, even this chart, which pegs the market cap/employee of Nvidia at $95 million, doesn’t come close to what the market decided one particular Nvidia employee is worth: As ChatGPT, which helped me make these charts, helpfully noted: Nvidia gained nearly $1 trillion in market capitalization following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. That gain alone exceeds the entire inflation-adjusted market capitalization of ExxonMobil in 2008 ($638 billion). It only takes an individual. The Huang Odyssey To describe the two-week odyssey of Nvidia’s then-and-now-CEO Jensen Huang as surreal is an understatement; what you can’t argue, however, is that it was unprecedented: it was only three Thanksgivings ago that Sam Altman was deposed and reinstated as OpenAI CEO over the very same weekend (two Max Verstappen Las Vegas Grand Prix wins, I might note). That said, I didn’t think that this episode would end the same way, and said as much on Sharp Tech : whereas Altman was taken out by a somewhat ham-fisted internal coup and restored through pressure from the private company’s investors and employees, Huang appeared to be targeted by a much more systemic campaign by powerful actors leveraging the media and barely disguised insinuations of malfeasance to leave the Nvidia board with no choice but to act. And, to be sure, Huang gave his enemies plenty of ammunition; I’ve invoked the phrase “Show me the man and I’ll show you the crime” over the past few weeks, but it’s worth acknowledging that Huang basically asked his critics, “Which one?”, at least as far as his sexual proclivities were concerned. At the same time, it sure seemed like no one cared about Huang’s affairs, including those with subordinates; the real crime appeared to be Huang’s resolute advocacy for selling chips to China, his refusal to do any more than the bare minimum to abide by export control rules, and, his most ardent critics allege, turning a blind eye towards actual smuggling. I’m not here, today at least, to litigate these accusations; I covered much of it in last week’s Article Obituaries (alternate title for today: Resurrections ). And, more broadly, this isn’t an Article focused on normative analysis; Huang’s Chinese interactions are going to be investigated by a Democratic Congress empowered by the anti-AI wave at the ballot box, and his personal moral failings would, for nearly any other executive, leave no question about the inevitability of their early retirement. Rather, I am struck by the extent to which Huang is, quite obviously, not any other executive, and how his reinstatement is the apotheosis of how tech is transforming business, just as AI is the apotheosis of information technology. It only takes an individual. The End of Managerialism In 1941, James Burnham, a former Trotskyist, wrote The Managerial Revolution , where he argued that the increasing complexity of industrial society, what with its massive returns to scale, technological complexity, and enmeshment with government, would increasingly div

articles.title: Different rules for the boss
articles.snippet: Of course, bosses have always been in favor of this. It’s one of the attractions of being the boss. A consistent set of rules is easier to understand and enforce. One set of rules for behavior, reward and consequence is easier to justify from a moral perspective as well. And yet, as Sahlins and Graeber wrote about in On Kings , the subjects of kings often approve of their royalty having different rules. The king comes from away, he (and it’s often a he) has a different origin and a different destiny. Different rules for a different sort of person. Superman comes from Krypton, not from Smallville. Someone who can act without facing consequences is a demonstration that he isn’t an ordinary person, and that is the closest thing on earth to a god. For some, “He doesn’t play fair” isn’t a flaw to be overlooked. It’s a credential. The challenge for kings is that once the subjects decide that there is no magic, the past transgressions aren’t considered a sign of power, they’re the end of the line. Monarchy is brittle. Fun while it lasts, perhaps, but it often ends poorly.

articles.title: [AINews] Jensen Is Back! and OpenAI Shows Its Pretraining Curve, joined by Microsoft
articles.snippet: Congrats to Sierra on tripling last year’s $10B valuation , and to Z.ai for releasing GLM 5.4 , their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller Inkling Mini 2 from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories… Jensen Huang is back . Eleven days after announcing his resignation , Nvidia announced his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors. View post on X ↗ The board voted unanimously after more meetings with Jensen on Sunday and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka the Treasury Secretary and the President dialing into the board meeting ). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control. As Matt Levine points out , with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light. OpenAI put its pretraining loss curve on the record. In Perplexity and Intelligence , Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki plotted base-model log-perplexity back to GPT-3.5 (on their internal held-out coding dataset … which has notable caveats ): View post on X ↗ Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. Lower is better. GPT-3.5 was around 0.99 and GPT-4 around 0.91. When OpenAI put a model around 0.76 (GPT6 Astra) to work on open math problems, hundreds of frontier math problems started falling quickly . Pachocki extrapolates that another jump in capabilities could come around 0.68–0.70. This is all in context of pacing the frontier . Pachocki proposes that labs agree on a first limit to development and spell out what would let them cross it, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitoring. Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman gave the first win by cosigning and joining in, running MAI-2 Base on OpenAI’s evaluation set and reporting 0.819. We’d need at least a couple more top labs to join this effort for it to gather steam as a real self-regulatory limit, most notably of course, Anthropic. Sponsored by Backblaze B2 If your data is growing faster than planned, you need storage that grows with your business, feeds flash and GPUs with terabit-scale throughput, and doesn’t charge egress. Backblaze B2 has delivered capacity tier storage for twenty years, manages more than six exabytes, and is trusted by leading neoclouds, labs, and gen AI companies. Growth shouldn’t be something you sweat. We’ve got room for whatever you’re building. Try it out! Enquiries and feedback to business@latent.space AI Twitter Recap OpenAI Publishes Its Pretraining Perplexity History and Proposes Shared Development Limits The disclosure : Jakub Pachocki's essay "Perplexity and Intelligence" publishes five years of OpenAI base-model log-perplexity on a fixed held-out dataset. It argues for industry-wide limits based on perplexity and other measurements, with further progress gated on milestones in understanding and monitoring AI behavior, such as a successor to chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors ( essay thread ). Policy framing : Sam Altman quoted the proposal for a first common limit with concrete exit criteria ( quote ). He tied it to the standards commitments in the White House Accords ( accords ). Endorsements : Greg Brockman highlighted the warning that alignment progress is unlikely to keep pace with pretraining acceleration ( gdb ). Mark Chen called the numbers formerly "sensitive IP" and asked other labs to disclose their key metrics ( markchen90 ). Claimed findings : Losses below 0.8 coincided with emergent capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics ( excerpt ). Thresholds and timing : OpenAI expects further "transformative capabilities" in the ~0.68–0.7 window and describes a steep acceleration in 2026 ( summary ). Internal model : An unreleased internal model already sits below GPT-6.2 Astra. Pachocki says pretraining could see an "avalanche" like the recent one in math as soon as 2027 ( scaling01 ). Community extrapolations (unofficial) : Dan Hendrycks infers ~3–5×/yr compute-efficiency gains since GPT-4, possibly 100×+ this year ( hendrycks ). One fit, using the internal model at 0.732 against 0.761 for the released model, reaches 0.70 between January and March 2027 ( fits ). Microsoft joins : With OpenAI's permission, Microsoft AI reported MAI-2 Base at 0.819 on OpenAI's eval set. It shares OpenAI's tokenizer and lands in GPT-5.6 Sol base-model territory. Mustafa Suleyman suggested bits-per-byte for future cross-lab comparisons ( mustafasuleyman ). Open-model mapping : Elie Bakouch used MAI as a bridge to place open models on OpenAI's curve ( plot ). He labels the further chaining through Inkling bpb a "very weak approximation" ( details ). Lucas Beyer's caveat : Inkling's held-out codebase may be largely agent-generated, which would make bridge-based placements look too optimistic ( giffmana ). Methodological critiques : Critics raised several confounds: Tokenizer bias : Common limits could favor OpenAI over Anthropic because of tokenizer differences ( davidmanheim ). Post-training compute : Post-training likely accounts for more than 75% of FLOPs, so pretraining perplexity may be the wrong pacing metric ( stochasticchasm ). Synthetic data : Part of the steep curve may come from a growing share of model-generated pretraining data ( Azaliamirh ). Missing context : Without model sizes or compute figures, it is hard to separate scaling from algorithmic progress ( Grad62304977 ). OpenAI's response : Staff say the eval is fixed over time and excludes model-generated code ( johnohallman ). Will Depue added that it is "held out, frozen, tokenizer agnostic" ( willdepue ). articles.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
articles.snippet: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look. I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark. articles.title: Heart, the Heretic: The Forgotten Visionary Jane Ellen Harrison on Critical Thinking, Emotional Imagination, and How to Fix the World
articles.snippet: “If we are to be true and worthy heretics, we need not only new heads, but new hearts, and, most of all, that new emotional imagination… begotten of enlarged sympathies and a more sensitive habit of feeling.” UPDATE 2025: This book is now back in print as the third title in Marginalian Editions . When the Inquisition persecuted Galileo for advancing the rude truth that Earth is not the center of the universe, the charge against him was heresy — the same charge on which Joan of Arc was burned at the stake for her crusade for political reform. We have had many words for heretics over the epochs — rebels, radicals, freethinkers — but they have always been the ones to dislodge humanity from the stagnation of the status quo, to illuminate our blind spots, dismantle our unexamined biases, and jolt us out of our herd mentality. Without those devoted to seeing reality more clearly and possibility more wildly, we would still live in a world haunted by superstition and governed by dogma. The power and dignity of this most courageous human mindset is what the pioneering classicist Jane Ellen Harrison (September 9, 1850–April 15, 1928), who brought the culture of Ancient Greece to the modern world, explores in her magnificent essay “Heresy and Humanity,” found in Alpha and Omega ( public library ) — the out-of-print essay collection that gave us Harrison on the art of growing older , published just as humanity was being dehumanized by its first World War. Jane Ellen Harrison Harrison writes: The word “heretic” has still about it an emotional thrill — a glow reflected, it may be, from the fires at Smithfield, the ardours of those who were burnt at the stake for the love of an idea. Heresy, the Greek hairesis , was from the outset an eager, living word. The taking of a city, its expugnatio , is a hairesis ; the choosing of a lot in life or an opinion, its electio , is a hairesis ; always in the word hairesis there is this reaching out to grasp, this studious, zealous pursuit — always something personal, even passionate… To be a heretic today is almost a human obligation. In a sentiment Bertrand Russell would echo in timeless manifesto for freedom of thought , Harrison adds: The gist of heresy is free personal choice in act, and specifically in thought — the rejection of traditional faiths and customs. Art by Olivier Tallec from Louis I, King of the Sheep A century and a half after Emerson inveighed that “masses are rude, lame, unmade, pernicious in their demands and influence,” she considers what makes heresy so difficult yet so necessary to the health of society: All traditional views are held with such tenacity, such almost ferocity, because they belong to the class of views induced, not by individual experience, still less by reason, but by collective, or, as it is sometimes called “herd,” suggestion. This used to be called “faith.” The belief so held may or may not be true; collective suggestion is not in the least necessarily collective hallucination. Mere collective suggestions — that is the interesting point — have the quality of obviousness; they do not issue from the individual, but seem imposed from outside, and ineluctable; they have all the inevitableness of instinctive opinion… Hence they are held with an intensity of emotion far beyond any reasoned conviction. To doubt them is felt to be at once idiocy and irreverence. Inquiry into their rational bases is naturally, and in a sense rightly, resented, because they are not rationally based, though they may be rationally supported. It is by convictions such as this that a society of the homogenous kind — a society based on and held together by uniformity — lives and thrives. To attack them is to cripple and endanger its inmost life. Observing that the development of science is what pivoted heresy from damnable to desirable in society, Harrison contrasts sensemaking by empiricism with sensemaking by authority: Science classifies, draws ever clearer distinctions; herd-suggestion is always in a haze. Herd-suggestion is all for tradition, authority; science has for its very essence the exercise of free thought. So long as we will not take the trouble to know exactly and intimately, we may not — must not — choose… We must follow custom; we must accept the mandates of [those] who enforce tradition. […] Science opens wide the doors that turned so slowly on tradition’s hinges, and opens them on clean, quiet places where we breathe larger air… It is well to remember our debt to science — our inward and spiritual as well as material debt. Art by Rockwell Kent , 1919. (Available as a print and as stationery cards .) And yet, Harrison argues, the heretic needs more than science — the heretic needs humanity. She writes: Science broke the binding spell of herd-suggestion. For that great boon let us now and ever bless and praise her holy name. She cleared the collective haze, she drew sharp distinctions, appealing to individual actual experience, to individual powers of reasoning. But by neither individual sense — perception nor ratiocination alone do we live. Our keenest emotional life is through the herd, and hence it was that, at the close of the last century, the flame of scientific hope, the glory of scientific individualism that had blazed so brightly, somehow died down and left a strange chill. Man rose up from the banquet of reason and law unfed. He hungered half unconsciously for the herd. It seemed an impasse: on the one side orthodoxy, tradition, authority, practical slavery; on the other science, individual freedom, reason, and an aching loneliness. […] We live now just at the transition moment; we have broken with the old, we have not quite adjusted ourselves to the new. It is not so much the breaking with the old faiths that makes us restless as the living in a new social structure. Art by Olivier Tallec from Louis I, King of the Sheep At the root of this new social structure, she observes, is not the old cult of homogeneity but the rec

articles.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
articles.snippet: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool): Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script , thanks Claude): Ladybird (72925) [240 MB] └── Hub (72926) [61 MB] ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB] ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB] ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB] ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB] ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB] ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB] ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB] ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB] ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB] ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB] ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB] ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB] ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB] └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB] Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site). I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool . It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too. The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite , which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error: undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages') I filed an issue about this , then found a FIXME annotation in the source code. The October explosion The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI , describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex. Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months: That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements. This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark , they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari! How did they do that? Coding agents: Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing . I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October. Should you use Ladybird? Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser: This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts. I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings. articles.title: How does Orchard AI fit into John Deere’s technology portfolio?
articles.snippet: John Deere said Orchard AI’s plant-level crop insights will bring more precision to its technology. | Source: John Deere John Deere has acquired Orchard AI, a San Francisco-based company that develops crop intelligence systems for high-value crop growers. Orchard AI uses vehicle-mounted, AI-powered cameras to capture data for every individual tree, vine, or plant across a farm. The system analyzes hundreds of images per tree, giving growers a detailed view of crop conditions. It also gives accurate yield estimates, precise fruit counts, fruit size and color data, canopy measurements, and more. The company also offers its FruitScope software platform, which enables growers to visualize and use this data to make more informed farm management decisions. “We started Orchard AI to give our growers the crop intelligence they need to help them farm more profitably and sustainably than ever before,” said Charlie Wu, the CEO of Orchard AI. “Everything that we do is in service of our growers, and joining John Deere lets us accelerate our mission. Together, we aim to bring the benefits of AI -powered crop intelligence to every grower across the globe.” Submit your innovation now! John Deere said the deal strengthens its ability to help growers make more informed decisions throughout the growing season. The company plans to combine Orchard AI’s plant-level crop insights with its own expertise in precision agriculture , equipment, and farm technology. “Everything we do starts with helping our customers succeed,” said Tim Marquis, the director of Farm Systems Innovation at John Deere . “This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field. By bringing these capabilities together, we have an opportunity to help growers make more informed decisions across their operations and get more value from the technology they already rely on.” Inside John Deere’s growing technology portfolio By combining Orchard AI’s crop intelligence with Deere’s equipment and technology., the company said growers can better understand what their trees need and act at the right time. This acquisition is part of John Deere’s increasing focus on integrating advanced technologies into its portfolio. John Deere’s recent journey in acquiring robotics and AI companies started in 2017 when it acquired Blue River Technology for $305 million. Blue River Technology developed computer vision and machine learning technology that enables agricultural sprayers to identify weeds and selectively apply herbicides. A few years later, it acquired Bear Flag Robotics for $250 million. Bear Flag retrofitted autonomy stacks onto existing tractors. The company used cameras, lidar, and radar technology to give tractors redundant, 360-degree situational awareness on farms. In January 2022, John Deere unveiled its first fully autonomous tractor, which incorporated some of the technologies it acquired over the years. The machine combined Deere’s 8R tractor, TruSet-enabled chisel plow, and GPS guidance system with new advanced technologies, Deere said at the time. After releasing its autonomous tractor, John Deere continued making acquisitions to fill out its technology stack. It acquired intellectual property from Light, which specializes in depth sensing and camera-based perception for autonomous vehicles, in May 2022. In 2023, John Deere acquired SparkAI, a New York-based startup that developed human-in-the-loop technology to help robots resolve edge cases in real-time. Most recently, the company acquired GUSS Automation, a developer of autonomous sprayers, in 2025. The companies had already been working together for years, with John Deere being an exclusive provider of GUSS sprayers. The acquisition indicated John Deere’s interest in high-value crops, such as orchards and vineyards, which GUSS specializes in. articles.title: Management consulting is not a thin wrapper on intelligence
articles.snippet: By Rod Moshtagi and Sayash Kapoor. Moshtagi is a researcher at the Harvard Kennedy School and was previously a senior associate at PwC. In summer 2026, he was a GovAI fellow advised by Kapoor, and the research for this essay began as part of the fellowship. Many discussions of AI’s economic impact rest on the implicit assumption that most knowledge work is a “thin wrapper” on intelligence. In this view, the main job of a knowledge worker is to process information. Once AI can match the quality of expert responses in a domain, it should be able to take over most of the work in that domain. Management consulting is a compelling example. The visible outputs of consultants, such as research summaries, slide decks, and financial models, primarily comprise processing information , work that AI already excels at. If the main function of a consulting firm is to provide information, AI looks like an existential threat. Many commentators have drawn this conclusion. In 2025, The Free Press warned that “ the consulting crash is coming .” An analyst told Axios that consulting firms are “ going to run out of work .” In February 2026, the CEO of the AI startup Mercor predicted that “in the coming two years, we’re going to have chatbots that are as good as the best consulting firm.” In this essay, we argue that apocalyptic predictions about consulting misunderstand both the value of consulting firms and how new technologies change the demand for consulting. We analyze different value propositions of consulting with an eye towards how AI affects them, provide a framework for thinking about the impacts of general-purpose technologies (including AI) on consulting, and recommend how consulting firms can adapt to AI. We make three main arguments: Part 1. Apocalyptic predictions about consulting misunderstand what clients pay for. We break down consulting firms’ work into five sources of value. Analysis is the most visible, but clients also pay for judgment, coordination, credibility, and accountability. AI has improved dramatically at analysis. But training AI to have judgment (such as deciding what questions to ask and interpreting evidence) has proven harder. As AI capabilities improve, that might change. But even if AI gets good at judgment, companies still need to persuade competing managers within the firm to agree on recommendations, especially when those recommendations negatively affect them. They need to give key decisions credibility with decision makers such as the board. And they need someone to answer for the results when things go wrong. Consulting firms provide the coordination, credibility, and accountability for all of these. Part 2. Clients’ AI integration needs are creating demand for consulting. Past general-purpose technologies, such as business computing and the web, did not just make existing work cheaper. They changed the nature of what clients needed help with, and in the process, they created new work for outside experts, including consultants. Early evidence shows that AI is doing the same. Realizing the benefits of AI requires organizational transformation, which is increasing the demand for consulting companies. Improvements in AI’s cybersecurity capabilities have also led to organizations taking cyber defense more seriously, and consulting firms are helping them strategize and implement defenses. Part 3. For consulting firms to capture this demand, they need to change how they operate. Our analysis in the previous parts does not mean that today’s consulting firms are safe. Clients’ own teams will compete for some of the new demand that we predict will arise due to AI. AI companies are building deployment businesses of their own, even as they sign partnerships with consulting firms. We argue that for consulting firms to successfully adapt to AI, they need to make changes to their operating model: building know-how that clients lack, developing in-house AI expertise and partnering with AI companies on deployment, and staying neutral across model providers. Table of contents Part 1: Apocalyptic predictions about consulting misunderstand what clients pay for Strategic judgment is hard to train into AI AI can produce advice, but not the coordination, credibility, and accountability needed to implement it Part 2: Predictions of consulting’s collapse ignore how general-purpose technologies change demand Past general-purpose technologies created new kinds of work for consultants Even for the work most directly affected by AI, such as research and analysis, lower demand isn’t a given. Analysis that every competitor can buy is no longer a competitive advantage Adopting AI is an organizational problem, not a software purchase Part 3: AI creates new demand for consultants, but consulting firms will have to change to capture it Consulting firms need to offer experience and skills that clients cannot build or sustain in-house Consulting firms need to adapt to AI faster than AI companies learn change management Consulting firms need to stay neutral across AI model providers Conclusion Part 1: Apocalyptic predictions about consulting misunderstand what clients pay for Clients pay for more than just the visible outputs of consulting. Building on previous analyses of the value that consulting firms provide , we categorize the five sources of value for consulting firms: Analysis and research: The visible outputs of consulting. This comprises building reports, financial models, and presentations to advise client companies on the problems they hire consulting firms to solve. Judgment: Deciding the scope and focus areas for the analysis, interpreting the evidence, and recommending a course of action for the client’s needs. Coordination: Reconciling competing interests across the company, securing cooperation and buy-in from important stakeholders, and managing the implementation of a decision. Credibility: Giving a recommendation weight due to the consulting firm’s expertise, reputation, and relation

articles.title: Merry Making: Play, Build and Create With NVIDIA Technologies This Holiday Season
articles.snippet: The elves don’t have to be the only ones busy in the workshop this holiday season. With the lights twinkling and the gift wrap out, it’s the perfect time to give someone — or yourself — a spark to take a hobby to the next level. For some, that means diving into a new game. For others, it’s video editing or even building a robot. NVIDIA technologies offer something for everyone on Santa’s list. Read on to unwrap the details. Make Time for One More Game With the holiday break here, everyone can be online to score bragging rights or explore a world that’s only been seen in video game trailers. For some players, an upgrade means a desktop that brings out the detail in every scene. For others, it’s a laptop they can take along when visiting family, or a way to play in the cloud on a device they already own. The right setup depends on where and what to play: GeForce RTX 50 Series laptops and desktops power the action. Built on the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, they feature fifth-generation Tensor Cores and fourth-generation RT Cores for AI-enhanced graphics, detailed ray-traced worlds and high frames-per-second gaming. NVIDIA RTX Spark PCs combine RTX graphics with NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform on a single superchip, bringing decades of NVIDIA innovation to slim, premium laptops and compact desktops on the familiar Windows platform. One PC can handle every workflow, from accelerated creation and immersive gaming to powerful local AI — with a variety of designs and all-day battery life. See games in a new light with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology, which boosts performance and enhances image quality. The newest feature, DLSS 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, infuses scenes with lifelike lighting and materials in supported games. Get a glimpse of NBA 2K27 with DLSS 5 . NVIDIA Reflex and G-SYNC make gameplay more responsive and fluid. Reflex reduces system latency in supported games, while G-SYNC displays use variable refresh rates to deliver smooth, tear-free gaming. The GeForce NOW cloud gaming service enables playing top titles anywhere. Stream supported games on compatible laptops, TVs, handhelds and more. Connect to supported game stores to play owned PC games, with more than 4,500 titles available across the service. Make Something Worth Sharing For creators with a project that’s been on the backburner, the right gift this season can be the push to finally make it happen. Maybe it’s holiday clips becoming a short film, a snowy scene coming together in 3D or a livestream that brings friends across time zones to the same virtual table. Creators can use NVIDIA systems — such as GeForce RTX 50 Series and RTX Spark devices — to keep up with the workflows, along with NVIDIA Studio tools and technologies for AI acceleration. Studio Drivers support video editing, 3D design and livestreaming. In supported applications, faster processing gives more room to experiment and refine. Build a Robot That Thinks Every robot starts somewhere. This season, it could be under the tree. Building a robot is an experiment in teaching a device to see or sense its surroundings. A first project might be as simple as using a camera to identify a candy cane or a gingerbread man, then moving on to an app that probes what the camera sees. Testing brings new questions. Can the robot recognize the candy cane under twinkling lights? Can it tell a frosted gingerbread man from an unfrosted one? Each experiment leaves more to improve and explore. The NVIDIA Jetson edge AI platform provides the hardware and software to build projects like these. It combines compact computers with the NVIDIA JetPack software development kit to help makers build robots, autonomous machines and intelligent devices. A Jetson Developer Kit is a gift to explore computer vision, generative AI and multimodal robot control, with the option to add cameras and sensors suited to various projects. AI runs directly on the device, processing information from its surroundings. When ready to take a prototype further, production systems powered by Jetson modules provide a path to deployment. See how Microduck comes to life with NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super , bringing together robot movement, visual understanding and natural-language interaction. With Hermes Agent and NVIDIA Cosmos, developers can explore how AI connects everyday requests with actions in the physical world. Bring an SO-101 arm to life with NVIDIA Jetson Orin and explore agentic robotics. Give OpenClaw a simple request, and watch it plan the steps, call NVIDIA tools and check the results. OpenShell runs the agent securely in a sandbox, controlling its access to models and robot tools. Based on ASPIRE skills, the system reuses lessons from past attempts to guide future tasks. Build a robot companion that chats, moves and understands what it sees, with NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt and Cosmos open models running locally on Jetson Orin Nano 8GB. For more advanced projects, explore vision language action models and world action models to enable increasingly sophisticated robotic behaviors — beyond simple perception and predefined actions toward understanding natural language instructions, reasoning, planning multistep tasks and interacting with the physical world. Dive into setup guides and project tutorials in Jetson AI Lab . Whether it’s a gaming upgrade, a creative project or a first robot, the right tools can open up new possibilities well beyond the holidays. Explore NVIDIA’s holiday lineup for gamers, creators and makers.

articles.title: NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang after 11-day absence
articles.snippet: So much for robotics being in its post-Jensen Huang era . Just 11 days after his resignation amid allegations of personal misconduct and concerns about potential national security risks involving China, NVIDIA has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO. The company announced today that its board of directors unanimously voted to bring Huang back . Huang also returns to NVIDIA’s board, effective immediately. NVIDIA said the board was satisfied with Huang’s candor and ability to lead the company. It also consulted with senior U.S. government officials before determining that his reinstatement poses no national security risk. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey Jones, NVIDIA’s board chair. The decision marks a dramatic reversal for NVIDIA. During the company’s earnings call on Nov. 17, Jones explicitly ruled out bringing Huang back, saying the board had unanimously accepted his resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. Just six days later, the board unanimously voted to restore Huang to the position he had held since co-founding NVIDIA in 1993. The reversal followed growing pressure from President Donald Trump, NVIDIA employees, investors and prominent technology executives. Trump publicly supported Huang’s potential return on Nov. 16, saying he would not object to his reinstatement. On Sunday, Nov. 22, Trump again urged NVIDIA’s board to bring Huang back. Submit your innovation now! Meanwhile, a “Stand With Jensen” petition attracted more than 200,000 signatures, including support from current and former NVIDIA employees, investors and technology leaders such as Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. NVIDIA also faced considerable financial uncertainty following Huang’s departure, with its market value falling sharply and questions emerging about who could replace an executive who had led the company for more than three decades. It remains unclear precisely what persuaded the board to reverse course. NVIDIA did not identify which government officials were consulted or disclose what information they provided. The company also did not say whether the public campaign influenced its decision. Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO following Huang’s resignation, will continue in her role as chief financial officer. Jones will remain board chair. “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.” Huang also thanked NVIDIA’s board, employees, shareholders and his family for their support, adding, “I can’t wait to get back to work.” National security investigation continues Huang’s reinstatement does not end the scrutiny surrounding his departure. NVIDIA said an independent board committee will continue investigating reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The committee has retained independent counsel, and Huang has committed to cooperating fully with the investigation. NVIDIA also recently established a National Security and Export Control Committee composed entirely of independent directors. The committee will oversee trade compliance and national security risks, with support from legal counsel and national security specialists. The company did not provide a timeline for completing its internal investigation. Huang’s return brings back robotics’ biggest champion Huang’s return also restores one of the robotics industry’s most visible advocates to the helm of a company that has become increasingly important to robot development. As The Robot Report previously examined , Huang has spent years promoting robotics and physical AI as major long-term opportunities. He has regularly featured robots in NVIDIA’s keynote presentations and helped bring greater attention to the industry’s potential. Under his leadership, NVIDIA expanded its robotics portfolio with technologies including Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, GR00T foundation models, Isaac ROS and Jetson computing platforms. NVIDIA has also invested in and partnered with robotics developers, including humanoid companies, as it works to establish its technology as a foundation for robot training, simulation and deployment. articles.title: Import AI 482: Huawei kernel benchmarks; airborne drone detection; and a national lab’s AI science benchmark
articles.snippet: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. Subscribe now Chinese researchers optimize Huawei chips with a kernel improvement benchmark: …AscendGYM will help China do its own form of RSI… Researchers with the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, a Chinese research organization, have built and released AscendGYM, “a kernel optimization benchmark for Ascend NPUs”. The purpose of AscendGYM is to make it easier to use AI to develop custom kernels for Ascend chips from Huawei – especially important given the export controls that prevent Chinese organizations from acquiring frontier Western semiconductors and forcing them onto Huawei. What AscendGYM does and contains: The goal is for AscendGYM to be the best way to evaluate the efficacy of AI-designed kernels as well as design new ones. The software is meant to help researchers answer this question: “Given a correct kernel implementation, can the specific agent further improve its performance for a target workload within an acceptable budget while preserving correctness?,” they write. “AscendGYM evaluates performance across multiple deployment cases, the best achievable performance for specific shapes and scenarios, and the optimization cost required to obtain these gains. Together, these dimensions characterize cross-case applicability, shape specialization, and optimization efficiency.” The software includes the AscendForge evaluation environment, which provides unified interfaces for “compilation, correctness checking, performance measurement, and feedback”. How well can AI models optimize Ascend chips? In tests, the single best model is Opus 5, followed by GPT-5.6, followed by GLM-5.3. They test out models in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode; Claude Code yields the best absolute scores, and GLM does well in it, while GPT does well in Codex. Opus 5 is more token hungry and GPT-5.6 more token efficient. Why this matters – ingredients for Chinese RSI: For AI systems to be able to build themselves, they need to be able to develop and improve the software that is used for their own training and inference. Software like AscendGYM will be an essential ingredient for allowing China to rapidly improve the efficiency of its own compute substrates. The software will also have a bearing on export controls, where it provides a route to improve the performance of Chinese chips and close the gap with Western alternatives. Read more: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs (arXiv) . Get AscendGYM here : AscendGYM (GitHub) . *** Lawrence Livermore scientists test out if AI scientists can communicate uncertainty about experimental results: …Can AI systems be appropriately conservative?… “An agent that reports a confident wrong number is worse than one that reports honest uncertainty, because nobody downstream can tell the difference,” write researchers from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in a new paper that tests out how reliably AI systems can give accurate score ranges even when dealing with uncertainty. Testing for uncertainty: The paper introduces SciResearch-Eval, “an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator”. The novel part of this eval is that “an agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth”. What they studied: They give AI agents a common materials science task – measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating a sample and fitting a heat-conduction model to its temperature response. “An agent receives a sample of unknown material, a simulator of heat conduction through it, one heating experiment, and budgets: four more experiments it designs, compute for simulations and fits, and a cap on actions. It must report the sample’s conductivity, heat capacity and rear heat-transfer coefficient with 95% intervals, and predict a measurement it may not run,” they write. “Hidden from the agent, the simulator may be under-resolved, physically wrong (the real sample has temperature-dependent conductivity, a glued joint, front-face radiation, or heat loss through its sides), or adequate but fed uninformative data”. Results – only the most powerful frontier models can do this : “When the simulator is missing real physics, only GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 are reliable at default settings; the Claude 5.5 models recover only at their highest reasoning setting, and older and open-weight models not at all.” These models are able to do well by automatically trying to measure where the simulator is accurate and where it is less accurate then bases their estimates on that, making them more resilient to the different ways the simulator gets broken in experiments. Why this matters – real scientists are careful, and so are powerful models: Papers like this are further indications that we’re entering an era of AI-driven science. Though many of today’s models can assist in scientific experiments, as this paper shows only a couple of the powerful models at the frontier are able to operate with such appropriate autonomous skepticism and inherent attendance to the scientific method that they can deal with unanticipated breaks in their equipment. This is both an indication of the science advancement to come and a sign of how the most powerful models are exhibiting more and more of an ability to generalize and make themselves robust to perturbations in their environment. articles.title: The two-sided power of subscription
articles.snippet: You can get this blog delivered to you every day, for free. The details are here: https://seths.blog/subscribe/ You can subscribe to streaming channels like Dropout (a new unscripted game show every time), MHz or RetroCrush (rare anime). You can subscribe to Apocabox if you’re a prepper in need of more stuff, or History by Mail, which will send you facsimiles of historical documents. And of course, you can subscribe to Elle Cordova on YouTube. But why? In an instant-on, find-what-you-want world, why spend the time or the money? Two things happen. The immediate one is that subscriptions are an asset and a signal. The creator of the product or service is more likely to do the work you seek if you give them a reliable way to get the work out there. This is why Google and others fight so hard to break the connection–they want to own your attention instead. The long-term one is that the arrival of your subscription is a prompt. It shows up on its schedule, not yours. It’s not just a reminder, it creates a pattern. Seventy years ago, a stack of Readers Digest or National Geographic magazines was a signal to visitors and to the homeowner as well. The same for the New Yorker twenty years ago. And not just for the cartoons. If you’re already a subscriber to the blog, thanks. If it hasn’t been getting to you, please check your promo folder or resubscribe. And mostly, please forward this to someone who might want to join in. When your colleagues subscribe too, you have a shared prompt to riff on. Bonus: My RSS reader is a treasure box of hundreds of subscriptions. The blog posts and the occasional XKCD have enriched my life and knowing that more will come opens up anticipation and creativity on my part. When in doubt, subscribe.

articles.title: How to Bear Your Desolations
articles.snippet: “You may have to break your heart, but it isn’t nothing to know even one moment alive.” The morning after a relationship of depth and significance long bending under the weight of its own complexity had finally broken with an exhausted thud, I opened the kiln to discover a month’s worth of pottery shattered — two pieces had exploded, the shrapnel ruining the rest. All that centering, all that glazing, all the hours of pressing letterforms into the wet clay — all of it in shiny shards. And meanwhile spring was breaking outside and a little girl in bright blue rain boots was jumping in a puddle, smashing the reflections of the clouds with savage joy. And I thought, this is all there is: breaking, breaking apart, breaking open. Breaking alive. Card from An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days , also available as a stand-alone print and as greeting cards . It is not an easy assignment, being alive. Coming awake from the stupor of near-living that lulls us through our days, awake to the knowledge that on the other side of the neighborhood ICE trucks are handcuffing people and on the other side of the planet children are dying in gunfire, while outside the first birds of spring are singing and everywhere people are falling in love and in some faraway mountain village a shepherd is singing under a thousand stars. And somehow, somehow, all of it has to cohere into a single world in which we, in all our incohesion, must live this single life. Ellen Bass reckons with all of this in her splendid poem “Any Common Desolation,” originally published in The Academy of American Poets’ poem-a-day newsletter and later included in James Crews’s lifeline of an anthology How to Love the World: Poems of Gratitude and Hope ( public library ), shared here with Ellen’s blessing. ANY COMMON DESOLATION by Ellen Bass can be enough to make you look up at the yellowed leaves of the apple tree, the few that survived the rains and frost, shot with late afternoon sun. They glow a deep orange-gold against a blue so sheer, a single bird would rip it like silk. You may have to break your heart, but it isn’t nothing to know even one moment alive. The sound of an oar in an oarlock or a ruminant animal tearing grass. The smell of grated ginger. The ruby neon of the liquor store sign. Warm socks. You remember your mother, her precision a ceremony, as she gathered the white cotton, slipped it over your toes, drew up the heel, turned the cuff. A breath can uncoil as you walk across your own muddy yard, the big dipper pouring night down over you, and everything you dread, all you can’t bear, dissolves and, like a needle slipped into your vein — that sudden rush of the world. Complement with Henry James on how to stop waiting and start living and Hermann Hesse on how to be more alive , then revisit Ellen’s magnificent poem “How to Apologize.” And if you are looking to break your poetry open, I couldn’t recommend her Living Room Craft Talks more heartily. donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). articles.title: Earning enrollment
articles.snippet: The single most important factor in learning is whether the student is actively engaged in the process. Eyes bright, hands up, curious and eager for the insight on the other side. Ask any teacher–students like this are a delight. The same is true for the work of professionals–from doctors to cashiers. Wanting to be there, open to interaction, eager for change–these are so obvious that we usually overlook them. In fact, the real work of anyone building an institution of learning or an organization that seeks to serve is simple: create the conditions for people to choose to actively participate. The lazy method is to wait for the self-motivated and take credit for the results when they show up. The hard work is to build the systems and culture that makes it more likely that you’re attracting, motivating and transforming the people who want to go where you can take them. Everything else is a bonus.

articles.title: The Most Powerful Attitude You Can Take Toward Your Life and the Life of the World
articles.snippet: “This fluke, single, huge, cross-indexed, thermodynamic experiment of a story that the world has been inventing to tell itself at bedtime is still in embryo. It’s not even the outline of a synopsis of notes toward a rough draft yet.” Perhaps the gravest violence we can do to ourselves is to live out our lives believing the world to be a fixity handed down to us by the authorities of history and life to be a matter of taking immutable givens. Daring to believe otherwise — to believe that even our smallest purposeful action alters the monolith of reality in some subtle, meaningful way — is an act of courage and resistance, an act of immense vulnerability to the possibility of disappointment, vulnerability the commonest cowering from which is cynicism. James Baldwin knew this when he issued his lyrical and impassioned insistence that “nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed,” that “we made the world we’re living in and we have to make it over.” Hannah Arendt knew this when she considered how we invent ourselves and reinvent the world , observing that “the smallest act in the most limited circumstances bears the seed of boundlessness, because one deed, and sometimes one word, suffices to change every constellation.” Art by Dorothy Lathrop , 1922. (Available as a print and as stationery cards .) Richard Powers knew this when he made his contribution to Take My Advice: Letters to the Next Generation from People Who Know a Thing or Two ( public library ) — artist and writer James L. Harmon’s wonderful 2002 anthology of wisdom from stellar minds , a decade in the constellating, envisioned as an eclectic contemporary counterpart to Rilke’s timeless Letters to a Young Poet , which had moved Harmon deeply when he first encountered it as a young man. Two decades before Powers won the Pulitzer Prize for his sylvan symphony The Overstory , he echoes Seamus Heaney’s exhortation to always remain “true to your own secret knowledge” and writes: Never forget what you were born knowing. That this fluke, single, huge, cross-indexed, thermodynamic experiment of a story that the world has been inventing to tell itself at bedtime is still in embryo. It’s not even the outline of a synopsis of notes toward a rough draft yet. Buy the plot some time. 19th-century Solar System quilt by Ellen Harding Baker, embroidered over the course of seven years as a teaching tool in an era when women were barred from higher education in science and a fraction of the presently known Solar System objects were known. (Available as a print and a face mask .) We buy the plot time with the currency of our conscious choices, the grand and the mundane alike — the daily actions that make us what we are, the people who make the world what it is. Powers writes: Take in more, consume less, recycle everything; book-keep all hidden costs; find out where you have been set down; lobby for a smaller market; get rid of your car and travel as widely as you can (yeah, walk: what the hell); try to say a little more than you mean; carry a pocket encyclopedia (ask for one without packaging) and when the entry on “Diffusion Constant” says, “for more information, see ‘Pastry War,'” see “Pastry War.” This latter sentiment might at first appear dated in the hindsight of two decades, in the epoch of Wikipedia. But it is actually all the more insightful and urgent today, for the quiet act of resistance at its heart has grown all the harder. What I most rue about the internet is that, for all its riches of readily accessible information, it has altered the texture of human curiosity, vanquishing that wondrous encyclopedic feeling of learning about the thing you hadn’t known you didn’t know but now greatly enjoy knowing. Somewhere along the way of choices being made for us by an insular tribe of technologists, discovery was sacrificed at the altar of search as algorithms perfected the mechanics of giving us more and more of what we already knew we wanted and believed, rendering the mind itself more and more a fixity. Would you be Googling “Pastry War” now had I not made this point about a point Richard Powers made long ago on the pages of a yellowing book I pulled from my bookshelf by some incomputable human impulse this morning? Those choices matter, Powers reminds us, even at the smallest scale. There is no fulcrum too small for the lever of change to lift from, but the lift must begin with lucidity. He writes: Take a full look at the worst. Acknowledge the figures: the runaway birthdates, the irreversible extinctions and ruined habitats, the meaningless economies fueled by waste, the exported shooting wars and their cover causes… Then work at whatever comes to hand. Useful or not, it makes no difference. Jumping in is the only calculus that emergency ever allows. Complement with Rebecca Solnit on rewriting the world’s broken stories with our actions , then revisit What If — a wondrous French picture-book about daring to imagine and build a different world for the children of tomorrow. donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). articles.title: The Only Three Distinctions Between People
articles.snippet: It may be that consciousness evolved to sieve the relevant from the incomprehensible allness of all there is, to parse the world into concepts and find an organizing principle for the chaos of them. Our cognitive inheritance is a restless yearning to fathom how things cohere and where they belong, a yearning we have given shape to in laws and labels, weights and balances, hierarchies and categories. It has served us well, this instinct to categorize in order to contain, giving us music, the laws of planetary motion, and democracy. But it also pulsates beneath every ism we have ever invented, beneath every stereotype and every genocide, beneath every algorithm that reduces us to variables then adds them up to sell the sum of who we are, beneath all the parcels of preconception we trade daily and mistake the barter a for a genuine encounter with one another. Two centuries ago, Nathaniel Hawthorne (July 4, 1804–May 19, 1864) offered a pithy, powerful antidote to this double-edged instinct. Nathaniel Hawthorne In a notebook entry from the autumn of 1836, penned shortly after his moving meditation on how not to waste your life , Hawthorne proposes a revision of our standard classification system for humanity — one that would rehumanize us with the simple awareness that what binds us is infinitely stronger than what divides us or by what affiliations we divide ourselves. He writes: A new classification of society is to be instituted. Instead of rich and poor, high and low, they are to be classed, — First, by their sorrows: for instance, whenever there are any, whether in fair mansion or hovel, who are mourning the loss of relations and friends, and who wear black, whether the cloth be coarse or superfine, they are to make one class. Secondly, all who have the same maladies, whether they lie under damask canopies or on straw pallets or in the wards of hospitals, they are to form one class. Thirdly, all who are guilty of the same sins, whether the world knows them or not; whether they languish in prison, looking forward to the gallows, or walk honored among men, they also form a class. Then proceed to generalize and classify the whole world together, as none can claim utter exemption from either sorrow, sin, or disease; and if they could, yet Death, like a great parent, comes and sweeps all through one darksome portal, — all his children. What a magnificent way to remember that down where the spirit meets the bone , we are all facing the same struggle: to feel safe, to feel seen, to wrest some meaning and some marvel from the ephemeral bewilderment of being alive. donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). articles.title: The manufacturing data gap holding back physical AI
articles.snippet: Robotics and physical AI companies have raised nearly $48 billion so far in 2026 , but the rollout of fully autonomous machines in industrial settings isn’t a given. For robots to step beyond controlled environments onto the manufacturing floor, they need real-world data to learn from. Most production facilities aren’t set up to provide it. Consider the welding process. For a robot to improve its technique autonomously, it needs to understand how changes in welding angle, travel speed, workpiece position, and other key parameters affect the finished result. Experienced technicians develop this understanding through years of hands-on experience, but much of that knowledge isn’t captured in a form robotics partners can use to train autonomous systems. Similar gaps exist in other manufacturing processes where technicians rely on experience to make adjustments that aren’t consistently documented. Manufacturers looking to deploy physical AI need to close this data gap. Without information connecting process decisions to production outcomes, even sophisticated robotic systems may struggle to adapt to changing conditions. These limitations could prevent manufacturers from achieving the efficiency and quality improvements they expect from physical AI. Why industrial data remains a barrier to physical AI Manufacturers already collect extensive operational data, but much of it was never structured for autonomous learning. Sometimes it is collected and never even reviewed at all! Relevant contextual information often sits in separate systems. A machine may record operating parameters while a quality management system captures inspection results, making it difficult to connect process decisions with finished-part quality. Manufacturing leaders are increasingly aware that these silos are an obstacle. According to the Manufacturing Leadership Council’s 2026 Smart Factories and Digital Production Survey , 37% of surveyed manufacturers cited a lack of data interoperability as a major roadblock to implementing their smart factory strategies, up from 22% in 2025. However, improving interoperability alone won’t get robots the data they need to learn. Manufacturers also need to ensure that production records can be tied to measurable quality outcomes. Submit your innovation now! 3 ways manufacturers can prepare for physical AI Preparing a factory for physical AI requires more than collecting additional data or connecting disparate systems. Manufacturers need to understand what information their robotic systems will rely on, how that data reflects real production conditions and whether it can help systems make reliable adjustments over time. Addressing these questions early, in collaboration with robotics partners, can help manufacturers identify gaps in their existing infrastructure and focus investments where they’ll have the greatest impact. Here are three areas to prioritize before deployment. 1. Capture data that reflects real production conditions Begin by identifying the production conditions your robotic systems need to recognize and respond to. Focus on capturing the complex interactions between the process parameters and quality outcomes to show how planned and unplanned changes in materials or equipment performance affect the finished product. Consider metal additive manufacturing , where factors like powder (or wire) characteristics, processing temperatures, and environmental conditions can influence a component’s final properties and characteristic defect structure. Connecting these variables with inspection results gives your robotics partners a clearer picture of which conditions contribute to defects or variations in quality. You can then use that information to train systems to recognize changing production conditions and develop more realistic simulations for testing their responses. 2. Connect data across the entire production process The data you capture won’t have much value if it remains isolated within individual machines or production stages. The next step is to create a digital thread that connects production conditions with inspection results and finished-part quality. I’ve seen this challenge firsthand in advanced manufacturing. AI-based image recognition is becoming table stakes for assessing quality within metal additive manufacturing printers, while downstream equipment such as heat-treatment furnaces may be far more difficult to integrate into the same system. Lior Susan of Eclipse rightly says: “If your physical asset isn’t generating real-time operational data, it’s a dead asset.” The disconnect creates gaps in the production history of a component, making it harder to understand how subsequent processing affects its final properties. To close those gaps, you need to connect equipment and quality management systems that weren’t designed to communicate. Start by identifying the data needed for a specific robotic application, then work with technology partners to establish consistent part identifiers and link process records to inspection results in a true digital thread. By starting with a targeted application, you can build the data connections to support physical AI without having to overhaul your entire production infrastructure at once. Submit your innovation now! 3. Build feedback loops around quality and repeatability Finally, establish how autonomous systems will be evaluated and when human oversight is required. Work with your robotics partners to identify which process adjustments can be made automatically and how the system will determine whether those changes improved production outcomes. In medical device manufacturing, for example, regulatory requirements often mandate validation of production processes to ensure consistent product quality. Changes to those processes may require additional testing and revalidation, limiting how freely AI systems can modify production parameters. articles.title: MiB: David Eichhorn, NISA Investment Advisors CEO, Head of Investment Strategies
articles.snippet: This week, I speak with David Eichhorn , Chief Executive Officer and Head of Investment Strategies at NISA Investment Advisors , a 100% employee-owned asset manager based in Clayton, Missouri, overseeing $483 billion in assets. He holds a BS.BA in finance and mathematics from Washington University in St. Louis, spent three years at J.P. Morgan Investment Management, and joined NISA in 1999. He became CEO at the end of 2020. We discuss his early career and return to St. Louis, how NISA has remained employee-owned and managed its leadership transition from founder Jess Yawitz, and how the firm builds liability-driven investment strategies for institutional clients. We also cover the firm’s systematic equity strategy, the current yield environment, and the risks and benefits of private credit, including the dangers of private credit making its way into pension funds and 401(k)s. A list of his current reading/favorite books is here ; A transcript of our conversation is available here Tuesday. You can stream and download our full conversation, including any podcast extras, on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , YouTube , and Bloomberg . All of our earlier podcasts on your favorite pod hosts can be found here . Next week, we speak with Holly MacDonald , Chief Executive Officer of Bessemer Trust , the privately owned multifamily office founded in 1907 by Carnegie Steel co-founder Henry Phipps. Previously, she served as Chief Operating Officer, overseeing technology, operations, and family office management while continuing to lead the investment team. Bessemer today oversees $250 billion in assets for about 3,000 clients across 22 offices, serving as trustee/co-trustee on over 15,000 trusts. They report a class-leading 99% ten-year client asset retention rate.
