articles.title: Emergent properties
articles.snippet: No system stays the way it began, and all systems evolve characteristics that surprise us. The rise of the automobile system led to roads and gas stations, of course, but also parking lots, drive-through fast food restaurants and drunk driving. The TV industrial complex was based on the effectiveness of advertising, and the ads that were among the most profitable were for beverages and snack foods, which made those industries ever more efficient and led to convenience foods and also widespread obesity. And factory farming feeds billions of people. Competitive pressures led to a rise in fertilizer use and a destruction of topsoil, which also dramatically shifts the climate. Any complex system will soon surprise us with its unanticipated effects.

articles.title: [AINews] Riemann Hypothesis proved...twice independently
articles.snippet: Within a few hours of each other ( timeline ), two mathematicians claimed independent proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics ( Scientific American ). Levent Alpöge of Anthropic first made his Claude-driven proof in a note released with Lean code (1.3GB worth, ~250,000 page equivalent) rather than a full paper. Elliot Glazer confirms that the formalized statement is GRH and puts the chance of a Lean bug well under 1%. So if it finishes compiling with no extra axioms, it is probably correct, and no human will ever have read all of it… …prompting Alessandro Masullo to release his 940 page, 100% human , work in progress proof he had been working on for the last 12 years (and had been undergoing secret manual review and revision per Kevin Hartnett ). This is the third in the trilogy of frontier math breakthroughs, following from the Navier Stokes solutions and the Quasi-Riemann bounding, but it doesn’t feel over. OpenAI's September Navier-Stokes claim is still the cautionary tale: critics argued that its Lean proof did not match the natural-language result. Both AI-claimed Millennium Prize results will take years to verify. Apart from the incredible accomplishment of the most famous problem in mathematics, one cannot miss the contrast that the AI-written solution is probably correct but incomprehensible , and the other solution is probably technically incorrect but understandable . Sponsored by Agentfield.AI Open models are ready. Most coding harnesses aren’t. On DeepSWE, CodeAF finished #1 of ten on the same open model, ahead of Claude Code, at the lowest cost per fix. Try CodeAF ! As Levent eloquently put it: “ Claude far outpaced me near the finish line . No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” This also ties into other AI themes we’ve covered on the podcast and on this newsletter: The nature of Slop : Levent says “ I am presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics. It being obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of "slop", I decided to only present Lean . ” One of the key tenets of the No Slop Manifesto is that you should understand what you ship (“ Slop is when we put less effort into producing something than we ask the consumer to spend understanding it. ”). And yet, this giant pile of Lean is verifiably correct and is incredibly significant in human history. Should we have delayed its release by a decade simply because we didn’t understand every single bit of it? Weak to Strong alignment : the typical experience of using agents is Strong to Weak - we are general intelligences guiding not-as-smart AI to do things we know how to do well. We also often expect AI to automate most work “within distribution”, and expect it to run into more trouble at the limits of capability where the “centaur” pattern of human-AI-collaboration is required. Levent’s lived experience is the opposite - collaborating with Claude only in the early stages and then leaving him far behind with the critical parts involving automorphic forms on higher-rank groups. We are starting to need Weak to Strong alignment — the open ended domain of controlling AI smarter than us. Backblaze B2 has delivered capacity tier storage for twenty years, manages more than six exabytes, and is trusted by leading neoclouds, labs, and gen AI companies. Growth shouldn’t be something you sweat. We’ve got room for whatever you’re building. Come and try it out ! articles.title: How to Criticize with Kindness: Philosopher Daniel Dennett on the Four Steps to Arguing Intelligently
articles.snippet: “Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?” “In disputes upon moral or scientific points,” Arthur Martine counseled in his magnificent 1866 guide to the art of conversation , “let your aim be to come at truth, not to conquer your opponent. So you never shall be at a loss in losing the argument, and gaining a new discovery.” Of course, this isn’t what happens most of the time when we argue, both online and off, but especially when we deploy the artillery of our righteousness from behind the comfortable shield of the keyboard. That form of “criticism” — which is really a menace of reacting rather than responding — is worthy of Mark Twain’s memorable remark that “the critic’s symbol should be the tumble-bug: he deposits his egg in somebody else’s dung, otherwise he could not hatch it.” But it needn’t be this way — there are ways to be critical while remaining charitable, of aiming not to “conquer” but to “come at truth,” not to be right at all costs but to understand and advance the collective understanding. Daniel Dennett (March 28, 1942–April 19, 2024), whom artificial intelligence pioneer Marvin Minsky has called “our best current philosopher” and “the next Bertrand Russell ,” poses an apt question that probes some of the basic tendencies and dynamics of today’s everyone-is-a-critic culture: “Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?” Daniel Dennett In Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking ( public library ) — the same fantastic volume that gave us Dennett on the dignity and art-science of making mistakes — he offers what he calls “the best antidote [for the] tendency to caricature one’s opponent” : a list of rules formulated decades ago by the legendary social psychologist and game theorist Anatol Rapoport, best-known for originating the famous tit-for-tat strategy of game theory. Dennett synthesizes the steps: How to compose a successful critical commentary: You should attempt to re-express your target’s position so clearly, vividly, and fairly that your target says, “Thanks, I wish I’d thought of putting it that way.” You should list any points of agreement (especially if they are not matters of general or widespread agreement). You should mention anything you have learned from your target. Only then are you permitted to say so much as a word of rebuttal or criticism. If only the same code of conduct could be applied to critical commentary online, particularly to the indelible inferno of comments. But rather than a naively utopian, Pollyannaish approach to debate, Dennett points out this is actually a sound psychological strategy that accomplishes one key thing: It transforms your opponent into a more receptive audience for your criticism or dissent, which in turn helps advance the discussion. Compare and contrast with Susan Sontag’s three steps to refuting any argument , and treat yourself to Dennett’s wholly excellent Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking . donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). articles.title: Medtronic’s Hugo surgical robot ready for bigger operation
articles.snippet: Medtronic’s Hugo surgical robot features a modular design that allows surgeons to use only the robotic arms needed for any given procedure. | Source: Medtronic Medtronic this week announced the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has cleared the Hugo robotic-assisted surgery system for use in general surgery procedures. The approval enables the modular, cart-based system to perform surgeries across the abdomen. The clearance covers all upper abdominal general surgical procedures, including cholecystectomy, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, ventral hernia, and small bowel resection. The FDA also cleared lower abdominal procedures of inguinal hernia and appendectomy. Combined, Medtronic said these procedures account for about 3.5 million surgeries annually in the U.S. “We started our U.S. journey in February of last year,” Rajit Kamal, the general manager of robotic surgical technologies at Medtronic, told The Robot Report . “We have been pleased with the progress we have made. We are in many leading hospitals in the country with our urology indication. Our general surgery further opens those opportunities for us and for our combined value proposition, not just for Hugo, but in service, training, support, touch surgery, and the broader portfolio.” Medtronic already has experience in many of these general surgery areas. The company said its technologies in open and laparoscopic approaches have been used for more than fifty years. Medtronic leverages experience abroad in the approval process Medtronic received CE marking for general surgery in Europe in 2022. This provided Medtronic with clinical data to support its U.S. submission. Globally, Hugo is on track to surpass 50,000 cumulative procedures by the end of the Medtronic fiscal year. “General surgery has been available on Hugo outside of the U.S., and it is our fastest-growing procedural mix, because we, as Medtronic, have a strong value proposition in general surgery,” Kamal said. “Many of [the surgeries] are multi-quadrant procedures where Hugo’s modularity provides better coverage, flexibility in port placement, and ability to reach the surgical sites.” Medtronic gained FDA approval for urology, a more common segment for surgical robots , in December 2025. The company also conducted a U.S. clinical study of Hugo for hernia repair, announcing in September 2025 that the system had met the study’s safety and effectiveness endpoints. At the same time, the company gained an investigational device exemption (IDE) to operate a clinical trial in the U.S. for general surgery. “We took two pathways [to gain FDA clearance]. One was we did a clinical trial in the U.S. and worked with the FDA and IDE, but we also leveraged the data from outside the U.S,” Kamal said. “I think it was a creative way of approaching this, and we were able to get a broader set of general surgery indications.” General surgery also represents the highest growth for Hugo system procedures outside the U.S., surpassing urology and gynecology. How is Medtronic using the latest advances in AI? Outside of bringing its existing technology to new markets, Medtronic is also interesting in exploring new technologies. This includes the latest advances in AI , which dominate conversations in the robotics industry today. Kamal said surgical care has three stages: preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative. He thinks AI can make a difference in each stage. “Pre-operative, you could use AI to plan a procedure, using imaging and all that to personalize it. You use AI intraoperatively to be able to identify anatomic structures, to be able to identify critical structures, and to be able to provide intraoperative guidance. You can use AI post-operatively as well to optimize the post-op recovery pathway,” Kamal said. In June, Medtronic gained FDA approval for its compute platform for the operating room, Touch Surgery Aide . The system brings AI insights to surgeons during surgical procedures. The platform uses computer vision and AI to analyze surgical video and provide real-time information to surgical teams. “We clearly see AI playing a very important role. Our intent is to bring AI features onto our Hugo platform and continue being that partner with the surgeons to use AI to provide them insights and continue to make improvements in terms of the patient outcome,” Kamal said. Robotics is changing how surgeons operate One of the biggest impacts of robotic surgery is on the surgeons themselves. Conventional laparoscopic surgery can be physically demanding, requiring surgeons to stand for long periods while manipulating instruments. Robotic-assisted systems like Hugo allow surgeons to operate from a seated console, potentially reducing some of that physical strain. “After decades of practicing, it takes a toll on their body. If you think about a robotic procedure, number one, you get a magnified 3D image, so you have clear depth perception. You’re sitting comfortably in a chair,” Kamal said. Additionally, the controls are more intuitive than the traditional imaging systems a surgeon would use in a manual procedure. “Any laparoscopic surgeon who is doing robotics will tell you that they don’t want to go back,” Kamal continued. Robotics could also help newer surgeons develop their skills. “If you’re a new surgeon coming in, just think about the amount of information you get if you are doing it robotically. You can see the surgical field much clearer,” Kamal said. “The instruments are a lot more precise and accurate. Now with AI, you get better features.” What comes next for Medtronic? Medtronic is continuing to make progress in the U.S. market. The company is running an IDE study for using Hugo in gynecology. The study evaluates Hugo’s safety and effectiveness when used during radical, modified radical or total hysterectomies, inclusive of those treated for malignancies. articles.title: The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification
articles.snippet: The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been “slop” — meaning low-quality output from a large language model. And with so much code being AI-generated now, avoiding slop has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use formal verification systems , which use mathematical proofs and logic to verify the correctness of software or hardware. With AI’s growing prowess at solving math problems , there’s now a number of AI companies offering formal verification systems. They include Harmonic , Theorem , Axiom Math , and a new entrant called &Truth (pronounced ‘and truth’). In this article we’ll look at some of the approaches these companies are taking. How formal verification is used in software and AI today In order to better understand the landscape of formal verification systems, we spoke to one of its leading proponents: Clark Barrett , &Truth’s co-founder and co-CEO. He’s also Corbel Professor (Research) of Computer Science at Stanford and was the co-creator of cvc5 , a popular automated reasoning engine used in formal verification. Without getting too in the weeds, cvc5 is what’s called a “solver” for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) , which Barrett says is widely used in companies like Amazon. For instance, cvc5 is used for specification analysis and test generation in Kiro , Amazon’s agentic development environment. “It's been fun to see my tools go from a good idea in the lab to cvc5 is now called billions of times a day in production pipelines at Amazon,” Barrett told us. Via a 2022 paper about cvc5 co-authored by Clark Barrett. When AI coding agent companies talk about “verifying” their work, it typically means agents running tests, critiquing their own output, or having another AI model judge it. So I asked Barrett how far short of real verification does that fall? “The main difference is really just, how do you know when you're done,” he replied. “So if you're testing, patching, scanning — using all these existing tools — they're quite good. I mean, they find a ton of problems. They raise those issues. But you're never quite sure, did I find all of them [the issues] or is there one more lurking there that my tool can't find?” &Atlas, the first tool of &Truth; it’s “a map of the world’s open-source code, starting with code written in the C programming language.” Lean’s role in formal verification &Truth builds on Lean , an open-source programming language and proof assistant . The company combines AI with automated reasoning techniques to construct proofs that Lean can check. Lean is a language used by frontier models to solve all manner of supremely difficult math problems . For instance, just this week GPT-6.2 Astra produced what Vals believes is “the first Lean proof of Smoktunowicz’s Gap Theorem.” Vals added that Anthropic also used Lean to formalize Fermat’s Last Theorem, a project of 13 million lines. The latest big math news is a report that Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he used Claude to prove the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and he posted the proof in Lean . Example of Lean code; via Lean project website &Truth is building what it calls a “verification machine” on top of the Lean framework, with the ambition of reading code “in any language, proving whether it satisfies precisely stated requirements , and enabling humans to trust it without having to understand every line.” “What Lean does is it just checks that you didn't make a mistake,” explained Barrett. “So you can think of it as a very sophisticated checker for mathematics.” This has implications for model training too. Axiom Math uses formal verification to provide correctness feedback for training its mathematical reasoning systems, with proof attempts helping improve future models. In an interview with Latent Space in June , Axiom CEO Carina Hong made the point that formal verification — and what Lean enables — isn’t just a defensive measure. “Formal verification, or verified AI, to us it's not just about handling or kicking out the lousiness, the hallucinations, the mistakes. It's about scaling brilliance. It's about super-intelligence.” Axiom develops AxiomProver , an AI system that generates Lean proofs, alongside AXLE , its toolkit for exploring, validating, and manipulating those proofs. Harmonic’s Aristotle , an “ automated theorem prover ”, uses Lean heavily in its offering. “Inside Aristotle, AI writes the proofs and Lean checks every step of them, so a result never rests on the AI being right,” states the company on its website. Harmonic’s workflow Cybersecurity and LLM-scaled formal verification Given the heightened level of paranoia about cybersecurity these days — some might say in the days leading up to AGI — formal verification systems seem like they’re needed more than ever. And Barrett confirmed that cybersecurity is a key focus for &Truth. “One really powerful use case for our technology is going through all the C code in the world, whether it be open source or closed source, and trying to ensure that it's memory safe. And then if it's not memory safe, we can point to: here's a problem with this piece of code, you need to fix it so that it's safe.” Security is also a focus of Theorem , one of &Truth’s competitors. “Verification is the only defense that holds while adversaries scale,” Theorem states on its homepage. Theorem’s proof-efficiency eval : “KB of machine code verified per hour on our proof-efficiency eval, by model release date, with 95% intervals.” Theorem has also collaborated with Anthropic on this topic, resulting in a blog post entitled “ LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale .” One of the more encouraging notes in the post is that formal verification, although currently token-expensive, is starting to get more token-efficient. articles.title: The Relief of Rock Bottom: George Orwell and the Secret Springboard of Success
articles.snippet: It happens to everyone — to kings and paupers, to astronauts and poets. Nothing will protect you from it — not money, not love, not perfect health — for it spares no life that is fully lived, not the sunniest or the most privileged or the best planned. It begins with the wall — the one you hit over and over and over, not breaking through. And then, after the exhausted collapse, the bottom. The floorboards of despair, cold as granite, absolute as gravity. But then something extraordinary happens — something George Orwell (June 25, 1903–January 21, 1950) captures perfectly in a passage from Down and out in Paris and London ( public library ), recounting his experience of abject poverty while trying to become a writer, working in restaurant kitchens in Paris and wandering London as a tramp. George Orwell at the peak of his success What Orwell observes of material poverty applies equally to the spiritual poverty of hope and meaning we call despair: When you are approaching poverty, you make one discovery which outweighs some of the others. You discover boredom and mean complications and the beginnings of hunger, but you also discover the great redeeming feature of poverty: the fact that it annihilates the future. It annihilates, he means, anxiety about the future, for when you have nothing left to lose, there is nothing to worry about losing. That is the relief of rock bottom — a feeling that is “a great consolation” when you are at your lowest, and one that “everyone who has been hard up has experienced”: It is a feeling of relief, almost of pleasure, at knowing yourself at last genuinely down and out. You have talked so often of going to the dogs — and well, here are the dogs, and you have reached them, and you can stand it. It takes off a lot of anxiety. Two millennia before him, Marcus Aurelius had anchored his meditation on turning suffering into strength in the same premise: Be like a headland: the waves beat against it continuously, but it stands fast and around it the boiling water dies down. “It’s my rotten luck that this has happened to me.” On the contrary, “It’s my good luck that, although this has happened to me, I still feel no distress, since I’m unbruised by the present and unconcerned about the future.” What happened could have happened to anyone, but not everyone could have carried on without letting it distress him. Here, the Stoic perspective converges with the Buddhist, best articulated by Pema Chödrön in her timeless field guide to transformation through trying times : Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over to annihilation can that which is indestructible be found in us. And that is the thing about rock bottom: Not only does it hold, but it is there you discover the part of you that also holds — the bedrock of your being unassailable by all the loss, all the failure, all the frivolities of chance. Orwell, being neither a Stoic nor a Buddhist, understood the universality of his experience. “It is a fairly trivial story,” he writes at the end of his memoir — trivial because its essence is so common, no matter the guise; trivial because it touches an elemental truth: The relief of rock bottom is not that you have sunk to it but that, having survived it, you can only rise. Art from Reweaving the Rainbow . (Available as a print and more .) The manuscript of Orwell’s memoir was twice rejected, including by T.S. Eliot at Faber & Faber. In a fit of despair, Orwell tossed it into his friend Mabel’s garbage bin. She fished it out and, without his knowledge, took it to a literary agent she knew. We could say that the rest is history, but the selective collective memory we call history is an erasure machine for the myriad failures behind every success, for the rock bottom that is so often — so much oftener than our culture likes to admit — the springboard for the redemption of our suffering. donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). articles.title: 2026.47: Down in DC
articles.snippet: Andrew made the fatal mistake of getting his hopes up for the Wizards; on Sharp Text he wonders how it all went wrong. (Photo by Todd Olszewski/Getty Images) Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery! As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings . On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week. Obituaries and Exceptionalism. After several days to mull the shocking departure of Jensen Huang, Ben’s article on Monday delivered an omnibus obituary for a variety of American eras that may now be ending. Tracing the decisions that made Huang great, the strategies that made him a target, the implications of his demise for the rest of the tech ecosystem, and a shift in the U.S. government’s perspective on tech companies — and specifically AI companies — to which Huang never quite adapted, Monday’s piece was both comprehensive and poignant. — Andrew Sharp Arguments About Agents. Recurring Stratechery guest and advertising expert Eric Seufert is often aligned with Ben in his view of the digital advertising landscape, which is why this week’s Stratechery Interview was fun: Ben is a big believer in the potential upside in agentic commerce, while Eric has been (correctly) calling BS on a variety of hyped agentic commerce stories and trends over the past year. Both of them made their case Thursday, and it was sandwiched between thoughts on how Muse plans to monetize, why the market have misread Google’s recent earnings report, and ChatGPT’s progress building an ads business. — AS Ben Gets a Duo. In the middle of a heavy week of Nvidia takes and ominous infrastructure failures, I was delighted to find out that Ben not only purchased an iPhone Duo, but loved it . Come for his review at the end of Tuesday’s Update , and then stay for his discussion with John Gruber on Tuesday’s Dithering . We doubled back (Duo’d back?) to discuss all of it at the end of this week’s Sharp Tech , including some hands-on testing, comparisons to the iPhone Air, and a variety of shots fired at the iPhone Pro. — AS Presented by As AI models improve, you might expect the market will consolidate around a handful of providers. But user data tells a different story. Among OpenRouter customers spending at least $100 a month, the median number of AI model families in use has doubled over the past year , from three to six. Even as AI models become more capable, businesses are using more models, not fewer. This makes sense when you consider that intelligence isn’t one-dimensional. A model that’s exceptional at writing code may not be the fastest at answering customer questions, or the most economical at processing millions of documents. The question is shifting from “which AI model should we build on?” to “which model should handle each task?” The answer, increasingly, is ‘it depends.’ Which is great for flexibility, less great for simplicity. OpenRouter, which recently joined Stripe , allows businesses to access and govern hundreds of models with the flexibility to optimize for cost, performance, and reliability as the market evolves. Learn more at openrouter.ai . articles.title: Video Friday: Drone Squeezes Itself to Fit Through Tight Spaces
articles.snippet: Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion. Humanoids 2026 : 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CA Enjoy today’s videos! Drones navigating cluttered spaces often encounter openings narrower than their bodies. We present a design method that jointly optimizes a quadrotor’s geometry and how its two side arms bend on contact. The resulting prototype folds from 31.3 centimeters to 14.1 cm wide on contact and flies through a 15-cm opening. [ Paper ] via [ Autonomous Robots Lab ] Thanks, Kostas! TeCoBots are soft, snakelike robots that can work alone and can also grab onto each other to form chains, loops, and branches, building a new body for each task. A single robot can inch like a worm, roll across gravel and grass, climb inside a pipe, and lift a 2.5-liter water bottle. The claw it uses to grab objects is the same one it uses to grab another robot, so linking up needs no extra docking hardware. Linked together, the robots do things that none can do alone. [ TeCoBots ] Thanks, Mahmud! AHEADance is a humanoid robot that makes up its dance as the music plays. It listens to the song as it streams in, takes a guess at what the next half second of music will sound like, and then moves to match the style of whatever is playing. When the music stops, it stands still and waits, and when the music comes back, so does the dancing. Curious what it would do with your favorite song? Play it through the live demo on our project page and watch the robot have a go. [ AHEADance ] Thanks, Chengxu! I am...not at all sure how I feel about this. [ Arc Lab ] Most affordable dexterous hands use tendons, and anyone who has worked with them knows the pain of re-tensioning and replacing them. I wanted to see whether rigid linkages could get you humanlike dexterity without that maintenance, and so far the answer looks like yes. Each finger has three actuated degrees of freedom, the hand can grasp and manipulate a wide range of objects, and the whole thing is 3D-printed for less than US $650 in parts. [ PHD‑Hand ] Thanks, Neel! I’m not sure that this is an entirely faithful representation of the capabilities of this robot goose , but it’s so cute that we’ll let it slide. For now. [ Robot Works ] You’ve seen data-collection gloves. You’ve seen teleoperation gloves. But this is different. What if the glove itself IS the robot hand? [ TriMI ] Can we treat a flapping wing like a rotary wing? In our latest IEEE [Robotics and Automation Letters] work, we developed CROBAT, a fully actuated quad-thopter with wing-thrust vectoring, enabling independent position and attitude control. The robot demonstrates full-pose flapping flight and tilted perching, showing a pathway toward flapping-wing robots that go beyond navigation toward physical interaction. [ Paper ] One robot can work. Two robots can team up. Meet CoMind—Be My Eye, the first framework for proactive, task-aware context sharing in multirobot collaboration. Robots share selected task context with each other, proactively and in real time. Shared vision is no longer science fiction. [ Astribot ] Today Spot is working with people and for people to make our jobs and our communities safer, more reliable, and more intelligent. See what tomorrow brings. Ugh, ouch! Atlas, don’t DO that. [ Boston Dynamics ] Fraunhofer IPA has been doing humanoid robot research since before humanoid robots were cool. [ Fraunhofer IPA ] LIMO ULTRA is AgileX Robotics’ newest embodied AI robot-development platform for robotics education, research, and hands-on development. [ AgileX ] In 2022, an AI drone beat world-champion pilots in head-to-head races—with no human at the controls. This is the story behind that breakthrough. This 25-minute documentary takes you behind the scenes of SWIFT, the autonomous racing drone developed by the Robotics and Perception Group at the University of Zurich. Meet the researchers and champion pilots, follow the preparations, and watch human skill face artificial intelligence on the racetrack. [ University of Zurich Robotics and Perception Group ] This Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute seminar is from Ben Burchfiel, cofounder and CTO of Walden Robotics : “Learning in Production: Building Physical AI at Walden Robotics.” Walden Robotics is a full-stack company building both the hardware and physical AI for general-purpose manufacturing robots. Walden was founded in January 2026 and deployed its first robot into production manufacturing two months later. It’s still there, and the fleet has been learning on the job ever since. Our core conviction is that the best physical AI will be built via a continuous cycle of deployment and learning grounded in real work. I’ll share lessons from the frontier of end-to-end learning in production manufacturing and why we believe physical AI has reached an inflection point. [ CMU RI ]

articles.title: MassRobotics launching marine robotics facility on Boston Harbor
articles.snippet: CRABI Robotics performs in-transit cleaning and inspection of marine vessels. | Source: MassRobotics MassRobotics is developing a marine robotics facility at the historic Boston Fish Pier. The new facility will marine technology startups a space to build, launch and test robots on Boston Harbor. Construction is underway through a partnership with the Massachusetts Port Authority (Massport). MassRobotics plans to open the facility in early 2028, with programming starting throughout 2027. “Boston has always been a harbor city, and some of today’s most exciting robotics work is happening in and under the water. Marine startups tell us that finding a place to test is one of their biggest hurdles,” said Tom Ryden, the executive director of MassRobotics. “With the Fish Pier steps from our headquarters, founders can build in our shop in the morning and test in the harbor by afternoon. We’re grateful to Massport for this partnership and excited to help make Boston a global center for marine robotics.” The Fish Pier facility facility will be outfitted with testing equipment for marine robotics, including a water tank, a float alongside the pier for direct water testing, and lifting and launch equipment for getting vehicles in and out of the harbor. MassRobotics currently supports more than 100 resident startups from across the globe. The Fish Pier adds a new dimension to what it offers them and opens its doors wider to companies working in the blue economy. Submit your innovation now! Access to water testing Access to water for testing is often one of the biggest challenges for marine robotics startups. Testing an underwater vehicle or ocean sensor usually means renting boat time, borrowing a tank or traveling to a remote site. The Fish Pier facility removes that barrier. Companies can design and fabricate in the MassRobotics machine shop, then walk their prototype to the pier and put it in the harbor the same day. That tight loop between building and testing means faster iteration and lower costs for early-stage teams. CRABI Robotics, one of MassRobotics marine startups, develops an underwater hull-cleaning robot. It started as a three-person startup with an idea about how to make oceans cleaner. “For ocean startups, getting to the water is one of the hardest parts. A facility on the harbor, steps from where you build, will help the next marine company move a lot faster than we could,” said Levi Gershon, CEO of CRABI Robotics . The post MassRobotics launching marine robotics facility on Boston Harbor appeared first on The Robot Report .

articles.title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #220
articles.snippet: Cover Image by Runway Hi friends 👋, Happy Friday and welcome back to our 220th Weekly Dose of Optimism! What a week to be alive. Since we spoke last Friday, GTA 6 is finally out, Anthropic is public, Starships are reusable, leukemia may not be as deadly, we may be able to live on the open seas, and… there’s just so much more. I think we might have both the highest density of great things in the Main Dose and the longest section of Extra Doses to date (there are 10 down there, including Anthropic and new Google models). Almost everything in Extra Dose would have made the top 5 even like 3 months ago. Plus, I’ve been having a lot of fun building a new notboring.com . You can click on a bunch of the companies on the home page for little Easter Eggs, check Roundup for all of the day’s top not boring-relevant stories, and Scarce Asset Tracker for the completed and upcoming sales relevant to what I wrote in Scarce Assets . I even built a better reading experience for all of our Essays . Enjoy! And let me know what else you’d like to see, so I can tell my agents to build it. Let’s get to it. This Week’s Weekly Dose is brought to you by… Runway If you want to blow your family’s mind over Thanksgiving, bring their ideas to life with Runway . Runway is building foundational AI for how the world creates. 65M+ people use Runway to generate, edit and produce video, images and audio with 80+ top media models. You can read my essay with co-founder Anastasis Germanidis to learn more on where Runway is headed beyond video. Nvidia, Amazon, Lionsgate, Chime, and 95%+ of the Fortune 100 are part of a growing community of teams, founders, and independent creators using Runway to make national TV spots, social ads at scale, launch videos and more. You can also use Runway in ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Cursor, Replit and more via the Runway MCP . Create any idea with Runway now (1) SpaceX’s Mechazilla Catches an Orbital Starship Humanity is one giant leap closer to being multiplanetary. Over the weekend on Starship Flight 15, Ship 42 launched from Starbase, Texas, reached orbit, deployed a batch of Starlink satellites, spent more than 22 hours in space, survived fiery hypersonic re-entry, flipped upright, and dropped cleanly into Mechazilla’s chopsticks. The SpaceX team made one of the greatest engineering feats in human history look easy. SpaceX has already caught Super Heavy boosters before, which was already absurd. Catching the orbital upper stage , the part that goes into orbit carrying the payload to complete a mission, was the final boss of rapid, full reusability. The final boss is dead. While the booster is more expensive at around 70% of Starship’s cost, it is somewhat easier to reuse given that it carries the upper stage up and comes right back. Having proven that the booster is reusable, the upper stage was like 90% of the marginal cost per flight. Having to make a new one each time would leave Starship with a hard floor around $30-40M per launch, but making it reusable means that the marginal cost of launch drops to something like $2-10M per launch, or $20-100/kg versus Falcon 9’s $1,000/kg internal cost. SpaceX still has plenty of work ahead on heat-shield durability and turnaround time before Starships are flying as repeatably as planes, of course, but the goal is to send up about two a week by the end of 2027, hundreds per year by 2029 ,and multiple per day beyond that. They’ll carry satellites and data centers and drug factories and eventually all sorts of things we’ll need to thrive in space and on other worlds. For now, just watch the slow-motion footage above and marvel. Humans rock. (2) Leukemia Vaccine Cuts Risk of Death by 41% in Phase 3 Trial Video created with Runway At this point, you know how we feel about cancer here at the Dose. Hate it. It’s been a big year for us cancer haters, and the streak continues. On Tuesday, SELLAS Life Sciences and Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center announced positive topline results from the pivotal Phase 3 REGAL trial of galinpepimut-S (GPS), an immunotherapeutic vaccine for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). AML is a brutal blood cancer with roughly a 33% five-year survival rate that kills around 11,500 Americans every year. The trial followed 126 patients whose AML had relapsed, who had fought their way back into a second (or later) remission, and who weren't eligible for a stem-cell transplant. The patients were a high-risk group with very few options left. And GPS extended their lives. Patients who received GPS alone (with no chemo alongside it) had a median overall survival of 24.0 months, compared to 14.7 months for patients on investigator's choice of best available treatment. That's more than nine extra months of life and a 41% reduction in the risk of death . Huge. While it’s not a total cure, we seem to be entering a period in which a number of therapies are able to extend patients’ lives while researchers around the world work to find more permanent cures. Meaning, an extra nine months both nine months and a call option on much longer. This isn’t the first promising vaccine this year. Back in Dose #207 , we covered Merck and Moderna’s personalized mRNA melanoma vaccine that cut recurrence or death by 42% in Phase 3. The exciting thing about GPS isn’t custom-built from an individual tumor like that one, but an off-the-shelf peptide vaccine, which should make it faster, cheaper, and more widely available if approved. Even better, the WT1 protein shows up in a number of blood cancers and solid tumors, so GPS may be effective against more than just AML. Say it with us… get fucked, cancer! (2a) Pancreatic cancer pill trial saw tumours vanish Keep saying it with us. I don’t even know what to say anymore. I got to my computer to wrap up the Dose, opened up X, and the first tweet I saw was one from the BBC saying that there’s a new pill for pancreatic cancer that shrunk tumors in one in 12 patients so completely they were undetectable in scans, and stoppe

articles.snippet: As we previewed on our Know Before You IPO pod , Anthropic set its IPO price at $83 and today $ANT closed at $97.17, up 17% from the offering price ( drifting -5% to $92.60 after the close) . The $81.3B offering overtook SpaceX's June IPO as the largest in history. Dario and Daniela ( Dario’s remarks , Founders’ letter ) used the occasion to say Anthropic would pace training and deployment based on whether it could keep its systems safe and under human control. Their Class F shares carry 50.1% of voting power on most shareholder matters. Expect the lockup expiries to weigh on the stock price as about a trillion dollars of shares free up over the next year, while Anthropic has to keep the world’s top model ... for now . AI News for 11/18/2026–11/19/2026. We checked 12 subreddits and 544 accounts on X . Search past issues in the AINews archive . AI Twitter Recap Anthropic listed on Nasdaq under $ANT, priced at $83, and opened 34% higher, putting it near a $2T valuation. Listing: Anthropic rang the Nasdaq opening bell ( @kimmonismus , @yacinelearning ). The official account posted a media-only launch item that drew by far the day's highest engagement ( @AnthropicAI ). Opening trade: $ANT opened at $111.50 , which is $28.50 (34.3%) above the $83 IPO price ( @TheRundownAI , @kimmonismus ). Pre-open indications were up ~32% at ~$110 ( @kimmonismus ). Record raise: The $81.3B raised beats SpaceX's $75B (June) as the largest IPO ever ( @TheRundownAI ). Net proceeds: Expected net proceeds are $104.8B including a concurrent private placement. Fully diluted valuation was ~$2T at the open ( @kimmonismus ). AMD investment: AMD agreed to invest $2.5B in Anthropic alongside the IPO. The same morning, AMD fell after a Hunterbrook report that a US-blacklisted Chinese server maker kept shipping newer AMD firmware ( @kimmonismus , source ). CEO statement: Dario Amodei published IPO remarks with a strong safety commitment (details below) ( @AnthropicAI ). Employee wealth: The average employee could be worth >$40M , per SEC filings and investors ( @kimmonismus ). Anthropic's 5,300 founders and employees are now worth more than the bottom third of US households, about 45M families ( @SteveRattner ). Dario Amodei's IPO remarks (official position) Personal framing: Dario and Daniela lost their father to a disease that became curable a few years later. Dario cited CRISPR's decades-long path from discovery to treatment. Core thesis: Powerful AI working with humans "could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade." He stressed that only early results exist so far. Named risks: Misuse by individuals or nation-states, economic disruption, and loss of control. Listed safety work includes bio/cyber safeguards, alignment training, and interpretability ("like an X-ray"). Key commitment: "We will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business or political pressure." Strategic framing: The IPO "only strengthens our resolve." He restated the "race to the top," which should work "regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time" ( @AnthropicAI ). Financials and data points from the S-1 and analysts Low cash burn: Anthropic raised ~$140B and still holds ~$132B on the balance sheet. That implies it "burnt like under $10 billion" to get here, per Tanay Jaipuria (Wing VC) on Latent Space. He called the burn the S-1's biggest surprise, "in a positive way" ( @FounderClipsHQ ). Use of proceeds: Proceeds are slated largely for data center leasing, which makes SpaceXSI (the Colossus landlord) an indirect beneficiary ( @kimmonismus ). A critic noted that Elon "rented them an entire Colossus cluster" despite past attacks on Anthropic ( @LinusMixson ). Google's stake: Google owns 13.7% of Anthropic stock ( @NielsRogge ). Teortaxes argued Google could still "fumble this by continuing to reinforce Anthropic with TPUs" ( @teortaxesTex ). After-tax reality check: The median employee likely takes home closer to ~$5M after taxes than the ~$50M headline figures suggest ( @futurenomics ). Product standing on IPO day: Anthropic is #1 lab on Code Arena WebDev, with Claude Fable 5.2 at 1824 , +27 over the next lab ( @arena ). Arena also posted a lineage visual from Opus 4.5 to Opus 5.5 Max ( @arena ). articles.title: Robotics enters its post-Jensen Huang era
articles.snippet: Jensen Huang keynote at CES 2025. | Credit: NVIDIA Days before Christmas in 2023, Serve Robotics was on the verge of bankruptcy. A major investor pulled out of a committed funding round, leaving the developer of sidewalk delivery robots unable to make payroll and just days away from running out of cash. With few options remaining, Serve Robotics co-founder and CEO Ali Kashani reached out to NVIDIA co-founder Jensen Huang. “We spoke at 6 a.m. the next day, and later that day I was having dinner with his executive team to find a way to bridge the company,” recalled Kashani. “Within days, they led a financing round that brought us back to life.” Four months later, Serve Robotics was ringing the bell at Nasdaq to celebrate its public listing. “I have heard similar stories from many other founders, as well as current and former NVIDIA employees, whose lives Jensen’s actions have changed,” Kashani said. Over the past several years, few people outside the robotics industry have done more than Huang to elevate its profile. Clad in his signature black leather jacket, Huang routinely dedicated portions of his marathon keynotes to robotics. He showcased humanoids on stage, introduced development tools, highlighted startups, championed open models and research, and made the case that robots would transform the world. He also put NVIDIA’s money behind that vision. Now, one of robotics’ most influential advocates is gone. NVIDIA’s board accepted Huang’s resignation on Nov. 12 , and CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor. A large stage for robotics For an industry that spent decades fighting for mainstream recognition, Huang provided something few robotics executives could: one of the biggest stages in technology. “Jensen was fantastic in painting the vision,” said Yaro Tenzer, co-founder and CEO of RightHand Robotics. Tenzer said Huang helped expand investors’ imaginations about what robotics could become. NVIDIA said during its third-quarter earnings call that its physical AI revenue nearly tripled year over year and is on track to exceed $25 billion in fiscal 2027. While that represents a sizable and rapidly growing business, it still accounts for only about 6% of NVIDIA’s projected annual revenue of more than $400 billion. And physical AI encompasses more than robotics. The attention Huang afforded robotics was disproportionate to its short-term commercial contribution. “NVIDIA introduced its Isaac robotics platform back in 2017, and Jensen kept robotics in his keynotes and in the company’s long-term story year after year,” said Deepak Jayaraj, vice president of hardware engineering and manufacturing at agricultural robotics developer Four Growers. “I think that steady attention made it easier for founders to make the case to investors.” Unlike Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose robotics advocacy is largely centered on his own company’s products, Huang promoted an ecosystem of developers, many of whom compete directly with one another. NVIDIA stood to benefit financially regardless of which robotics companies succeeded. But that business model also positioned Huang to become an advocate for the broader industry. Providing infrastructure Perhaps NVIDIA’s lasting contribution to robotics will be the development infrastructure it built under Huang. Its portfolio spans much of the robotics development stack, from GPUs and CUDA for AI training to Omniverse and Isaac Sim for simulation, Isaac Lab for robot learning, GR00T and Cosmos foundation models, Isaac ROS software, and Jetson embedded computing. Jan Zizka, co-founder and CEO of warehouse robotics developer Brightpick and co-founder of machine vision specialist Photoneo, experienced NVIDIA’s impact firsthand. Zizka said Photoneo participated in an early-access program for NVIDIA’s Jetson TX1 computing platform. “He was almost pushing the market to make it happen,” Zizka said, pointing to Huang’s willingness to invest in emerging markets before demand fully materialized. NVIDIA’s investments in open research and software helped lower barriers to entry for developers. Zizka noted that its efforts in embedded computing also encouraged competitors, including AMD and Qualcomm, to pursue robotics opportunities. Under Huang, NVIDIA became one of robotics’ most prominent strategic investors, backing companies including Figure AI, NEURA Robotics, Skild AI, Wayve, Waabi, and Serve Robotics. Beyond capital, an investment from NVIDIA provided an endorsement that could help startups attract additional investors, employees, and customers. “Jensen’s style will be hard to copy,” said Jayaraj. “I’d judge whomever it is by which robotics programs they keep funding.” “NVIDIA has a business reason to stay in, since many robot companies train and simulate on its compute long before they ship at scale,” he added. “The keynote time and the early bets on young teams are the parts that could fade.” Losing an advocate inside NVIDIA Huang’s enthusiasm for robotics was perhaps just as valuable inside NVIDIA as it was outside the company. Its robotics teams had an advocate at the highest level of the organization. Having earned considerable credibility with investors through previous long-term bets, Huang enjoyed a latitude his successor might not. NVIDIA’s next CEO will also inherit growing competition in its core data center business and potentially greater political and regulatory scrutiny following the Democrats’ strong performance in the midterm elections. Robert Little, co-founder and former CEO of ATI Industrial Automation, is particularly concerned about how opposition to data center construction could affect NVIDIA’s ability to fund its longer-term investments. “Robotics is being propped up from the money that’s being created in the data centers for NVIDIA that affords NVIDIA to have a team of people developing product for robotics,” Little said. Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
articles.snippet: Open video on YouTube ↗ Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work. Jump to the MCP discussion → "Issue tracking is dead" When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues. Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads. Jump to the "issue tracking is dead" discussion → The AI budget behind $100M in months The thing speeding up purchases right now, Cristina says, is AI budget. Companies carved out money for AI tools that didn't exist before, and any product that fits inside it skips the usual fight for spend. At some companies that budget is very high. It's already starting to change. Buyers are signing one-year deals and paid pilots, not three-year contracts, because nobody knows what they'll want in two years. And some overnight-$100M stories are a handful of $30 to $40 million contracts with defense companies or giant law firms. That's a very different business from Linear's 40,000 paying customers on what was, until June, entirely seat-based pricing. When those one-year deals come up for renewal, we'll find out whose ARR was real. Jump to the AI budget discussion → Linear threw out its 2025 enterprise roadmap Three weeks after joining in 2023, Cristina crossed "move upmarket to enterprise" off Linear's company goals. It had one salesperson. She went after growth-stage companies that would have to rip out an existing tool instead, the same way Stripe won new businesses long before it won switchers. Linear finally declared an enterprise push in 2025, with a roadmap full of features for large organizations. Then agents happened. Linear built an MCP server, an agents platform with a whole new set of APIs, and integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot. None of it was planned, and a lot of the enterprise work never got done. Cristina chose to race ahead anyway. Competitors waited, and enterprises started putting Linear on their shortlists. Jump to the enterprise roadmap discussion → No SDRs, no forward deployed engineers Linear has never hired a single SDR. Cristina thinks the qualification call wastes the customer's time: they want a demo, not questions about their budget. AEs do their own outbound, with tooling to keep it personal. It doesn't do forward deployed engineering either. Linear should be easy enough to adopt that nobody needs access to your systems. Solutions engineers sell alongside enterprise AEs instead, sometimes building a working ServiceNow integration overnight to show a prospect it can be done. In three and a half years, Cristina has never had an escalation over a bad support experience. articles.title: Why Linear says Issue Tracking is Dead — Cristina Cordova, COO
articles.snippet: Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work. Jump to the MCP discussion → "Issue tracking is dead" When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues. Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads. Jump to the "issue tracking is dead" discussion → The AI budget behind $100M in months The thing speeding up purchases right now, Cristina says, is AI budget. Companies carved out money for AI tools that didn't exist before, and any product that fits inside it skips the usual fight for spend. At some companies that budget is very high. It's already starting to change. Buyers are signing one-year deals and paid pilots, not three-year contracts, because nobody knows what they'll want in two years. And some overnight-$100M stories are a handful of $30 to $40 million contracts with defense companies or giant law firms. That's a very different business from Linear's 40,000 paying customers on what was, until June, entirely seat-based pricing. When those one-year deals come up for renewal, we'll find out whose ARR was real. Jump to the AI budget discussion → Linear threw out its 2025 enterprise roadmap Three weeks after joining in 2023, Cristina crossed "move upmarket to enterprise" off Linear's company goals. It had one salesperson. She went after growth-stage companies that would have to rip out an existing tool instead, the same way Stripe won new businesses long before it won switchers. Linear finally declared an enterprise push in 2025, with a roadmap full of features for large organizations. Then agents happened. Linear built an MCP server, an agents platform with a whole new set of APIs, and integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot. None of it was planned, and a lot of the enterprise work never got done. Cristina chose to race ahead anyway. Competitors waited, and enterprises started putting Linear on their shortlists. Jump to the enterprise roadmap discussion → No SDRs, no forward deployed engineers Linear has never hired a single SDR. Cristina thinks the qualification call wastes the customer's time: they want a demo, not questions about their budget. AEs do their own outbound, with tooling to keep it personal. articles.title: The Cost of Human Frailty: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Test!
articles.snippet: In a month full of big stories, perhaps the biggest business story was the fall from grace of Jensen Huang and the consequences for Nvidia, investors, and the rest of the AI trade. The initial story, with its potent mix of personal fallibility and security concerns, related to Jensen’s affair with Alice Huang, who news stories labeled a Chinese spy, though the evidence on the ground is still thin. I had planned to write about the story then, but on the road in Asia and with teaching commitments, I put it off for a few days, and over those days, the story took a turn, with stories of dalliances with Nvidia employees. Last week culminated with Nvidia’s board asking Jensen to step down, and his agreeing, perhaps bringing to an end one of the more eventful and productive stints as a CEO in corporate history. I have no desire or standing to debate the moral aspects of this story, and I will let others take sides on whether the board should or should not have fired Jensen. In this post, I will focus on the question of what Jensen stepping down as CEO might mean for Nvidia’s value, and whether after the market correction over the last three weeks, the market has overreached. What does a CEO do? What does a CEO do for a business? Given the many tasks that go into creating, building, and running a business, it should come as no surprise that the list is long, but I will classify them broadly into groups: Storyteller: Every business is built around a story, and that story drives its valuation and sometimes its pricing. While that story is grounded in the company’s products and the markets that it seeks, it is the top manager’s job to craft and tell the story to investors, employees and to consumers. Clearly, the significance of this component of a CEO’s story will shift, depending on where the company is in its life cycle, with its importance being greatest at either end of the life cycle. B usiness manager: It is of course CEO’s job to manage the business that they are put in charge off, but that can span the spectrum from building a business model, for young companies, to working on ways to scale up a business for high growth firms to defending a business model for mature businesses to scaling down the model, as the company enters the declining phase. People leader: Organizations are composed of people, including suppliers, employees and customers, and it is the top management’s job to lead these people, though the nature of that leadership will also shift as a company ages. Early on, when a company is still seeking out a business model and faces failure risk, it is to inspire people with vision and direction. As companies grow and mature, it is to create a corporate culture that retains employees, as competitors try to lure them away. In decline, when a company is shedding employees and shrinking, it is finding a way to do so as humanely as possible and find a soft landing, without destroying morale. Public face: For better or worse, the CEO represents the public face of the company with investors, regulators and others, and the role they play will vary across groups and across the life cycle. With investors, CEOs frame the vision/narrative for young companies and are key to drawing in fresh capital, whereas with mature firms, especially if they are publicly traded, managers interactions are with institutional investors, where they try to manage expectations and frame results. With regulators and politicians, the CEO’s role is sometimes to play defense, when their companies are in the crosshairs and facing regulatory questioning, and sometimes to play offense against competitors. Succession planner: There is a final aspect of a CEO’s job that is often ignored but can be key to extending a company’s life cycle, and that is preparing for a succession, where a new management is readied, for a handover, when it comes due. Clearly, the importance of creating succession plans increases as top managers age, and especially so at companies that are transitioning from one stage of the life cycle to the next. In sum, while the list of roles that CEOs play and the functions that they provide is long, the role and functions that get emphasized will shift as companies move through the life cycle. Early in the life cycle, it is the visionary component that is front and center, moving on to business building and people leader as the company's business model takes form, and as the business scales and matures, the primary mission becomes playing defense (against competition, regulators and governments), and managing succession. How much does a CEO matter? A hundred years of formalized business education has been built on the premise that CEOs matter, and that having good management at the top of a business can make the difference between success and failure. While I do not disagree with that broad premise, the effect of good management can be greater at some firms and smaller at others, with five determinants: Macro versus micro: Businesses that are driven more by macroeconomic movements, such as those in interest rates or commodity prices, will be less affected by who manages them than companies whose success can be traced to company-specific actions on which products to produce, how to price them and where to market them. Thus, management will matter more at a consumer product company than at a commodity company since the former’s success will depend upon its management decisions a great deal more with the latter. Competitive advantage: The nature of the competitive advantages possessed by a business can also affect how much management matters. In companies with long-standing and legacy competitive advantages, management has more of a caretaking role, than at companies that constantly need to reinvent their competitive advantages. While we do not intend to downplay the challenges that managers at Coca Cola and Aramco face, when managing the company, they face less of a challenge than managers at Costco, a comp

articles.title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
articles.snippet: NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers , providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference. Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure. To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS . Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1 , Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1 , Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65. Helping Enterprises Customize and Deploy Open Models Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding the models and services available through Microsoft Foundry to help developers bring these capabilities into business applications. Microsoft’s serverless Programmed Training offering gives developers control over post-training workflows while Foundry manages the underlying infrastructure. Enterprises can focus on their business data, evaluating model responses and improving model behavior. Foundry Managed Compute adds support for deploying custom model weights, helping connect model customization with deployment through Microsoft’s managed services. EY used Programmed Training in Microsoft Foundry to adapt NVIDIA Nemotron open models for classifying corporate purchasing records, improving accuracy on its evaluation dataset by 55% and lowering cost by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models. The work demonstrates how enterprises can customize open models for specialized business tasks. The expanded NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 lineup on Foundry Managed Compute supports different requirements across enterprise applications. Nemotron 3.5 Super is designed for long-running agents working across coding, research and business workflows, while Lightning supports applications that need fast responses and tool use. Complementary models help agents find relevant information with Nemotron Embed and Rerank, extract structured information from documents with Nemotron Parse and detect harmful content with Nemotron Content Safety. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt — designed for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning — and Transcribe, for speech recognition, are coming soon. Bringing AI Closer to Enterprise Data NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding deployment options beyond the cloud, helping organizations run models and agents closer to their data while maintaining control over their infrastructure and operations. Expanded support for Nemotron 3.5 in Foundry Local brings capabilities for reasoning, coding and tool-using agents to Azure Local environments. Retrieval models help applications find evidence across text, document images, charts and tables. Azure Local will also support NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners, giving organizations additional options for deploying AI on premises. Azure Local is expanding to NVIDIA Jetson Thor and Jetson Orin edge AI platforms to support industrial applications such as machine vision, robotics and autonomous operations. NVIDIA physical AI models, including Cosmos , are also being brought to Foundry Local. On Windows PCs powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark , NVIDIA and Microsoft will showcase local large language model experiences at Ignite, demonstrating how developers can run AI applications directly on devices. For organizations using Cloud PCs, the companies are bringing Direct Stream capabilities to GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs. These capabilities support demanding graphics applications with up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second and low latency, even over challenging networks. A limited preview is open for sign-ups, with public preview planned for early 2027. Connecting Scientific AI With Microsoft Discovery For scientific research, NVIDIA BioNemo Agent Toolkit and NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit are expanding into the Microsoft Discovery catalog , bringing models for life sciences, drug discovery and materials and chemical science into Microsoft’s agentic research platform. BioNeMo Agent Toolkit helps scientists use natural language to run computational biology workflows in Microsoft Discovery, with agents coordinating the tools and model calls needed to carry out the work.
