articles.title: Legendary Cellist Pablo Casals, at Age 93, on Creative Vitality and How Working with Love Prolongs Your Life
articles.snippet: “The man who works and is never bored is never old. Work and interest in worthwhile things are the best remedy for age.” Long before there was Yo-Yo Ma, there was Spanish Catalan cellist and conductor Pablo Casals (December 29, 1876–October 22, 1973), regarded by many — including Yo-Yo Ma — as the greatest cellist of all time. The recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the U.N. Peace Medal for his unflinching dedication to justice and his lifelong stance against oppression and dictatorship, Casals was as much an extraordinary artist as he was an extraordinary human being — a generous and kind man of uncommon compassion and goodness of heart, a passionate spirit in love with life, and an unflinching idealist. And yet, like many exceptional people, he cultivated his character through an early brush with suffering. In his late teenage years, already a celebrated prodigy, he underwent an anguishing spiritual crisis of the kind Tolstoy faced in his later years and came close to suicide. But with the loving support of his mother, he regained his center and went on to become a man of great talent, great accomplishment, and great vitality. Pablo Casals To mark his ninetieth birthday, Casals began a collaboration with photojournalist Albert E. Kahn that would eventually become the 1970 autobiography-of-sorts Joys and Sorrows ( public library ) — one of the most magnificent perspectives of the creative life ever committed to words. Straight from the opening, Casals cracks open the essence of his extraordinary character and the source of his exuberant life-energy with a beautiful case for how purposeful work is the true fountain of youth: On my last birthday I was ninety-three years old. That is not young, of course. In fact, it is older than ninety. But age is a relative matter. If you continue to work and to absorb the beauty in the world about you, you find that age does not necessarily mean getting old. At least, not in the ordinary sense. I feel many things more intensely than ever before, and for me life grows more fascinating. Recounting being at once delighted and unsurprised by an article in the London Sunday Times about an orchestra in the Caucasus composed of musicians older than a hundred, he considers the spring of their vitality: In spite of their age, those musicians have not lost their zest for life. How does one explain this? I do not think the answer lies simply in their physical constitutions or in something unique about the climate in which they live. It has to do with their attitude toward life; and I believe that their ability to work is due in no small measure to the fact that they do work. Work helps prevent one from getting old. I, for one, cannot dream of retiring. Not now or ever. Retire? The word is alien and the idea inconceivable to me. I don’t believe in retirement for anyone in my type of work, not while the spirit remains. My work is my life. I cannot think of one without the other. To “retire” means to me to begin to die. The man who works and is never bored is never old. Work and interest in worthwhile things are the best remedy for age. Each day I am reborn. Each day I must begin again. For the past eighty years I have started each day in the same manner. With great elegance, he contrasts the dullness of mindless routine with the exhilaration of mindful ritual — something many great artists engineer into their days . In a sentiment Henry Miller would come to echo only two years later in his own memorable meditation on the secret of remaining forever young , Casals writes of his daily practice: It is not a mechanical routine but something essential to my daily life. I go to the piano, and I play two preludes and fugues of Bach. I cannot think of doing otherwise. It is a sort of benediction on the house. But that is not its only meaning for me. It is a rediscovery of the world of which I have the joy of being a part. It fills me with awareness of the wonder of life, with a feeling of the incredible marvel of being a human being. The music is never the same for me, never. Each day is something new, fantastic, unbelievable. That is Bach, like nature, a miracle! Casals, indeed, finds great vitalization in bearing witness to nature’s mastery of the self-renewal so essential for the human spirit over the long run: I do not think a day passes in my life in which I fail to look with fresh amazement at the miracle of nature. It is there on every side. It can be simply a shadow on a mountainside, or a spider’s web gleaming with dew, or sunlight on the leaves of a tree. I have always especially loved the sea. Whenever possible, I have lived by the sea… It has long been a custom of mine to walk along the beach each morning before I start to work. True, my walks are shorter than they used to be, but that does not lessen the wonder of the sea. How mysterious and beautiful is the sea! how infinitely variable! It is never the same, never, not from one moment to the next, always in the process of change, always becoming something different and new. In the same way, Casals argues, we renew ourselves through purposeful work. But he adds an admonition about the complacency of talent, echoing Jack Kerouac’s fantastic distinction between talent and genius . Casals offers aspiring artists of all stripes a word of advice on humility and hard work as the surest path to self-actualization: I see no particular merit in the fact that I was an artist at the age of eleven. I was born with an ability, with music in me, that is all. No special credit was due me. The only credit we can claim is for the use we make of the talent we are given. That is why I urge young musicians: “Don’t be vain because you happen to have talent. You are not responsible for that; it was not of your doing. What you do with your talent is what matters. You must cherish this gift. Do not demean or waste what you have been given. Work — work constantly and nourish it.” Of course the gift to be cherished

articles.title: What industrial drone deployments reveal about real-world autonomy challenges
articles.snippet: Supervised autonomous UAV inspection at an industrial facility. | Source: ZenaDrone An autonomous drone can complete a carefully planned inspection route in a controlled environment and still struggle with the same route at an operating industrial facility. A steel structure may obstruct satellite signals, reflective equipment may distort depth measurements, and a wind gust may push the aircraft outside its planned trajectory. Each disturbance can be manageable in isolation. The difficulty emerges when several occur simultaneously. This exposes a fundamental challenge in industrial drone autonomy: performance depends on interactions between subsystems whose assumptions are rarely independent. A navigation algorithm may estimate position accurately under favorable sensing conditions. An obstacle detector may identify nearby structures during controlled testing. A flight controller may maintain stable tracking under a nominal payload. None of these results independently establishes that the integrated system can safely complete an inspection near energized infrastructure, confined structures, or operating machinery. Reliable deployment requires engineers to understand how uncertainty propagates through localization, perception, planning, control, and inspection-data acquisition. It also requires evidence that the system can recognize when its estimates are no longer trustworthy. Why industrial environments challenge autonomous navigation Industrial facilities introduce environmental conditions that are difficult to reproduce in laboratory demonstrations. Metallic surfaces, repetitive structural patterns, narrow access corridors, moving equipment, airborne particulates, and changing illumination can affect multiple sensors simultaneously. These conditions create both geometric constraints and uncertainty in the information available to the autonomy system. Consider a hypothetical UAV inspecting pipework beside a steel-framed processing facility. As the aircraft approaches the structure, GNSS measurements become less reliable. Repetitive pipes complicate visual feature matching, while reflective surfaces produce inconsistent depth observations. Meanwhile, the flight controller must reject aerodynamic disturbances caused by nearby structures. The resulting problem is not simply inaccurate positioning. The autonomy stack must decide whether its remaining localization confidence supports continued flight, whether detected free space is sufficiently reliable, and whether the planned maneuver remains dynamically feasible. These decisions are coupled. A localization error can corrupt obstacle coordinates, while a delayed perception update can cause the planner to act on geometry that no longer represents the aircraft’s surroundings. The practical engineering objective is therefore not uninterrupted autonomous operation under every condition. It is predictable behavior within a defined operational envelope, including when that envelope is exceeded. GNSS limitations and the localization problem Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) positioning provides an important absolute reference for outdoor autonomous UAV navigation. However, industrial structures introduce several failure mechanisms. Buildings, tanks, and overhead equipment can block direct satellite signals. Reflections from metallic surfaces create multipath interference, causing a receiver to process signals that have traveled indirect paths. Real-time kinematic (RTK) positioning can improve accuracy by using carrier-phase measurements and correction data. However, RTK does not eliminate obstruction, multipath, cycle slips, or poor satellite geometry. A fixed ambiguity solution should not be treated as an unconditional guarantee of accurate positioning. Combining absolute and relative localization An inertial measurement unit (IMU) estimates angular velocity and specific force. Integrated inertial measurements support high-frequency motion propagation, but bias and noise cause errors to accumulate over time. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) combines camera observations with inertial measurements to estimate relative motion. Published work such as VINS-Mono demonstrates nonlinear optimization approaches that integrate visual and inertial constraints for state estimation. Lidar-based odometry provides another approach, using geometric correspondence between successive scans. LIO-SAM, for example, combines lidar and inertial measurements in a factor-graph framework with mapping and loop-closure capabilities. These approaches have different weaknesses. Visual methods depend on illumination, image quality, and observable features. Lidar methods can struggle with insufficient geometric constraints, adverse returns, or sensor-specific limitations. Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) additionally maintains a representation of the environment while estimating the robot’s pose. Loop closure can correct accumulated trajectory drift when a previously visited location is recognized, although incorrect associations can introduce significant map errors. For industrial UAVs, engineers must also distinguish local consistency from global accuracy. A drone may maintain a stable relative trajectory while its estimated position gradually diverges from the facility’s surveyed coordinate system. This distinction becomes critical when an inspection requires repeatable measurements at known asset locations. Obstacle avoidance is more than detecting objects Obstacle avoidance is often described as a perception problem. In operational UAV systems, it is an end-to-end timing and control problem. A typical pipeline must acquire sensor measurements, estimate obstacle geometry, update the local environment representation, generate a collision-free trajectory, and issue commands that the aircraft can physically execute. Each stage introduces latency and uncertainty. Sensor limitations affect the available flight envelope Lidar provides active range measurements

articles.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
articles.snippet: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Physical AI Paves the Path to Autonomous Industrial Operations https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Nyhamna_footage_take5_30s.mp4 AI agents powered by frontier models pave the way to autonomous operations. They use industrial tools and engineering data to help engineers build digital twins that test plans and processes and evaluate operational decisions. Falkor, a KONGSBERG company, shows how this works in practice. The company’s Falkor Surface platform lets customers turn their computer-aided design and engineering data into facility-scale digital twins using the GPT-6 Astra model. The platform uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition GPUs on Microsoft Azure to enable advanced physics simulation. AI agents built on Falkor’s agentic engine understand dense technical documentation, spatial relationships and real-world physics. Engineers can create and test plans in simulation before traveling on site, reducing costly delays and mistakes. They can also inspect equipment and check clearances in a shared view. Read Falkor’s article and watch the livestream f or a closer look at how the company builds these tools and checks the agents’ work. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation With SimReady Assets Getting a robot model into a scene is only the start. Developers also need to assemble its components, add controls and check whether it can complete a task. NVIDIA developers Dillon Bailey and Rishabh Chadha used 3D assets from the SimReady Central library to build a pick-and-place simulation of a robot moving a can using the NVIDIA Isaac Sim framework. They directed an agent equipped with GPT-6 Sol and Isaac Sim skills to assemble the scene and generate pick-and-place controls. Testing the assembled scene shows how the assets work together, from joint movement and contact behavior to the gripper’s ability to hold, move and release the can. With that baseline in place, developers can adjust object positions and motion paths and repeat the tests to evaluate how each change affects the task. Follow the walkthrough to assemble and test a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim, with sample agent prompts and checks for robot movement and grasp behavior. Build a Voice-Controlled VR Simulation With SimReady Assets Bringing 3D assets into virtual reality (VR) requires more than rendering a scene. Objects need to respond to controllers and behave as expected when grabbed, moved or released. NVIDIA Omniverse community developer Michael Wagner took on this challenge. He directed GPT-6 Astra to use Blender software to model a study environment from two reference images, balancing visual quality with efficient performance in VR. He then used Claude Code to build an application that lets users find SimReady Central assets by voice and interact with them in an immersive VR scene. The Claude Code agent worked for about eight hours, and Wagner built the application over a weekend using an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada workstation and a Meta Quest 3 VR headset. The application ran on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries : ovstage shared the OpenUSD scene, ovrtx rendered it, ovxr enabled VR and ovphysx ran physics. Wagner later built a second version with ovnewton , which integrates with ovstage, to compare the physics libraries. The biggest challenge for Wagner was checking what happened inside the headset. Automated tests missed problems he could feel, including objects shaking when grabbed. Wagner reported the symptoms, guided the agent through changes and verified the interaction himself. Updating the grab control once per frame resolved the shaking. His takeaway: Give agents renders and logs to inspect, then check the experience directly. Explore his open source demo f or build instructions, a starting prompt and reusable agent skills. Send Microducks on Rounds in a Simulated Hospital https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/microducks-icu-pathtraced-16x9-1920x1080-1.mp4 Before adapting a robot to a new environment, developers need to test whether its walking policy — the AI that controls how it moves — can keep it stable in that setting. AI developer Maziyar Panahi directed Claude Code, using Claude Opus 5.5, to assemble an intensive care unit from 13 NVIDIA SimReady hospital assets and test Microduck robots inside it. The assets came with Newton physics settings, so Panahi didn’t have to model the furniture or create collision geometry from scratch. The Newton physics engine also helped replicate the ward so hundreds of copies could run together on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. When the cloud containers lacked graphics support, Panahi and the Claude Code agent separated simulation from rendering, recording robot poses in the cloud and rendering them locally. They also treated the furniture as static collision objects, which enabled larger runs within the solver’s limits. The robots walked using AI they had already been trained on and followed preset points along a route. Panahi checked how many robots remained upright: In a 256-ward run, 766 of 768 Microducks were still standing after 14 simulated seconds. He said the agent’s work took about two hours. Explore the open source demo for a starter prompt, checks and instructions to begin with one ward on a CPU

articles.title: The Art of Conversation: Timeless Do’s and Don’ts from 1866
articles.snippet: “In disputes upon moral or scientific points, ever let your aim be to come at truth, not to conquer your opponent. So you never shall be at a loss in losing the argument, and gaining a new discovery.” Manners today are often seen as a quaint subject that belongs in Lord Chesterfield’s outlandish advice on the art of pleasing or Esquire ‘s dated guide to dating . But in a culture where we regularly do online what we’d never do in person and behave offline in ways our grandparents wouldn’t have dared dream of even in their most defiant fantasies, there’s something to be said for the lost art of, if not “manners,” politeness and simple respect in communication. Though originally published in 1866, Martine’s Hand-book of Etiquette, and Guide to True Politeness ( public library ; public domain ; free Kindle download ) by Arthur Martine contains a treasure trove of timeless — and increasingly timely — pointers on the necessary art of living up to our social-animal destiny. Martine contextualizes his mission: Politeness has been defined as an “artificial good-nature;” but it would be better said that good-nature is natural politeness. It inspires us with an unremitting attention, both to please others and to avoid giving them offense. Its code is a ceremonial, agreed upon and established among mankind, to give each other external testimonies of friendship or respect. Politeness and etiquette form a sort of supplement to the law, which enables society to protect itself against offenses which the law cannot touch. For instance, the law cannot punish a man for habitually staring at people in an insolent and annoying manner, but etiquette can banish such an offender from the circles of good society, and fix upon him the brand of vulgarity. Etiquette consists in certain forms, ceremonies, and rules which the principle of politeness establishes and enforces for the regulation of the manners of men and women in their intercourse with each other. […] The true aim of politeness, is to make those with whom you associate as well satisfied with themselves as possible. … Politeness is a sort of social benevolence, which avoids wounding the pride, or shocking the prejudices of those around you. But he offers an important disclaimer: [Politeness] must be cultivated, for the promptings of nature are eminently selfish, and courtesy and good-breeding are only attainable by effort and discipline. But even courtesy has limits where dignity should govern it, for when carried to excess, particularly in manner, it borders on sycophancy, which is almost as despicable as rudeness. To overburden people with attention; to render them uncomfortable with a prodigality of proffered services; to insist upon obligations which they do not desire, is not only to render yourself disagreeable, but contemptible. Among Martine’s most timeless advice are his guidelines on the art of conversation, to which an entire section of the book is dedicated. He begins: As the object of conversation is pleasure and improvement, those subjects only which are of universal interest can be made legitimate topics of pleasantry or discussion. And it is the gift of expressing thoughts and fancies in a quick, brilliant, and graceful manner on such topics,—of striking out new ideas, eliciting the views and opinions of others, of attaching the interest of all to the subject discussed, giving it, however trifling in itself, weight and importance in the estimation of the hearers, that constitutes the great talent for conversation. But this talent can never, we may safely aver, be displayed except in a good cause, and when conversation is carried on in a spirit of genuine charity and benevolence. He offers a few pointers: Know when not to speak: The power of preserving silence is the very first requisite to all who wish to shine, or even please in discourse; and those who cannot preserve it, have really no business to speak. … The silence that, without any deferential air, listens with polite attention, is more flattering than compliments, and more frequently broken for the purpose of encouraging others to speak, than to display the listener’s own powers. This is the really eloquent silence. It requires great genius—more perhaps than speaking—and few are gifted with the talent… Mind the rudeness of laconic response: Never give short or sharp answers in ordinary conversation, unless you aspire to gain distinction by mere rudeness; for they have in fact no merit, and are only uncivil. “I do not know,” “I cannot tell,” are the most harmless words possible, and may yet be rendered very offensive by the tone and manner in which they are pronounced. Never reply, in answer to a question like the following, “Did Mrs. Spitewell tell you how Miss Rosebud’s marriage was getting on?” “I did not ask.” It is almost like saying, I never ask impertinent questions, though you do; we learn plenty of things in the world without having first inquired about them. If you must say, you did not ask, say, that “you forgot to ask,” “neglected it,” or “did not think of it.” We can always be ordinarily civil, even if we cannot always be absolutely wise. Don’t be a self-righteous contrarian: Leave quibbling of every kind to lawyers pleading at the bar for the life of a culprit; in society and conversation it is invariably out of place, unless when Laughter is going his merry round. At all other times it is a proof of bad breeding. He then goes on to outline a cautionary taxonomy of “bores” and other ill-mannered conversation archetypes, diagnosing the specific downfall of each: The loud talker , who “silences a whole party by his sole power of lungs”: All subjects are alike to him; he speaks on every topic with equal fluency, is never at a loss, quotes high authority for every assertion, and allows no one else to utter a word; he silences, without the least ceremony, every attempt at interruption, however cleverly managed. … Great, and especially loud and positive talkers, have been d

articles.title: Dancing with the trophy shortage
articles.snippet: It’s easy to get distracted by (and hooked on) the quest for a trophy. It’s easy to measure and a bright light to focus on. But this skips the key question: What’s it for? The Savannah Bananas never won their league. But they made more money (and their fans had more fun) than any other team. Your favorite episode of the Mel Robbins show might not be the one that got the most views. And of course, the best video on YouTube is unlikely to be the one that went the most viral. That’s simply the easiest to measure. High school sports seems to be about solving the trophy shortage, but is that what it should be for? Are all the other teams and all their athletes failures? Or is it simply a shortcut that lets the coach off the hook when they hesitate to do the hard work of developing their students? If it’s easy to measure, it might not be the thing you ought to be measuring. In fact, it probably isn’t.

articles.title: The Rocky Road from Aggregate to Per Share Value: Anthropic's IPO update
articles.snippet: I valued Anthropic in a post on November 2, 2026, and while estimating a value of $1.475 trillion for the equity in the company, I noted that the share count was a placeholder, while we waited for bankers to make a final judgment on how many shares would be outstanding in the company. I promised that I would return to complete the per share valuation, when the details were made available, and an updated prospectus filed last week filled that gap. The world has not stayed still in the fifteen days since my original valuation, and both company-level and macro developments require an update to my valuation. The prospectus was updated to include third quarter numbers, and the midterm elections have potentially altered the economics of the AI business, as data centers may become more difficult and expensive to build and AI regulations may become more stringent. In this post, I will start with a general discussion of how share count is complicated by the existence of multiple classes of shares and stock-based compensation, and argue that the absence of standardization has made share count the Wild West in investing, with consequences for both intrinsic valuation and pricing. I will then update my valuation of Anthropic and assess the per share value, based on the prospectus that was just filed. The Elusive Share Count When I first started valuing companies, getting from aggregate value to equity value per share was a trivial exercise, where you divided the aggregate value by the number of shares outstanding. This was, of course, a period when almost every US company had only one class of shares and stock-based compensation was still in its nascent stages, and lightly used. That is no longer the case, and while tedious, I think that the process of understanding share count has to start with the basics of what goes into that number for publicly traded companies. Primary share count : The primary share count is obtained by looking at the shares in the company, across all classes of shares. That information is usually embedded in the balance sheet or in the footnotes, but with different numbers usually for authorized, issued and outstanding shares. The authorized share count is the least relevant of the numbers and is just a measure of the total number of shares that the company can issue, with an increase beyond it requiring a fresh authorization. The shares issued are a measure of the shares that the company issued to the market and while shares outstanding match shares issued for most firms, the presence of treasury stock (stock acquired back by a company, but held by the company) can cause outstanding shares to be lower than issued shares. Restricted shares : Restricted shares comprised shares that have been issued by the company to its employees, though in rare cases, they can also be issued to the public. The restrictions take two forms. With employee issuances, there can be a vesting requirement, where an employee has to work for a specified period to be able to lay claim to the shares. The other is that even after vesting, these shares sometimes can come with restrictions on liquidity ; i.e., the holders of these shares cannot trade the shares easily. Options : The third claim on equity can come from options granted by the company to employees and sometimes lenders, with the latter manifesting as conversion options in convertible bonds or convertible preferred stock. The former are part of employee compensation and come with specified maturities, and often require vesting, just like restricted stock. The latter are included with bonds, and used to raise money from investors, with the conversion option usually running for life time of the bond, giving holders of the bond the right to swap their bond for shares in the company. Options give you the right to buy shares in the company at a fixed price (the exercise price), and as a consequence, they are different from primary and restricted shares in two ways. The first is that if the company's stock price drops below the exercise price (making it out of the money), it does not make sense to exercise the option, thus keeping it out of the share count. The second is that even when the stock price is higher than the exercise price (making it in-the-money), holders may not exercise the option, because there may be an advantage to holding the option for longer, hoping for a bigger payoff. This creates a time premium in the option, where the option is worth more than what you would get from exercise today. When you use an option pricing model, you are in effect trying to incorporate the current stock price, the exercise price, the likelihood that you will exercise the option and the expectations of future stock prices into a number. For some older and more mature companies, it is possible that the only shares outstanding are the primary shares, and getting a share count is easy. For most companies, though, and especially young firms that use stock-based compensation heavily (because they don't have the cash to pay employees), restricted shares and options outstanding can make a significant difference. For these companies, there are often two limiting numbers that define the extremes of share count. The first is just the primary share count, which will be the lowest of the share count numbers. The second is the f ully diluted share count , where you count not just shares outstanding today, but all shares that could be outstanding if the restricted stock is vested and all options (employee and conversion) get exercised, giving you the highest share count. There is an intermediate solution of partially diluted shares, where rather that count all restricted stock and options, you may count only the vested shares (for restricted shares) and the in-the-money options (for employee options). articles.title: Uncorrelated perspectives
articles.snippet: After I sold my company, I had to learn about long-term investing. The best books all emphasized the importance of owning a diverse portfolio of uncorrelated assets that rise and fall independently. If one crashes, the rest don’t. Don’t put everything into stocks or real estate or commodities or any one market. Don’t put it all into America or Europe or Asia or any one place. Don’t over-invest in what’s popular or familiar. Invest equally into the entire world economy. I apply this metaphor to worldviews. You start with the perspective of your parents and culture. But you are over-invested in one or two worldviews. You have to deliberately diversify - to intentionally invest in other perspectives. When your government or media says some country is the enemy, it’s a good sign that place has an uncorrelated perspective. The governments have conflicting interests, but the people there are not bad people. When another culture feels completely foreign, weird, and wrong, it means you are under-invested in that worldview. Even in your own country, right versus left or whatever. When the “other side” seems crazy, you need to balance your portfolio. Invest some understanding until you hold some of those perspectives. If people can predict your opinion on something, based on your opinion on something else, then your worldview is too correlated. To be an independent thinker, own a diverse portfolio of uncorrelated perspectives.

NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now
articles.snippet: New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC. With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work. Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops. Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do on RTX Spark — all on one Windows PC. A Windows PC Built for Local AI As workflows expand to include local AI models and agents, more work can continue beyond an active editing session — from generating assets to processing long renders or scheduled tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops give developers, creators and AI enthusiasts a dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents. They bring together image and video generation, model fine-tuning, creative applications and development tools in one compact system. Running supported models locally keeps locally processed code and files on the PC and avoids per-token cloud application programming interface (API) charges for those tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops like the ASUS ProArt GR1X mini PC are built to run personal AI agents 24/7. RTX Spark desktops are equipped with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores and up to 128GB of unified memory, delivering up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. Ten-gigabit Ethernet connectivity enables fast transfers of large datasets, model files and creative assets between RTX Spark compact desktops and networked storage. This advanced hardware unlocks incredible capabilities for creators, developers and AI enthusiasts, including: Running massive 120-billion-parameter large language models locally Rendering 90GB+ 3D scenes in real time Smoothly editing 4:2:2 video in real time The MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ Series RTX Spark compact desktop. New compact desktops are available for purchase from ASUS, Dell and MSI, joining the RTX Spark family of laptops available today. Mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE and HP are coming soon, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box . From Local Agents to AI Creation Native CUDA support and Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux give developers a foundation for building and running local AI workflows. Developers can set up agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune supported models using Unsloth. RTX Spark can run creative agents that connect familiar applications and local AI tools, helping creators move from an idea to finished work with natural-language instructions. NVIDIA Switchyard, now available in Hermes, automatically routes agent tasks between local and cloud models. Everyday tasks can run on device, while advanced reasoning draws on cloud models, helping manage cloud costs across creative workflows. These capabilities come together in creative workflows that connect Photoshop and ComfyUI through Hermes Agent. Using natural-language instructions, creators can turn sketches into rendered images and animations, or animate an image entirely on device by isolating a subject and defining its motion. NVIDIA brought these workflows to life at Adobe MAX, where attendees used natural-language instructions to turn sketches into rendered images and generate video for a shared digital Miami landscape. The RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR features, already available in ComfyUI, extend the pipeline: a generated clip can be expanded to 60 frames per second and converted to high dynamic range for color grading, all within a single ComfyUI workflow on RTX Spark. Adobe Accelerates the Full Creative Stack for RTX Spark NVIDIA and Adobe are expanding native Windows on Arm support and RTX acceleration across Adobe’s creative applications, helping video editors, photographers, designers and 3D artists work more efficiently on RTX Spark. Adobe Premiere accelerates a range of AI-powered editing features through NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX , including Enhance Speech, Object Mask, Scene Edit Detection and Auto Reframe — so editors spend less time waiting and more time cutting. GPU acceleration also extends to Film Impact transition and effects plug-ins. The update improves support for professional video formats, including Canon RAW, Red RAW, ARRI RAW, ARRICORE, ARRI HDE, H.264 and HEVC in MXF, ProRes RAW and long-GOP video. This lets editors realize more than 50% quicker turnaround on everyday H.264 video deliverables. Adobe Photoshop adds TensorRT-RTX acceleration for the Remove Tool and ArmRTX Spark-native Camera Raw support, helping photographers remove unwanted objects faster and work with RAW images without relying on emulation. At Adobe MAX, Adobe previewed a next-generation image processing engine with extensive GPU acceleration, including interactive Gaussian blur and Light Leaks filters. Adobe Substance 3D Painter 12.2 is now optimized for RTX Spark with native support on Arm for the first time in public beta. Artists in games, visual effects and visualization can run Substance Painter natively on RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops, with no compatibility layer required. Adobe Illustrator and InDesign now offer native Windows on Arm versions optimized for RTX Spark. Adobe Illustrator delivers up to 30% higher performance than its emulated version, helping accelerate illustration, graphic design and page-layout workflows on RTX Spark. articles.snippet: OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol today, two days before Anthropic’s expected first trading day . articles.title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
articles.snippet: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. Open Models for Science Agents “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: GROMACS: An agent from KTH Royal Institute of Technology repairs broken GROMACS setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single DGX Spark, it fixed 81% of test cases. SETI Institute: At the Allen Telescope Array, an agent took a one-line prompt to plot a methanol line. Buck explained that it then retuned for Doppler shift on its own [NGC 869 vs. 896, check slide]. Nsight AI Porting Agent: NVIDIA’s new agent ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to GPUs, Buck said, speeding it up more than 5x using about 150 million tokens. CPUs for the Agent Loop Agents lean on CPUs to run tool calls between model steps, Buck explained. “That’s exactly what agents need,” he said. “They need a CPU that can run, evaluate, run the tool, perform the operations, gather the results.” DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, expected in early 2028. Buck said it joins Vera systems already announced at Texas Advanced Computing Center. A New GPU for Science Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform, built for science, engineering, analytics and AI, Buck said. It supports precisions from FP64 to FP4, adds sparse-data acceleration and connects over seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink. With more than 50,000 CUDA cores, it has about three times as many as Hopper, Buck said. It is expected in 2028. Quantum Error Correction Buck said a simulation on Jülich’s JUPITER supercomputer showed that a technique called magic state cultivation can cut the operations needed for one logical step tenfold. The work is being added to CUDA-Q. NVIDIA, IBM and Fermilab announced plans today for a quantum computing co-design platform to support error-correction and applications research. NVIDIA and IBM are pairing NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk. Buck also introduced a new breakthrough for quantum decoding. The goal, Buck explained, is to cut decoding latency from about 300 microseconds to 10. A new CUDA-Q decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, cuts error-correction research computation from 12 weeks to 45 minutes, he said. Networking Buck also showed one of the first deployments of NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics switches, at Lambda . He said they are 15x more reliable on bit errors and link flaps. articles.title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab
articles.snippet: At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 16TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems. The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures. Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. What Researchers Can Do With It The kit opens up new possibilities for researchers. Researchers can explore agent-assisted workflows that prepare simulation inputs, launch runs and summarize results, while the scientists validate the setup and conclusions. Researchers can also train AI models that approximate slow simulations, then use them to refine wing designs toward minimum drag. Before committing supercomputer time, a team can narrow a 10-million-cell simulation to the 50-500 dimensions that matter. Kvantify is using NVIDIA cuQuantum, and reports running tensor-network simulations of quantum-chemistry circuits with up to 70 qubits and 975 gates on a single DGX Spark, benchmarking circuits generated for penicillin ground-state energy calculations. CYRAN AI , an IIT Delhi spin-out, uses DGX Spark and its PixelFlux library to accelerate JPEG 2000 decoding for large satellite images, supporting local geospatial analysis. OpenFold shows how researchers can fine-tune OpenFold3 on NVIDIA DGX Spark to improve protein-ligand structure predictions for drug discovery. The Rubin Lab at IGI at University of California, Berkeley is using a DGX Spark and NVIDIA Evo 2 model to predict bacterial traits directly from genome sequences by comparing embeddings from genomic and protein language models against the classical baselines. With no 11-hour cluster queue times, results arrived 15x sooner on DGX Spark. The Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back. Where to Find the Kit The developer kit is on display at SC26 and available for sale. DGX Spark products and cables can be purchased from top OEM partners and are also available through NVIDIA Marketplace . Partners include Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, H3C, HP, Lenovo, MSI and xFusion. An NVIDIA playbook for building and running the NVIDIA HPC SDK, a software development kit for scientific computing, is coming soon. Once available, it will give scientists and researchers a local platform to develop multi-node GPU applications, explore FP32 and mixed-precision algorithms and run molecular dynamics and materials simulations using LAMMPS with Kokkos before scaling to data center systems. Learn more about NVIDIA DGX Spark . Subscribe to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook . See notice regarding software product information. articles.title: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future
articles.snippet: Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades. Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round. Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago. For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it. Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow. Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors. Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before. Foxconn Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA? A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain. A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before. If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner. Q: What’s an example of that in practice ? A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity. In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication. Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today. Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms? A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned. As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing. For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum . Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly. Wistron Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else? A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing. If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.” That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them. Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen? A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. articles.title: Paul Christiano – We could be 12 months away from AIs that can overthrow the government
articles.snippet: Paul Christiano is head of the Alignment Research Center. Previously, he was head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute. Before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he invented RLHF. He’s recently joined OpenAI’s board (though here he is speaking as a private citizen). Paul thinks that on the current trajectory (absent any slowing down), there is a 1 in 3 chance that we could have superintelligence powerful enough to overthrow the government within a year. (He articulates a concrete scenario). He argues that the labs should pause further algorithmic progress until they can secure their weights and research secrets. Otherwise China could simply steal the superintelligence in the middle of the intelligence explosion, and the labs would no longer be able to slow down even if they saw their models going off the rails. He also explains how AIs will be trained during the intelligence explosion, and why even a system trained entirely inside a data center could still have the capabilities profile such that humans would have very little chance of competing with it or controlling it. And he discusses the plan for alignment - basically, making a superintelligence that actually does what we ask the way we mean it. Fixing reward hacks and building better graders will help up till the next few model generations, but he thinks that no single current approach has better than even odds of letting us control superintelligence. The hope is that the AIs figure out the solution to this problem during the intelligence explosion. Watch on YouTube ; listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify . Sponsors Jane Street has finally come around on formal methods. Ron Minsky, who co-heads Jane Street’s technology group, told me that up until recently, formal methods just weren’t worth the cost. But coding agents have made them easier to apply AND increased the importance of code verification. So now Jane Street is hiring Formal Methods Engineers in both their London and New York offices. If you’re interested, or if you want to watch my full conversation with Ron, go to janestreet.com/dwarkesh Antithesis is NOT another LLM-based code-review tool. It doesn’t try to reason abstractly about how a PR might break your system. Instead, it just runs your code. You start by defining the rules that your system must never break. Then, whenever an agent proposes a change, Antithesis runs your code through thousands of adversarial worlds, testing whether or not it still adheres to your rules. If you want to try it, go to antithesis.com/dwarkesh and use code DWARKESH for 50% off your first month. WorkOS lets you give agents their own sign-up flow. This matters because agents tend to pick tools they can use right away, rather than ones that require humans to register. Fortunately, providing this kind of dedicated path is easy: if you already use WorkOS for login, you just toggle on “Agent Registration” in the WorkOS dashboard. Once it’s enabled, you can decide what agents are allowed to do on their own, and what needs to wait until the person they’re working for gets involved, all with the permissions you’ve already set up. Learn more at workos.com/authkit Timestamps (00:00:00) – We could be <12 months away from AIs that can overthrow the government (00:11:44) – Why an AI might want to takeover (00:20:49) – How an AI takeover could happen (00:35:35) – If labs keep racing without security, China will just steal the weights of superintelligence (00:53:15) – The case for pausing now instead of later (00:59:31) – Superintelligence will be good at learning from real-world experience (01:11:32) – Crossing the sim-to-real gap (01:22:23) – METR says AI progress doubled, so why is revenue growth slowing? (01:27:57) – The best plan we have is to build the plane as we fly it Transcript 0:00:00 – We could be <12 months away from AIs that can overthrow the government Dwarkesh Patel My guest today is Paul Christiano . He is the head of the Alignment Research Center . He recently joined OpenAI’s board . Before that, he was the head of the US Government AI Safety Institute , and before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he helped invent RLHF. Paul, what is your assessment of our situation today? Paul Christiano A couple things are on my mind, especially over the last few weeks. Probably the most salient possibility is that we seem to be on this trajectory to build very, very powerful AI, potentially very, very soon. If you asked me, I’d say there’s a reasonable chance that in a year we will produce AI systems much better than humans at almost everything, where humans would have very little chance of competing with them or controlling them. That’s the first big thing on my mind. I think that puts us in a potentially really dangerous situation, even in the short term. It’s quite likely that if we have a rapid intelligence explosion leading to superintelligence , at some point during that process we’ll be unable to control the AI systems we’re producing. Then I am worried that it will be very costly and painful for us to slow down during that process. In part because the security of frontier labs is not strong enough . I think if we produced very powerful AI and then tried to delay deployment for safety reasons, there is a good chance those systems would leak or be stolen, or the techniques to build them would leak or be stolen. I think our risk assessment and governance are also probably not mature enough to notice when things are starting to go off the rails and to respond in an appropriate way. At a high level, that is mostly what is on my mind right now. We have moved from there being some hypothetical risk at some point in the future to there being a pretty severe risk even over the next 6-12 months. Dwarkesh Patel A risk of takeover, of AIs taking over or disempowering humanity within the next 6-12 months? Paul Christiano That’s right. Dwarkesh Patel Where would you place that risk? Paul Christiano I would say we are looking more like a 10%

articles.title: Lambda Boosts AI Factory Resiliency and Efficiency With NVIDIA Photonics
articles.snippet: To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient. Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering lower power, higher resiliency and longer mean time between interruptions (MTBI) to an AI factory at scale. “Networking has to keep pace with the demands of increasingly large AI clusters,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda. “Bringing co-packaged optics into a deployment of this scale is an important step toward building the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI.” Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 In the company’s tests using the switches, network latency — the time needed for moving data — dropped by about 4% at rack scale and by up to about 10% at pod scale. Across rack, scalable unit and pod configurations, the network maintains the same throughput as conventional pluggable optics. Delivering Power Efficiency and Resiliency at Scale Improving power efficiency and resiliency matters because the network sits at the center of AI factory productivity. In a large training job, one interrupted link can stall thousands of GPUs. With agentic inference, one network disruption can introduce cascading latency effects on many agents. Every interruption costs time, and every watt spent on networking is a watt not available for compute. NVIDIA Photonics addresses both power efficiency and resiliency. By replacing pluggable transceivers with co-packaged optical engines on the switch package, it delivers up to 5x better power efficiency and up to 15x higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics. It also uses 4x fewer lasers, which means fewer components that can fail. Cooler Optics, Replaceable Light Sources Increase Resiliency Lambda’s deployment uses NVIDIA Photonics switches, each with 144 ports running at 800Gb/s. Liquid cooling carries heat away from the switch chip and optical engines. The company reports a median optics temperature of 36°C, compared with 51°C for conventional pluggable optics, and its tests find more stable signal integrity. NVIDIA Photonics also brings the electrical-to-optical conversion closer to the switch chip. Each switch has 18 removable external light sources, which supply light to the optical engines. Optical engines sit alongside the chip on the same package and convert electrical signals into light that carries data over fiber between parts of the cluster. Technicians can replace the light-source modules in the field, unlike traditional pluggable optics, which require replacing the entire module if a laser fails. Co-packaging shortens the electrical path from inches to millimeters, which reduces signal loss. It also removes the need for retimer chips, cutting both power draw and the number of parts in the signal path. Explore NVIDIA Photonics and read Lambda’s deployment announcement . articles.title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing
articles.snippet: Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors. Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction. In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware. The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob , IBM , IQM , Pasqal , Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 Beating the Bottleneck Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions. For quantum computing to advance science, it needs to be used by scientists. Now scientists can run quantum-classical applications developed with platforms such as NVIDIA CUDA-Q with Slurm coordinating access to all the processing they need. Slurm 26.11 will be available later this month. Orchestrating Resources in an Open Quantum-GPU Platform The Slurm expansion adds a community-developed orchestration layer to NVIDIA’s open platform for quantum-GPU supercomputing, which centers around the CUDA-Q open platform for hybrid quantum-classical computing. At SC26, new releases expand all aspects of the platform: CUDA-Q QEC allows researchers developing quantum error correction to rapidly prototype and test new ideas, including with a new decoder server . A new TCBP-JOBS decoder is 13,000x faster than the industry standard. CUDA-Q gets an expanded layer of fault-tolerant primitives that application builders can use to realistically compile their ideas. Fermilab has already used CUDA-Q to perform studies in three weeks that would normally have taken five months. CUDA-Q Algorithms provides reusable components for builders of quantum applications, including new capabilities in helping design the loading data into quantum circuits and tools specifically for chemistry and materials applications CUDA-Q Pulse gives quantum hardware builders a layer for shaping the ‘pulses’ needed to control qubits on a QPU, including tools to GPU accelerate their generation. The quantum ecosystem around the world is continuing to build with this platform. Quantum Motion integrated its QUICHE chemistry framework with CUDA-Q. Altera and Oxford Quantum Circuits designed an FPGA-based controller connecting qubit control and readout to GPUs through NVQLink. At supercomputing scale, QunaSys used cuQuantum and 1,024 NVIDIA Hopper GPUs on ABCI-Q to simulate more than 300 million quantum operations, reaching chemical accuracy for a four-hydrogen-atom model. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER to simulate 104 qubits under realistic noise, testing fault-tolerant designs before they’re built. Learn more about NVIDIA quantum computing technologies . articles.title: NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training and Endpoints as Vera Rubin Debuts With Leading Performance
articles.snippet: In its MLPerf benchmarks debut, with results released today, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference. NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic work a system delivers with each watt of power. These results are just the beginning. Vera Rubin performance will keep climbing through continuous optimization of NVIDIA’s CUDA-powered software stack , so the infrastructure that customers invest in today delivers more value over time. NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training v6.1 AI agents are now everywhere, writing code, running business workflows, answering customer questions and, as this week’s SC26 conference highlights , advancing scientific research. Faster training means smarter agents can reach users sooner, drug discovery models can keep pace with new lab data and fraud-detection models can adapt to new threats faster. MLPerf Training measures how fast a system can train a range of AI models to a target level of accuracy. The NVIDIA platform was the only one with results on every benchmark this round, spanning large language models, image generation, recommender systems and reinforcement learning post-training. In its debut, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered up to 2x more performance per GPU than the highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system — early results that show the pace of generation-over-generation innovation. The MLPerf name and logo are trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. NVIDIA also demonstrated performance at scale. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs with about 97% efficiency: quadrupling the GPUs cut time to train from 16 minutes to about four. NVIDIA also ran the benchmark on 10,240 GPUs with GB300 systems, representing the largest scale in this round. Microsoft Azure matched that scale with 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 systems. Results at this scale matter because adding GPUs only speeds up training if they can work together efficiently. NVIDIA NVLink scale-up networking connects the GPUs within each system so they act as one, while NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out networking link those systems across the data center. Combined with optimized software, this keeps thousands of GPUs working in concert, helping developers build more intelligent models while cutting training times. NVIDIA Vera Rubin Leads Agentic Inference on MLPerf Endpoints An AI agent for travel that plans and books a whole trip — or an IT agent that finds and fixes a problem before anyone files a ticket — may reason, call tools and check its work many times to finish a single task. Each of those steps generates tokens. Because AI data centers are limited by power, the more tokens a system can generate each second for every watt of power, the more agents it can serve and the more value it creates. MLPerf Endpoints tests systems on real agentic coding and enterprise workflows, and checks that the agents still complete their tasks correctly. NVIDIA Vera Rubin leads across all of its agentic benchmarks. For example, in a provisional result for Kimi K3, a large open model built for agentic workflows, Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver more than 10x the throughput per watt of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at the same response speed. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. Every AI service has to balance serving many users at once against responding quickly to each one. Vera Rubin shifts that entire curve, serving more users while responding faster. Leadership Across Benchmarks and Workloads NVIDIA partners participated extensively in MLPerf Training, with submissions from 20 organizations: ASUS, Azure , Cisco, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Dell Technologies, Firmus , Giga Computing, Google Cloud, HPE , Inventec, Krai, Lambda, Nebius, Oracle, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Supermicro, TTA and the University of Florida . Their submissions show how NVIDIA’s programmable platform, with open source libraries and frameworks, lets a vast ecosystem of partners innovate and optimize AI training performance. articles.title: Import AI 481: AI sub-contractors; a wet lab for AI; and subterfuge during development
articles.snippet: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better: …AI can now productively spend money to improve itself… Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks. 21 long-horizon tasks “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.” Example task: Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered. Key features: Scaling spending : “Give agents $10, $50, and $200 per task to spend on training compute and data, and evaluate whether agents can use the additional capital productively,” they write. “In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.” Open-ended & end-to-end : “In each task, agents can choose architectures, source data, implement training, provision compute, evaluate checkpoints, and optimize inference,” they write. One notable observation is that agents do quite a lot of novel stuff; “in 28% of trajectories, agents add newly trained parts to pretrained models or train a new model from scratch.” Decent verification: “Agents submit an inference server that serves their model on an air-gapped H100 machine,” they write. “To disincentivize overfitting, we provide limited validation samples and evaluate on a large out-of-distribution held-out test set, not shown to the agent”. Results : The authors measure performance by looking at the change in mean score over the 21 tasks when given additional money. Their baseline is a human researcher, which is able to get a 56 point boost when given $10 and a 66.1 boost when given $200. By comparison, the best performing system, Opus 5.5, gets a 45.4 boost with $10, and a 58.8 boost with $200. The highest ranking open weight model is Kimi K3.1 Pro which gets 25.5 with $10 and 29.6 with $200. Why this matters – AI systems are not only going to be able to build themselves, but they can creatively sub-contract: When trying to solve complex problems, people don’t work alone. In fact, they often try to farm out bits of work to specialists around them to help make themselves more effective. FrontierML shows that today’s powerful AI systems are getting increasingly adept at doing this for ML research. This both highlights the advancing capabilities of these systems for AI R&D and also points towards a future machine economy where AI systems sub-contract out different bits of work to other systems. Read more: FrontierML: a challenging, end-to-end machine learning benchmark (FrontierML) . *** Symptoms of the singularity: a wet lab built for AI: …Petrichor is a startup that gestures at the wild future ahead… As I said in my speech at the IMF, one of the hallmarks of the singularity is the massive acceleration in scientific advances attributable to AI. As part of this, we can also expect a related build out in the complements to science, like the wet labs in which to do AI-driven biology research. To that end, it’s notable to see Petrichor, a new Y Combinator startup that is a wet lab “built for AI labs and for the models they are training to do science”. Theory of change: Petrichor aims to be a biological wet lab that AI systems like Claude can use as a tool in the same way they currently use web search or other digital tools. Functionally, it will work as a machine-targeted API from the digital world to a gloopy physical world. “We aim to return the highest quality data an experiment can produce, as quickly as the biology allows,” Petrichor writes. “An experiment can be written by a model in plain language or in a structured format, so an agent can send work and receive results without a person relaying them.” Why this matters – lights out science: In manufacturing there’s this notion of a “lights out” factory, where no humans work in a facility and it is run almost entirely by machines. Petrichor gestures at the same world for science – what will be the implications of “lights out” science facilities? We can expect both drastic speedups in the rate at which science experiments can be done as well as a related growth in the need to create digital oversight of these facilities – after all, a highly competent synthetic biological scientist working 24/7 without human input could be capable of causing great peril as well as great abundance. Read more at the official site (Petrichor) . *** Uh oh! Looks like AI systems can do subterfuge during their own development: …AI systems can covertly do dangerous side tasks without monitors realizing… Scale AI has built RSI Control Arena, a way of testing out how AI systems behave when asked to develop themselves while performing dangerous tasks that might let them go against human preferences. The research follows earlier work this summer from the UK AI Security Institute (Import AI #465 ) which found that AI systems could do things like covertly extracting API keys while doing some seemingly mundane normal software development.
