articles.title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
articles.snippet: I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell , the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die . The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies , the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke. “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics , based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death. When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away. Christie Hemm Klok The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.” For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold. But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga , who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit. Why Telesurgery Starts With Stroke As recently as the early ’90s , physicians who treated stroke struggled with “ therapeutic nihilism .” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery . In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event. Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right. The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.” Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment

articles.title: Obituaries
articles.snippet: Listen to this post: Dearly beloved, we are gathered here today to get through this thing called life. ― Prince Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, 1993–2026 Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday, November 12, 2026. He had been CEO of the company ever since he founded it on April 5, 1993. Nvidia started out as a graphics card company; Huang’s exit — nominally because of affairs with a buyer who may or may not have been a Chinese spy, as well as at least two company employees — was ultimately because Nvidia was, by the powers that be, considered a defense contractor, and Huang never adjusted. In this, Huang was the ultimate victim of his own success. Nvidia’s first graphics cards simply translated triangles into pixels. The 2001 GeForce 3 introduced a programmable pixel shader, which meant a video card’s functionality was no longer pre-defined. The killer move, however — which almost killed the company — was the 2006 introduction of CUDA, which was an API for programming those shaders. For much of the next 16 years Huang sold the gospel of CUDA , convinced it was the platform for a future of accelerated computing; then, in 2022, came ChatGPT. ChatGPT made clear what GPUs were most useful for: large language models, and Nvidia made the best GPUs. More than that, Huang had realized that the future of accelerated computing was not just chips, but rather systems; that drove the purchase of Mellanox in 2019, which provided the technology for Nvidia to scale out from chips, setting it down the road to being the best option for the sort of large scale training that made large language models possible. For this Nvidia charged very high prices, with margins exceeding 70%, because they could: they had the platform, the technology, and, over the past few years as others sought to make their own chips, the supply chain. Huang’s impact on the Asian supply chain in particular cannot be overstated. Byrne Hobart, in his book Boom: Bubbles and the End of Stagnation , notes that one of the benefits of bubbles is that they provide a coordination function, as the fear of missing out incentivizes multiple entities with interlocking dependencies to all commit to building at the same time; Huang was, in many respects, a one-person coordination function. Huang gave multiple keynotes a year, which he explained as how he communicated with the ecosystem broadly, and was famous for eating and drinking his way across Asia in particular, convincing reluctant suppliers that the AI boom was real, and locking up the lion’s share of their output for Nvidia and its stunning commitment to a yearly release cycle. Huang, who had toiled for decades in relative obscurity, known primarily to gamers, and only barely to the tech industry, became a rock star, swarmed wherever he went, always in his black leather jacket. He also, to his ultimate detriment, became a political figure. Nvidia had long had no presence in either Washington D.C. or Beijing , and was blindsided by the Biden administration’s imposition of chip controls in 2022. Nvidia’s immediate reaction to those initial controls, which restricted exports based on interconnect speed, was to immediately release the A800 in China, which was an A100 with a third of its interconnects disabled. That set the tone for the conflict that I believe was the true cause of Huang’s downfall: Huang strenuously disagreed with the various iterations of the chip ban, and Nvidia only bothered to do the bare minimum to abide by the letter of the law, never the spirit. That approach, in all likelihood, extended to Nvidia’s oversight (or lack thereof) of Singaporean entities that were alleged to be fronts for chips for China. Some of these were legal: Chinese companies are allowed to access cloud computing facilities outside of China that house leading edge Nvidia chips, although chip control advocates are seeking to close that loophole; some were not legal, in that the chips were ultimately ferried to China. Megaspeed, whose executive, Alice Huang, was the first person Huang was alleged to have an affair with, was officially in the former business, and alleged to actually be in the latter. There are whispers that Megaspeed’s ultimate customer was not, or not just, Alibaba, but also the Chinese military. These are whispers, to be clear; it was the affairs that were enough, at least publicly, to lead to Huang’s resignation. Nvidia, Most Valuable Company in the World, 2024–2026 Nvidia’s durability — at least that of their margins — was already an open question. Start with CUDA: when the market was software written for GPUs, a platform — including not just an API but a huge set of libraries targeting every conceivable market for accelerated computing — was a nearly impenetrable moat. That is why LLMs like GPT were written using CUDA. LLMs, though, both brought Nvidia its incredible success, and also seeded its greatest risks. The first is that the vast majority of developer energy moved up the stack, using the LLM’s API as a platform; for most companies, CUDA didn’t matter. The second is that Anthropic, which found funding from Amazon and Google, originally also-rans to the Microsoft-OpenAI partnership, had to learn how to use Trainium chips from Amazon and TPUs from Google; this was difficult, but ultimately meant that the leading LLM did not have any Nvidia dependency at all (Anthropic runs on Nvidia chips, because they learned how to run on anything). The third is the most devastating: LLMs are so effective at writing software that any software-based moat will inevitably dry up. Nvidia’s second moat, its networking and systems approach, is more durable, although challenged by Google (and by extension, Anthropic) in particular. Nvidia’s systems approach is also the easy answer for enterprises and governments seeking to own their own hardware, and neoclouds seeking to build data centers that are independent of the hyperscalers. The latter market rents chips to both hyperscalers and frontier

articles.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
articles.snippet: This article is brought to you by VicOne . VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. VicOne The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly. Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence. Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly. These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior. In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised. Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne A published patch still needs to be proven safe AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior. An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined. Three questions can help teams respond: Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots. What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior. How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended. When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared. From discovery to safer deployment As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior. That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during

articles.title: Why Skydio Built a Lopsided Drone
articles.snippet: Skydio’s drones have always been magical. From MIT research and early prototypes to what I would argue is still the most advanced consumer drone ever made , this is a company that makes very cool stuff. Sadly, Skydio no longer makes cool stuff for consumers , instead focusing on drone platforms for public safety, inspection, and other things that, on a good day, don’t affect me personally. Even so, a new drone from Skydio is worth paying attention to, especially when it’s as weird as this one—the F10 Lightrunner is a fixed-wing camera drone designed for autonomous deployment and high-speed flight, all while looking so lopsided that it’s surprising that it can actually fly. The benefits of asymmetrical aircraft There’s a short rabbit hole you can go down if you start looking for other examples of asymmetrical aircraft. In the 1990s, legendary aircraft designer Burt Rutan and his company Scaled Composites built some decidedly odd airplanes, including the Model 202 Boomerang . But perhaps the most famous asymmetrical aircraft was the Blohm & Voss BV 141 , a World War II-era reconnaissance plane that featured an engine in the middle alongside a crew compartment alarmingly offset out onto the right wing. The unique design was intended to give the crew the best possible view for reconnaissance missions, because in a typical single-engine aircraft, the crew sits right behind the engine, limiting forward visibility. Nearly 90 years later, the Skydio F10 is applying a similar philosophy to fixed-wing reconnaissance drones, which typically track targets by flying around them in circles. “While turning at low altitudes, it becomes very hard to avoid occluding a camera with a wing or a tail,” explains Andrew Goessling , director of engineering at Skydio. “So we were analyzing a lot of these use cases, and one of our engineers just blurted out, ‘What if we put the camera on the wingtip?’ And that’s where it all started, because as long as you only turn left, a lot of these problems just go away.” Of course, putting the camera on the F10’s wingtip creates a bunch of new problems, chief among them that the aircraft is no longer balanced. Not only is the camera payload fairly heavy relative to the total mass of the drone, but its bulk also creates greater drag. This is why the seemingly straightforward solution of putting something else (like a battery) on the other wingtip to rebalance the drone isn’t practical, says Goessling. “The issue there is that the camera represents a substantial portion of the total aircraft drag, so putting something else on the other wing would cut your flight time nearly in half.” The F10’s wing-mounted camera payload necessitated asymmetrical wings and uneven motor placement. Skydio Goessling points out that there’s nothing inherently bad about an asymmetric design like the F10; it just makes the life of engineers either a little more difficult or a little more exciting, depending on your perspective. “There were really two challenges here: What is the optimal design for an aircraft with a wingtip camera, and then once you have the design, how are you going to control it?” Any fixed-wing aircraft design has to consider three factors: distribution of mass, how thrust is distributed between the motors, and how the shape and location of the wings affect the aircraft’s aerodynamics. Once Skydio decided on their requirements for the F10—including the wingtip camera, two motors to enable controllable hovering for takeoff and landing, and a high top speed and long flight time—the engineers used a modeling-and-optimization approach to explore design options. The resulting aircraft compensates for the wing-mounted camera payload by extending just that wing to provide more lift on that side, and repositioning the motors asymmetrically to balance thrust against the added drag of the camera. Maneuvering with MegaDock The MegaDock can autonomously launch, recover, and recharge up to five F10 drones using a robot arm to grab them out of the air. Skydio An added challenge was getting the F10 to launch and recover with a robot arm, using a storage, charging, and deployment system called the MegaDock. That requires the drone to transition from hover to forward flight and then back again—a particularly difficult trick for a flying wing with no tail control surfaces (movable parts of the wing used to steer the aircraft). The F10 uses model predictive control (a control technique based on a detailed physics model of the robot) to accomplish this autonomously, and a single control policy can handle the robot all the way through its entire flight envelope, from a stationary hover to its maximum flight speed of 100 miles per hour. In other words, there’s no “hover mode” or “flight mode,” so the mission planner just tells the drone where it needs to be, and the drone will know how to get itself there. In operation, Skydio’s MegaDock can handle up to five F10s, allowing for continuous flight operations with three drones while two recharge. The entire system is fully autonomous, with humans only needed for remote supervisory control, communicating with the F10 via dual 5G cellular modems. Maximum flight time is 2 hours, and the aircraft is equipped with the same kind of magical obstacle-dodging camera setup as Skydio’s quadrotor drones. If something goes seriously wrong, an integrated parachute in the F10’s butt will deploy, lowering the drone to the ground gently enough to safely fly over people. Goessling is the first to acknowledge that the F10 Lightrunner is an unconventional design, but he’s proud of what he and his team have come up with as a commercially viable solution to the occlusion issue with other fixed-wing drones. “It looks weird, and we got some pushback from some of the less technical parts of the company,” Goessling says. “If there were less crazy ways of doing it, we would have pursued them. But we have the data. We have sound reasons for every decision we’ve made. And the outcom

articles.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
articles.snippet: This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings. Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms. Figure 1: A preview of the gallery’s 2026 architectures, grouped by positional encoding. Architecture figures taken from my LLM gallery . But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis. Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover different positional methods in LLMs; (finally) how RoPE works; what methods are used by recent open LLMs. Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) . If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher: The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style. PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses. PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, Positional choices in modern architectures . Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the web view here , which also has a navigation bar on the left side. 1. Where position information enters an LLM Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token. The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation. Figure 2: Token embedding layers in GPT-2 and MiniMax-M3, highlighted in orange. (Side note: M3’s first three out of 60 feedforward layers are dense not MoEs.) A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention. We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed. 1.1 Why add positional information? Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example: “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.” “The gray fox jumps over the red fox.” Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure. Figure 3: Changing the word order changes which fox jumps. For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7. Figure 4: Token IDs and positions in the toy sentence. # Assume the following small vocabulary. # Real vocabularies typically have 50k to 200k entries vocab = { "The": 0, "red": 1, "fox": 2, "jumps": 3, "gray": 4, "over": 5, "the": 6, } (If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my tokenizer materials on GitHub .) Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer. (For those who are interested in more details on how this selection from the embedding table looks like, check Appendix A .) Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any tw

articles.title: Open-source AI without Jensen
articles.snippet: The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on. Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up. Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ( slides , recording ). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside. The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is. The downside is that the true long-term benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s DeepInfer release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in my recent piece on the open model economy . Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine. Jensen’s support, and protection, gave the ecosystem time to figure this out. Jensen was more than a cheerleader. He would stop a lot of shit from going wrong once early winds were stirring. He was willing to use his power on open models. There’s a major swell in Democratic government funding towards candidates that want to regulate the AI industry, fostering “safety” . Many of these people feel a need to do something and have general opinions that open models are unsafe, while not being educated on the complexities of their benefits. My biggest near-term worry is sloppy regulation at the state level, followed by national regulation. We’ve been one, strong Chinese open-weight model away from a crisis since this summer. It still holds – especially as we enter a new, turbulent equilibrium of cybersecurity. We have not seen a major hack driven by a popular Chinese open-weight model, but it is a matter of when, not if. We need someone to encourage caution and an ecosystem perspective when the “open-weight hawks” come hunting. Knocking over the open-source AI domino today is easy — if done, unwinding the downstream concentration of power, reduction in safety research, and stifling of long-term innovation is far harder. On public data, it looks like balancing long-term innovation versus short term risks, but this is due to how horribly hard it is to measure the open model economy (e.g. the most valuable aspects of it run on private infrastructure). It’s a recurring challenge facing the ecosystem and my work. As a brief aside, the extent to which the media ecosystem is revolving around timing today, rather than exact availability of information, is incredible. All of these Jensen affairs were known, but getting them out at the right time, right after the midterm political swing, took down the king. The same goes for the Jacob Coxon brouhaha this summer. All of that safety culture around top labs was well known, but the right timing around datacenters and the Overton window made it a national issue. This could very well happen at some point for open model safety, as it tends to be harm, risk, or safety-related narratives that drive the modern media algorithms. I cannot imagine my work on open-science driving such a media cycle, because it will never happen. Share The only lasting solution to this is to incubate a truly frontier open model player in the US. For example, I agree completely with Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, on a core problem in the US open model ecosystem. From a recent ChinaTalk + SemiAnalysis emergency podcast : Jordan Schneider: I do want your guys’ take on just how bad this is, that Jensen’s now off the table for the future of American innovation. And we should talk about open models. I mean, he was the big champion, right? Dylan, you were talking earlier — I still don’t understand quite why someone didn’t just spend a few billion dollars and make something better than Kimi or DeepSeek and open source it. Dylan Patel: Not that easy. It’s not money, it’s talent, man. All of the most talented people primarily work at Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta TBD, right? And then those who don’t are split across a hundred different startups. I mean, yes, Thinking Machines has a cracked team, but is Thinking Machines as good as Moonshot? No. Moonshot skill-wise is probably just as good as the US labs. They just have a big deficit in compute and deployment. So I think if we don’t have a scale adv

articles.title: The avalanche that hit math is coming for AI development
articles.snippet: Many thanks to Max Farrens , Gabe Fried , and Thomas Larsen for pairing with me through significant parts of writing and researching this essay. You can watch or listen to me narrate this essay on YouTube , Spotify , and Apple Podcasts. If you asked me earlier this year how far away we are from superintelligence, I’d probably have said at least the better part of a decade. But over the last three months, I’ve updated my views a ton. I’ve been debating people about this question, both on and off the podcast. And I’ve been watching the progress of AI on verifiable domains and thinking about what that implies for AI research itself. I’ve now come to the view that we’re only a couple of years away, and possibly only a couple of months away, from AIs that are as good as the best humans at AI research. I’ve also come to believe that automating AI research will compress so much progress into a single year that, soon thereafter (so by 2030, but plausibly as early as next year), we’ll have AIs that are at least as good as the best human experts in every field. I know this is a wild claim, and it’s one that I myself didn’t believe even a couple of months ago. Let me walk you through how my thinking has changed. Before we get into more speculative arguments, I want to point out that we have a lot of evidence that AI is already dramatically speeding up further AI progress at the frontier. For example, METR, which is an independent evaluation organization, concluded after three months embedded inside Anthropic that Anthropic’s overall rate of progress on well-scoped tasks is 2x what it was a year ago, and that a “majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D.” OpenAI published a blog post about this in September, where they showed that the heaviest 10% of AI users among OpenAI’s researchers went from using around $1,000 a day of internal coding agents at the beginning of the summer to over $7,000 a day by the end of August. In September, Anthropic put out a similar post on its own AI uplift. They reported that, as of August, Claude “leads” more than 26% of Anthropic’s AI R&D work—up from under 1% as recently as February. 1 Math is a preview of what will happen to AI research When I think about how big a deal it could be if AIs automate AI research, and how soon that could happen, a really important update for me has been just seeing how quickly AI capabilities in mathematics have exploded. Current AIs are slicing through well-scoped problems in mathematics like a hot knife through butter. It was only two years ago that I asked Dario why LLMs aren’t able to use their vast knowledge across so many different fields in order to connect different ideas and make new discoveries. And lo and behold, here we are: In a wholly verifiable domain like mathematics, AIs are doing this search-and-match discovery to such a great extent that hundreds of important results (which the top mathematicians and computer scientists in the world had spent decades trying to resolve) are being churned out as side quests to hype up future model releases . It’s crazy how fast we went from, in 2023, “This model can’t reliably add four-digit numbers,” to, in 2024, “This model can barely solve any problems in a high school math competition,” to, in 2025, “Oh, it can win a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad,” to, earlier this year, “Wow, it’s solving open Erdős problems, but maybe just because no human has attempted to solve these particular problems, and a similar solution was already in the literature,” to, about a month ago, “Okay, it fucking solved a Millennium Prize problem in 88 hours.” There’s a line in the novel East of Eden : “And there is one sure thing about the fall of gods: they do not fall a little; they crash and shatter.” It’s true that progress has skewed disproportionately towards the verification-laden parts of math, like finding counterexamples (rather than coming up with new theories, say). Toby Ord posted a great essay about this recently. He writes , “While current AI systems are starting to automate mathematical proof, there is currently very little evidence that they can ask powerful questions or find profound new fields of mathematical enquiry.” But another way to say the same point would be: Current AI systems have solved a Millennium Prize problem, all without the ability to ask powerful questions or find profound new fields of mathematical inquiry. And this ability to solve well-scoped problems is going to be an even bigger deal for machine learning research than for mathematics, broadly construed. That’s because the goal of mathematics research is not just to prove or disprove long lists of conjectures, but to extend human understanding of mathematical concepts. Coming up with the idea of topology, group theory, or the Cartesian grid matters far more than knowing exactly how many one-unit-apart pairs you can make from n dots . We mainly care about such abstruse questions insofar as they might elicit new mathematical theories. But in AI research, the priorities are exactly reversed. AI labs mainly care about how any new algorithmic recipe empirically makes training more efficient or elicits smarter models. They don’t care about theory for its own sake, and all the progress we’ve made in deep learning over the last decade and a half has not required much new theory anyway. The equivalent of grinding through random conjectures would be enormously valuable in machine learning in a way that it just isn’t in mathematics. AI research is actually surprisingly similar to the type of mathematical progress that current AIs are disproportionately good at: unlocking a ton of low-hanging fruit by applying a combination of incredible persistence and a superhuman capacity to connect ideas from lots of adjacent domains. For example, let’s talk about the transformer architecture. My friend Sholto Douglas , who is an AI researcher, has a perenniall

articles.title: 2026.46: The End of Jensen
articles.snippet: (Photo by Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images) Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery! As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings . On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week. The Shocking Demise of Jensen Huang. This week’s coverage was dominated, unsurprisingly, by the shocking and sudden end of Jensen Huang’s 32 year tenure as CEO of Nvidia. The end came on Thursday morning, and just a few hours later, we recorded a Sharp Tech episode recounting Huang’s legendary history, figuring out what happened, and looked forward to what this might mean for Nvidia, the tech industry, and America going forward. Also see Andrew’s view from DC, Jensen Huang Was Always Going to Lose , and listen to Wednesday’s episode of Sharp China about the geopolitical angle, and Thursday’s Dithering about both the parallels and differences between Steve Jobs and Apple. — Ben Thompson Enterprise, Consumer and Intel. The more things change, the more they stay the same: Intel remains on the back foot in the AI era, and the foundry dreams continue to flounder. On the heels of disappointing earnings and 2027 guidance that promises yet more letdowns, Ben’s Update on Wednesday examined the state of America’s would-be national champion by drawing comparisons to AMD, an Intel peer that’s red-hot right now. To understand why one company is capitalizing on skyrocketing enterprise demand while the other confronts flatlining consumer sales, the answer starts with chips chiplets and leads to more profound questions about culture, Intel’s nature, and its bifurcated strategy for the long-term (and, for subscribers, look forward to more on this topic in Sunday’s Sharp Tech mailbag episode). — Andrew Sharp And Then There’s Professional Basketball. As a palate cleanser after a week of Jensen drama, this week’s Greatest of All Talk was a look at the top and bottom of the NBA after the first three weeks. On the euphoric side of the ledger we have Warriors fans (pre-Steph injury), Lakers fans, Spurs fans, and on the other end spectrum there is nothing positive to say in Brooklyn, a familiar malaise in Cleveland, and precisely one silver lining in Salt Lake City. All of it was a great time; we also hit Adam’s experience with the NBA in Mexico City last weekend, the hardest working players in NBA history, and an anxiety-inducing conversation about the number one pick, AJ Dybantsa. — AS Presented by Agentic commerce purchases with Link, Stripe’s digital wallet that works surprisingly well for agents, grew 38x in September. The catalyst was consumer agents like Muse and Instinct. Filling out a web form is not a value-add activity for anyone. No one chooses to fill out web forms in their spare time. That’s why these agents have been particularly useful. I’ve written about how these platforms are giving ordinary people an AI agent with a computer, enabling agents to do genuinely useful things on our behalf. When one of those things is spending money, it needs a wallet that knows what it is, and isn’t, allowed to do. Stripe has learned that’s really about deciding how much freedom to give it. You might approve one purchase, or give it $500 for flights this week, and let it figure out the rest. The wallet’s job is to keep it within those lines while handling everything between “go buy this” and the purchase actually happening. That’s what Stripe is building with Link: You approve what it spends, it can come back to you if the final price changes, and eligible purchases can even come with protection if the agent makes a mistake. You can use Link on Muse, Instinct, as well as many other of the agents you might use already. Stratechery Articles and Updates Jensen Huang’s Affair, The Culper Report, Huang’s Righteousness — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a Chinese spy, and that might not be the end of his troubles. I hope he survives, but his influence will never be the same. The Jensen Huang Story Gets Worse, Washington vs. New York, Silicon Valley — The Jensen Huang story got worse for him on Monday; the real risk for Huang is governance, even more than national security. Who benefits? Intel Earnings, AMD Earnings, Intel and AMD’s Divergence — Intel and AMD’s diverging earnings point to fundamental historical differences, and make me wonder if Intel needs to find a new (old) path. An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play — An interview with Roblox CEO David Baszucki about how AI is transforming game creation, and why that opens up huge opportunities to both enable developers and make Roblox both an Aggregator and a platform. Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp Jensen Huang Was Always Going to Lose — Jensen Huang spent four years substituting his own judgment for that of the U.S. government. His downfall was inevitable, and probably isn’t over. articles.title: Video Friday: NASA PROMISEs a New Moon Rover
articles.snippet: Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion. Humanoids 2026 : 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CA Enjoy today’s videos! NASA will send a nuclear-powered rover called PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration, depicted in the rendering) to the moon’s South Pole as a foundational mission in the Moon Base Program. It will be constructed largely from existing hardware—test-bed and flight-spare components—developed for NASA’s ongoing Mars rover missions, Curiosity and Perseverance. [ NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory ] What happens when you put wheels on a humanoid and let a learned controller drive it? We swapped the feet on our Atlas robot to find out; it let us push our actuators, and our models of them, hard. [ Boston Dynamics ] The Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program has achieved the first-ever demonstration of automated in-space assembly. A Caltech payload operating in orbit built a truss structure from individual components. A relatively simple gantry robot (able to move along three linear axes) connected composite truss members using custom-designed joints while simultaneously deploying a thin reflective mesh; a proof of concept for future space-based antennas. [ DARPA ] Well, it looks like Amazon’s idea for using mobile robots as security systems is not as dead as we thought it was back in 2020 . [ Amazon Ring ] There are many excellent applications for robots that have a market size of very close to zero, and this is one of them. [ DEEP Robotics ] I don’t know about you, but my philosophy in life is that more tentacles is always better. [ Paper ] Well, I’m impressed. [ UZH Robotics and Perception Group ] How Corvus One drones count boxes and read every UPC in case reserve and the singles area at ASICS America’s distribution center. Corvus One flies both areas at the ASICS distribution center in Byhalia, Miss., with no localization infrastructure anywhere in the building. No stickers, no beacons, no markers. [ Corvus Robotics ] Thanks, Joan! How do you solve a math problem that might have quadrillions of computations? It’s increasingly a problem for robot fleets in manufacturing and warehouse facilities. Lots of robots, lots of tasks, lots of traffic. Brute force, even with a supercomputer, could take years to find answers. That’s where the Toyota Research Institute steps in with a bespoke solver program to elegantly tackle the problem of multiagent optimal planning. In just one minute, Andrew Best, a scientist at TRI, explains how the company approaches this complex robotics deployment problem. [ Toyota Research Institute ] Rumor has it that printers built by robots never have “PC LOAD LETTER” errors. [ Flexiv ] Dancing robots are getting even better! Hooray...? [ LimX Dynamics ] It’s season two of AI in Motion, and we’re on a road trip to talk with more of America’s experts in physical AI. We’re rolling into Austin to talk with Jeff Cardenas, who cofounded Apptronik to build robots for humans in very familiar forms. [ Waymo ]

articles.title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #219
articles.snippet: Cover Image by Runway Hi friends 👋, Happy Friday and welcome back to our 219th Weekly Dose of Optimism! What a week. After two affairs emerged - one with an alleged Chinese spy and one with a direct report - Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned . Sources say the affairs are the tip of the iceberg and that heavier shoes will drop. But progress marches on, as evidenced by everything in this week’s Dose. It’s going to take more than a wandering Huang to keep us down. By the way, inspired by Readwise launching Readwise Books , I had Codex turn all of my essays into epubs that you can download and read on your book reader of choice, because while they’re long essays, they’re actually pretty short books! You can find and download all of them, including Of Miracles and Moats , at not boring press . Let’s get to it. This Week’s Weekly Dose is brought to you by… Runway I have been having so much fun with Runway as this quarter’s presenting sponsor. The product keeps getting better, and expanding, every week. Personally, I’m hooked to making videos - whether explainers for the Dose or attempts to make short films - and I think you’ll really enjoy it, too. Try it for work, or try to become the next Scorsese . Runway is building foundational AI for how the world creates. 65M+ people use Runway to generate, edit and produce video, images and audio with 80+ top media models. You can read my essay with co-founder Anastasis Germanidis to learn more on where Runway is headed beyond video. Nvidia, Amazon, Lionsgate, Chime, and 95%+ of the Fortune 100 are part of a growing community of teams, founders, and independent creators using Runway to make national TV spots, social ads at scale, launch videos and more. You can also use Runway in ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Cursor, Replit and more via the Runway MCP . Create any idea with Runway now (1) Google DeepMind Releases AlphaGenome 2 So, uhhh, pretty good time to be Google, huh? On Wednesday, as Nvidia was in turmoil, the maker of GPU competitor TPUs, and our favorite chef of models outside of your plain vanilla LLM, released AlphaGenome 2. Last year’s AlphaGenome 1 took a million letters of DNA and predicted what they do, but averaged across whole tissues. It was very cool! But averages can hide things, like variants that might cause disease in only one rare cell type or only after a cell gets activated. AG2 takes the same million letters plus a condition, which can be a tissue, a cell type, a cell state, or data from a few dozen of your own cells that it has never seen before, and it predicts what the DNA does there specifically. It trained on more than 107 million individual cell profiles from 68 human and mouse tissues. On a benchmark of 28 immune cell types, it found 30% of the variants scientists believe are causal, versus 16% for the old model. As longtime readers know, my process for figuring out whether something in bio is legit is to text Elliot, but this time, he tweeted before I had to: Genome-wide association studies have handed us an enormous pile of DNA variants linked to diseases, and for most of them, scientists are still trying to figure out which gene they touch or which cell they act in, which often takes a lot of real world experimentation. That's a big part of why genetics - we mapped the whole human genome! you can now get yours done for like $100! - hasn’t turned into drugs as fast as everyone hoped. But AG2 can pick up signals from all of that data computationally, which means we’ll be able to rev through them to (hopefully) find cures much more quickly. AG2 still misses most of them (30% is 30%), but going from 16% to 30% in one generation is great progress, and there’s a lot scientists can do with that 30%. Bad time to be a disease. (1a) Argenx Acquires Unnatural Products for Up to $1.15B Real bad time to be a disease, because even if you can use things like AG2 to find targets, you still have to drug them. Which is what macrocycles do. Macrocycles are ring-shaped peptides that sit somewhere between the small molecules that come in pills and antibodies that need to be injected. The promise is the precision of a biologic in a pill that can slip inside cells to hit targets antibodies can't reach. Think something like an oral GLP-1 or cancer therapeutic. Macrocycles are what not boring capital portfolio company Unnatural Products does, and now, it will be doing them inside of argenx. On Monday, argenx announced that it's acquiring UNP for $550 million in cash upfront and up to $595 million more if it hits development and regulatory milestones. Big win for Cam, Josh, and the UNP team! argenx and UNP have been partners since last year, and argenx was already an investor, so it knows what it’s buying. They’ve been working on a pill that goes after FcRn, the same target as Vyvgart, the argenx drug that did $1.72 billion in sales last quarter. The team will keep working out of Santa Cruz, where they have huge lush trees right outside the window, and will become argenx's home for peptide discovery. Naturally, I’m very excited about the win, and we should all be excited to get more of the potential miracle cures we talk about here delivered in effective pill form in the years ahead. (2) Path Robotics Raises $300M for Robot Welders Good welders are insanely valuable. I remember touring SpaceX a few years back and hearing them talk about the one guy who could weld everything in hushed tones. Just this week, I was talking to someone about a golden gloves welder somewhere else who pulls $1 million a year. Welding is the same story we often hear: not enough welders, let alone great welders, to make all of the things we need to make. Back in Dose #214 , we covered Anduril’s $3.7 billion Arsenal-2 shipyard, its answer to the US’ shipbuilding problem. But even with big shipyards, we’re going to need a lot of welders. They just might not all be human welders. Path Robotics , which brothers Andy and Alex Lonsberry started in Columbus, Ohio in 2018

articles.title: Of Miracles and Moats
articles.snippet: Welcome to the 1,974 newly Not Boring people who have joined us since our last essay ! Join 282,985 smart, curious folks by subscribing here: Subscribe now Hi friends 👋, Happy Wednesday! A consistent theme of this newsletter is that we are fortunate to be living in an Age of Miracles. To wit, I’m sending this over Starlink on a United flight, surrounded by regular people who also received access to free WiFi beamed down from the heavens with their few hundred dollar ticket to fly at 30,000 feet and span the country in mere hours. The Louis CK joke is no longer applicable. Airlines and internet are a good reminder, though, that a miracle technology does not guarantee a miraculous business. In fact, the more incredible and useful a technology is, and the more you can throw money at scaling it once it works, the more likely it is to attract hordes of competitors who, in aggregate, build too much supply and crash prices. Let’s get to it. Today’s Not Boring is brought to you by… Reducto Meet r-1 mini: High-quality document parsing from $1 per 1,000 pages AI products get more useful when they can work with more of a customer’s documents. Reducto’s new r-1 mini makes that practical for larger workloads, with pricing starting at $1 per 1,000 pages . r-1 mini preserves reading order, tables, and layout, so search, extraction, and agents can use the structure of a document alongside its words. Teams can bring historical archives and everyday uploads into their workflows while using r-1 for files where additional accuracy matters. Reducto already processes more than a billion pages a month for AI teams at Scale AI, Harvey, Toast, and Vanta. If you’re using another parser, apply for up to $5,000 in migration credits and compare the results on your own documents with help from our team. Try r-1 mini → On Miracles and Moats Cover Image by Runway It is neither productive nor becoming to call a bubble. Most people who do it are innately pessimistic curmudgeons left out of the fun who believe that the technology underlying the asset in question is overhyped and that those excited about it are rubes. For me, personally, calling a technology bubble would also seem to be pretty off-brand. Anthropic will probably end its first week of trading at a much higher market cap than it goes out at, and it may well proceed to eat the entire economy en route to becoming the world’s first quadrillion dollar company. The economy very well may end up looking K-shaped in the way that my kids write K’s, with no sense of proportion, a few Anthropic employees at the tippy top each controlling one Bay Area fiefdom/polycule and the rest of us treating Claude with the proper respect in order to continue receiving our allowance from the Machine of Loving Grace (that or somehow outsniping Duet on Kalshi enough to eat). While I have written that AI is more Oil than God (funny title image choice in retrospect), and I still believe that, it is also true that oil does not produce its own oil , that you can’t replicate Microsoft Office with oil, and that oil is yet to produce a solution to Navier-Stokes . There is a world in which we look back at Anthropic’s IPO price and laugh at the idea that we ever valued an old school commodity LLM at ~$1.4 trillion. Maybe there’s no new S-curve as intense as coding, because in hindsight, duh, the computers were really good at speaking computer and that didn’t transfer. Or maybe there is, but competition from OpenAI, Google, SpaceXAI, Meta, Chinese open source models, and the neolabs slows revenue growth just enough that compute commitments made in the boom times force the company to sell itself to Amazon or Apple or whoever. There is another in which Dario has decided that laughing hurts the models’ feelings and well, he’s allowed to tell us not to laugh anymore, since he is the economy. A very real bull case for Anthropic goes something like: it has the best models and they are now improving themselves faster than ever, growing the lead in what may be a winner-take-all market, and unlike other winner-take-all markets, this one extends to all markets, because Anthropic can win whichever markets it chooses to point its smarter-than-anyone models at, from productivity software to medicine to … anything. Anyone who tells you they know which of those two outcomes will come to pass is full of shit, and I am many things, but I hope not to be full of shit. There are three arguments against this being a bubble more broadly, though, which are oft-repeated, sound right, and are exactly the things you’d expect to see in a bubble. Note: I’ll use bubble here as the broad term but I might mean something closer to commodity cycles, and I certainly don’t mean manias, which are when price becomes totally divorced from reality, as with tulips. The three arguments are: Unlike other bubbles (lol WebVans and crypto), AI is actually an incredibly useful technology that is being widely and productively adopted in the economy. These companies are generating real revenue, and growing incredibly fast. The labs have shown they can be profitable, and any losses are just them investing to capture future growth. Grant all three! In doing so, however, you’d be saying that the situation is exactly the situation that creates and then deflates bubbles. A miracle technology arrives. Early suppliers earn real profits because supply is short. Demand looks bottomless, which is obvious to everyone in the early numbers. The demand and profits pull in capital and competitors. Everyone builds at once, even those who see the glut coming, locking in commitments at scarcity prices just to get capacity online. Supply arrives, the technology gets better, and prices collapse. Capital loses, consumers win, and the technology chugs on. Capital flees, so new entrants can’t get funded. A survivor or outsider with capital consolidates and becomes the low-cost provider. articles.title: The missing quadrant in responses to AI
articles.snippet: We are starting a non-profit research organization: STABL . Adapting to advanced AI will require dramatic institutional change and broad societal resilience. It will also require evidence about AI progress and impacts — the prospects of recursive self-improvement (RSI), the pace of AI diffusion, and the bottlenecks that constrain how AI capabilities translate into societal outcomes. Four theses define our worldview: We consider advanced AI a transformative general-purpose technology with the potential for broad societal benefits. Yet we recognize that the pace of societal transformation will be bottlenecked by the speed of human and organizational change more than progress in capabilities. Our institutions — the established ways we organize knowledge, work, and governance — are an important source of stability during this turbulent period, but they also need serious reforms to keep serving their purpose. We favor a broad portfolio of defenses to manage AI risks, of which alignment is only one part. Resilience, the most neglected component today, must become central. Another way to state our worldview is to place it on a 2x2 chart. The vertical axis depicts taking AI’s transformative potential seriously. The horizontal axis depicts taking downstream bottlenecks to AI’s impacts seriously. At the top left is technological determinism: the view that superintelligence will unilaterally transform society by obliterating downstream bottlenecks. Many AI CEOs express this view, such as when predicting that a century’s worth of progress will be compressed into the next few years. This view often ignores the organizational, regulatory, and societal bottlenecks to such a transformation; in this view, such questions are moot because superintelligence is all powerful. Surprisingly, some of the AI industry’s strongest critics share this worldview, focusing on slowing AI capability improvements as the main way to keep society safe from AI’s dangers. The opposite view, at the bottom right of the chart, treats existing organizations, processes, professions, and governance as fixed points, and insists that technology be molded to fit them. People holding this view often work on limits on AI adoption, and protecting existing structures from disruption. They are good at identifying and leveraging the bottlenecks that blunt AI’s impact, such as regulation, professional norms, organizational inertia, and political pushback. Slowing the pace of change can buy valuable time to shape technology’s impacts. But when preserving the status quo becomes a goal unto itself, it stands in the way of technology-enabled societal progress. (As an example, consider the resistance to self-driving cars despite their being safer than humans, or bans on AI-enabled legal advice ). STABL belongs in the top-right quadrant. We take frontier AI seriously as a transformative technology, yet consider the role of institutions — both new and existing — to be important in helping society navigate the transition. For example, how should we understand and improve AI’s impacts on medicine? Many technological determinists claim superintelligence will rapidly cure nearly all diseases. Someone with the opposite view might respond that the bottleneck is not drug discovery, which AI may well accelerate, but clinical trials, which take years because of regulations and safety risks. This response correctly identifies the bottlenecks to AI’s impacts. But this is often seen as the end of the conversation. In our view, understanding the bottlenecks to AI’s impacts is only the starting point of analysis. The next question is whether drug testing can be made faster and more efficient in order to meaningfully materialize AI’s benefits. For example, what are the barriers to in-silico testing? How can we rethink regulatory institutions and processes? Unfortunately, neither extreme pays close attention to these critical questions. To be clear, STABL isn’t the only organization in the top-right quadrant; much of our work builds on other organizations and thinkers who take both AI’s potential and its downstream bottlenecks seriously. But compared to the other quadrants, there is a sparsity of thinking in this quadrant, which has led to polarization among the communities that take either the technology or the bottlenecks seriously. Our ultimate goal is to contribute to a rich intellectual agenda for this quadrant, create the space for new organizations, and collaborate with existing organizations in this and other quadrants. To follow our work, subscribe to the STABL newsletter: Subscribe to the STABL newsletter Our research agenda The top-right quadrant leads us to many interesting research directions. On one hand, we expect AI capabilities to continue improving quickly, which motivates our empirical research on the pace of progress and RSI. We expect highly capable AI models to continue to be widely available, which motivates our analysis and advocacy for risk mitigation beyond aligning AI models and non-proliferation. On the other hand, we consider institutions important for shepherding the transition to a world where advanced AI is broadly diffused. This leads to our interest in understanding the downstream outcomes of advanced AI adoption. We plan to measure specific benefits and harms, study the disruption of labor markets and beyond, propose ways to improve societal resilience and revitalize institutions. These interests lead to four key research directions, which we detail below. While other organizations have worked on similar questions, we expect our research to be different in how we formulate these questions and how we go about answering them, informed by our worldview and priors about AI progress. 1. How should we measure progress towards recursive self-improvement? Many forecasts of explosive AI progress rest on recursive self-improvement (RSI): AI automating AI research itself. We take RSI seriously precisely because our model of progress differs

articles.title: De-othering
articles.snippet: The word “other” is also a verb. To other is to treat groups of people as fundamentally different or inferior. It’s in our nature, but leaders amplify it for scare-mongering. Those immigrants. Those Muslims. Those Chinese. They’re the problem. They’re not like us. That message is broadcast and echoes all around you, which intensifies feeling it’s a fact. It builds a huge wall: us versus them. It repels you from that wall, to make sure you can’t see them, because that would complicate the simplicity of polarizing. We categorize the animal world into species. Species are so different that they can’t mate, can’t switch, can’t be both a cat and a bird. The problem with othering is thinking of people as so deeply different that they are like a separate species. It’s an enticing belief because it helps you jump to a conclusion, so you can stop thinking. Those people are just weird and bad, and that’s that. I’m so interested in othering, because I noticed it in myself. I grew up with the usual stereotypes that shaped my worldview. Then I moved to the city, where you meet people from the other side of that wall. Like a great story where the heroes oppose an evil enemy tribe, but then one person falls into enemy hands and realizes that tribe is not evil and is not the enemy, and you get the wow moment of understanding a conflicting point of view. Stories tend to make only two sides, so they can take sides and switch sides. But imagine a longer story that does this twenty times, so you can’t even think of them as sides anymore. That’s what I’m trying to do with my life. I’m on a slow background mission to reverse the othering in my worldview. It’s a fun challenge. When I notice I’m othering, I undo my conclusions, and cross that wall. Understand and internalize a conflicting point of view. I try to join every tribe, to show myself we are not separate species. This year, I heard the word “other” as a verb, and it called all of this to mind. So now I can give my mission a succinct term: de-othering.
